item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Vanta 正在"反向定价"——它是 AI 时代第一家公开承认"我吃掉 token 成本"的公司，这不是认输，而是一场精心设计的"去金融化"反击
大多数讨论 AI 定价时都在争论 token、credit、outcome 哪种模式胜出。但 Christina 揭示了一个被所有人忽视的结构性真相：**一旦你按 token 收费，你就自愿把自己放到了与 Anthropic/OpenAI 的同一张比价表上**。用户会立刻问："你这个 token 是不是 Claude 的 4 倍价？那你有没有 Claude 的 4 倍好？"——这是定价学中最致命的"参照系陷阱"。
这里有个让人意外的推论：**token 定价本质上是把应用层公司"商品化"的加速器**。它表面上让你看起来像 AI 公司（高增长、使用量计费），实际上把你的毛利永远锚定在模型厂商的成本曲线上。Vanta 选择"吃掉成本、保持 SaaS 定价"，不是因为传统，而是因为她看穿了这件事：**在模型成本每 12 个月下降 10 倍的世界里，吃亏是一次性的，而被商品化是永久的。**
## 二、跨领域连接：Bil

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Inside the Robot Data Factory: Mecka's Josh Gao on Sensorizing Humans to Train Robots
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Mecka 正在建造的，不是"数据工厂"，而是人类身体的殖民地化基础设施

表面上 Mecka 是在"收集数据"，但如果你把它和整个工业史放在一起看，会发现一个让人毛骨悚然的类比——这是一次反向的工业革命。

  • 第一次工业革命：机器模仿人的身体（纺织机 → 手臂；蒸汽机 → 腿）。
  • 第二次：机器模仿人的神经（计算机 → 大脑的离散部分）。
  • 而 Mecka 正在做的是：把人反过来变成传感器节点，让人类的日常动作、肌肉收缩、指尖压力、Michelin 大厨的刀工，被"抽取"成可被机器复制的 token。

Josh 用了一个非常轻描淡写的词叫 "sensorizing humans"（给人装传感器）。但如果你把它和福柯的"规训社会"、或者 Shoshana Zuboff 的"监控资本主义"放在一起，会发现一个惊人的转向：过去 20 年互联网公司提取的是你的"注意力和偏好"，Mecka 提取的是你的"身体性知识"（tacit bodily knowledge）——那些你自己都说不清楚、只存在于你肌肉记忆里的东西。换句话说，Mecka 做的事情本质上是把 Polanyi 的"隐性知识"显性化——而这是 Michael Polanyi 在 1958 年断言机器永远做不到的事。

二、跨领域连接：Mecka 的商业模型，其实是米其林指南 + 淘金热补给站 + 东印度公司的奇怪三体合金

Josh 说未来的 SKU 会从"路边中餐馆"升级到"米其林餐厅"，再到"费德勒级别的网球"。这句话被他一笔带过，但它暗藏一个稀缺性的反转：

  • 在 LLM 时代，数据的价值在于规模（trillion tokens）。
  • 在机器人时代，数据的价值将迅速转向稀缺的专家身体——世界上只有几千个米其林三星大厨、只有一个费德勒。

这意味着 Mecka 真正的护城河不是"量"，而是对稀缺人类卓越性的独家采集权。这和米其林指南 1900 年的商业逻辑惊人一致：米其林卖轮胎，但发现要让人们买轮胎必须先让他们"开车去远方"，于是创造了"美食目的地"的概念。Mecka 卖机器人数据，但真正的生意可能是"身体奇观的策展人"——它将决定哪种人类技艺值得被保存、复制、永生。

一个让人意外的推论：顶尖寿司师傅、Noma 的主厨、费德勒，未来可能需要签"身体技艺独家授权"合同，就像音乐人签独家版权一样。你的手感、你的发力曲线、你的刀工节奏，会被估值、被证券化。这是一个还不存在、但即将出现的产业——身体性 IP。

三、隐藏的系统性真相："carbon life" 这句玩笑话，泄露了整个赛道真正的终局结构

Josh 自嘲说网站是发推前一晚做的，但他写下的 "teaching robots about carbon life" 却是整段访谈里最诚实的一句——比任何融资 pitch 都诚实。

注意他引用的三个科幻典故（Asimov、Ender's Game、Hitchhiker's Guide）有一个共同的终局结构：

机器把"生物性"视为最后不可征服的边疆，并因此开始试图成为生物。

把这个结构映射回今天的技术栈，你会看到一个被所有人忽略的递归：

  1. 机器人需要人的数据 →
  2. 人穿戴传感器把身体转为数据 →
  3. 机器人用这些数据模仿人 →
  4. 机器人部署后收集"失败数据"（Josh 自己提到的 flywheel）→
  5. 这些数据又会反过来改变人类对自己身体的理解（就像 FSD 改变了我们对"开车"的定义）

这是一个人-机互相训练的闭环，且这个闭环的方向并不是单向的"机器学会人类"，而是人类会被机器重新定义。想想看：当机器人学会了"费德勒式反手"之后，网球教练会开始用机器人反推"最优反手动作"去教孩子——人类的技艺会被机器人用过的那部分反过来标准化。

这就是 Mecka 真正的历史位置：它不是在"训练机器人"，它是在建造一个人类身体标准的中央数据库，一个未来可能像 ISO 标准、像 Unicode 一样基础的东西。谁拥有这个数据库，谁就在未来几十年里定义"人类正确的做事方式"长什么样。

而这件事最 absurd（Josh 自己最爱的词）的地方是：它可能是由两个加拿大年轻人、一个前稳定币开发者、一个前云厨房 SaaS 工程师，在他们还没意识到的情况下，顺手建立的。——这本身就非常 Hitchhiker's Guide。

📝 转录文本

Inside the Robot Data Factory: Mecka's Josh Gao on Sensorizing Humans to Train Robots

开场：Carbon Life 作为最终边疆

"There's an idea in science fiction that is when robotics and AI has ultimately fully generalized and solved all tasks that humans can do, the final frontier is going to be organic. Final frontier is going to be biological. And you see this in like Asimov, you see this in Ender's Game. You could even in Hitchhiker's at the very end — the planet ultimately was this giant organic computer trying to process and understand what the meaning of life was or what the question was."

[music]

Today I'm delighted to have Josh from Mecka on the show. Josh is founder and CEO of Mecka AI, which is building a data and deployment company for robotics. I — and I think the whole ecosystem — think that robotics is about to enter a golden age. And unlike LLMs where we had so much free human data from the internet, robotics is fundamentally data constrained, and I think your position in the ecosystem as the leading data factory to bring robotic data and physical data in distribution for models is just a really, really interesting perch.

So, I'm excited to use this conversation today to chat about: how does egocentric data and data collection work in robotics, what are the actual operations and economics of operating a data factory, and your overall thoughts on robotics research and deployment. Thanks for joining the show.

Josh: Amazing. Thanks for having me.

一、Mecka 是什么？

Q: Maybe to start off for those who aren't familiar, what is Mecka and how are you looking to impact the world of robotics?

Josh: So, Mecka is like you said — the data and deployment company for physical AI. What that means is today we create, we process, and ultimately we license a lot of the data that goes into training these robotics foundation models.

The big problem across robotics is that we don't have the luxury of the cold start that LLMs had with the internet. Fundamentally, a lot of this robotics data is three things: it's pixels, it's actions, and it's logic. And so we don't have access to a large amount of this curated and processed and clean data to be able to then train these models to understand what it is to be in the physical world.

So a lot of our job is pretty much to: one, create the different types of hardware such as sensorizing and wearables for humans; the different operations to go and collect and partner with individual contributors, businesses, tasks across different environments; and then ultimately post-process and own the quality gates to make these data sets useful and teach robots about the world.

二、机器人数据的经济可行性

Q: Without having been given the benefits of a giant free many trillions — maybe lots of trillions, trillions of trillions — of tokens of internet corpus, do you think that robotics, having to pay for and operationally collect all the data that's going into the mix, is even a feasible challenge? Is it economically feasible without having had the gift of the internet?

Josh: I think we still have the luxury of a lot of things that was given from the internet. So we aren't starting from zero ultimately.

I think you can see it across LLMs and data across LLMs. Pre-training data was always driven by the labs largely across web crawlers, things like that. It didn't become a large market. Today in robotics, we do see pre-training as quite a large market and that could be taken in several forms. So that could be that we are teaching video models how to generate more physics-grounded realities of what the world looks like. And we get to leverage all the work that has gone into VLMs and different types of world models before to make that possible.

Is it possible and scalable to get to that volume of data? I think that ultimately comes down to: what commercial use case can you unlock at which levels of scales of data. And our strong belief is along that journey that we will be able to unlock a lot of the simple pick and place tasks along the beginning of what we're creating, and towards that long tail that is going to be many orders of magnitude larger than it is today.

三、"Teaching Robots About Carbon Life"

Q: I did a little homework before this. Your website is very whimsical. It says that you are teaching robots about carbon life. What does that mean?

Josh: I actually made the website — [laughter] — like the night before we did our first tweet announcement or something like that.

There's an idea in science fiction that is when robotics and AI has ultimately fully generalized and solved all tasks that humans can do, the final frontier is going to be organic. Final frontier is going to be biological. And you see this in Asimov, you see this in Ender's Game. You could even in Hitchhiker's at the very end — the planet ultimately was this giant organic computer trying to process and understand what the meaning of life was or what the question was.

And so I think in the same vein for us: the human brain runs on just 20 watts, we are self-healing. And so along the journey of teaching and getting robots to fully generalize, we'll slowly show them what carbon life is made of.

Love that.

四、从金融科技到机器人的非典型路径

Q: You come from an untraditional background for robotics. I think you started in the fintech world and the sneaker world if I'm not mistaken. Tell me about how you and your co-founder found your way to robotics.

Josh: It was quite an interesting journey. Before this, I was building essentially a Toast for cloud kitchens. This meant we did everything from back of the house order management. At one point in my fourth year of university, I was skipping class to go deploy and install kiosks into rural Rochester, New York, where we had to stay all nights replacing a lot of these different front of the houses for restaurants.

My co-founder built a stablecoin — they ultimately sold to Coinbase — but he's been this very obsessive personality. He was a top thousand in four competitive games, including League of Legends.

And I think a big part of what brought us together — one, we're both Canadian, and two, we have this big science fiction grounding. The belief ultimately was that payment was a hard and difficult problem, but whatever we worked on next, we wanted to be something that seemed exciting, that the future was going to be incredible, and robotics seemed like a great space to get into.

Q: I remember walking into your office and immediately seeing those mechatronic robots and the Kawasaki Corleos on the wall. The inner child in you must be very happy about what you're doing these days.

Josh: Yeah, absolutely.

外来者的优势与挑战

Q: Coming from a non-robotics background, what do you think your advantages are in building this business? And where has it presented challenges?

Josh: I think the advantage is when we entered the space, we had to go and do this full discovery process. We reached out to hundreds of folks that were in the space that we appreciated. We read every paper that we got our hands on. We went to visit the different robot labs.

And what we saw in late '24, roughly GPT was taking off, robotics was still evolving from this traditional robotics era. It seemed obvious to us at the very least that data and compute would become very important across the industry.

So moving towards that, we got to read and see some of the papers like Ego4D from a fresh lens and say, "Hey, there's about 4,000 hours of this human demonstration data." And when you actually went in to look at the data, you would realize some of the data sets would be daily life of folks like bowling, for example. There was very broad use cases and potential applications at the 4,000 hour scale.

Coming into that with a fresh lens, we were able to from a first principles approach have a general intuition of what would be important, and then iterate very closely with people that were much smarter than us that had different views of what the future would be, and be able to stay close to iterate on what the product would become.

Q: Yeah, interesting. It seems like robotics has just changed so quickly as a field that almost coming from the field can be an advantage and a disadvantage — because people come from different eras of what's important in the training mix and things like that.

五、什么是 Egocentric Data？

Q: Maybe for our audience just say a word on: what is egocentric data? And I think you really started your company kind of making a bet behind it. Obviously it's much more distributed now, but what is egocentric data? Why did you decide to bet the company on it at the beginning?

Josh: Egocentric data is pretty much video data from humans demonstrating and doing tasks from a first-person POV. The high-level idea was that from the gap of human data to robotics data, you could close a lot of the vision gap where robotics experience the world from POV — can we also show it what it is like to interact with the world from first person as well?

Why we bet on it was pretty much — when we explored the space, a lot of what we saw was robotic state at the time was teleoperation, which was humans controlling robots to do demonstrations. It was very hard to scale at the time, and from what we saw across GPT and a lot of the principles of scaling up, we had to find ways to scale up data much more significantly.

Some of our early intuitions were that humans and robots share a lot of similarities. Humanoids were just starting to take off. Humans and humanoids look the same. Why couldn't we turn humans into this fleet-style learning that Tesla has, to be able to all contribute into understanding and ground the physics of the world?

Q: So what does that look like? You're mounting an iPhone on somebody's forehead and just letting them go about their day — or what does that look like in practice?

Josh: Yeah, when we first started, our very earliest pilot was we created a mobile app. We got all the Chinese aunties and uncles to record themselves cooking, cleaning, doing tasks. That obviously evolved a lot. We tried a number of things. We did UMI data. We did all the sorts at the beginning. And that's evolved quite a bit into all the custom hardware that we have to produce now, and all the different partnerships that we have to have across different industries.

Ultimately we're sensorizing humans. That's the broader category here.

力觉数据的重要性

Q: How important is it to get force data from the sensors? In self-driving, you don't really need force data as much. Whereas with robotics, especially with manipulation, you really care about how hard am I squeezing that door handle or picking up that egg. And it seems to me that video doesn't quite capture that. You might be able to approximate it, but doesn't really capture it. How important is capturing force data, and how do you think about getting that?

Josh: I think some of the substitutes for force data that we've seen would be approaches like wrist cameras currently across both humans and robots, and being able to see the contact time between the hand and the different objects that you interact with. That obviously is kind of a hacky way ultimately to get to understanding how much force in Newtons it takes to pull open a chair or twist a bottle cap.

I think force data will be incredibly important. It's actually one of the products that we've been building out, in that when you iterate with many different robotics foundation labs, you realize to close this gap we have to create new hardware. So we've been developing things like gloves for humans to wear, and in those gloves being able to collect the information in how much force it takes to do your daily life and different tasks.

六、数据工厂的真实运营

Q: I'd love to just spend a bit of time on the actual operations of a data factory, because there's so much money that's gone into the LLM data factories. There's so much money that is starting to be poured into, and I think will be poured into, the robot data factories. And the way they work is just mysterious and intriguing to me. So I'd love to ask you a bit about the operations of it if that's okay.

Josh: Yeah, let's do it.

Q: How does it work? If I want to make an extra buck, do I just sign up on your website to start putting a camera on my forehead and start sending you data? How does it work?

Josh: We actually have a lot of different approaches on the operator side.

One would be we have a direct consumer approach. Through direct mobile apps, can you sign up from anywhere in the world? Can you start contributing? Can you register which profession you're in? And can you get streamed a sequence of tasks to do such as cleaning your bedroom, cooking your breakfast, cleaning up afterwards? This is a very lightweight approach to get that diversity ultimately of this pre-training data.

The second approach is — ultimately there is so much more beyond the home to collect. So we had to build out a lot of this B2B engine and this muscle of being able to recruit businesses across this incredible taxonomy of all physical human work — bakeries, PCB manufacturing lines, everything to…

Q: Podcasting?

Josh: Podcasting [laughter] — there's not too much handwork here.

Q: [laughter] We should have equipped ourselves.

数据引擎背后的硬件挑战

Josh: That's ultimately how contributors come into the mix. But the actual data engine for the data factory is so much more sophisticated and much more painful than folks can expect — and that is that a lot of the things that we have to distribute into the world didn't exist until we designed and produced this hardware.

Even across tactile gloves — a fantastic example. There is nothing off the shelf that you can purchase and that you can wear and that reliably tells you how much force you are applying day-to-day and turn that into ready data sets for these different robotics foundation models.

So we have to have that hardware iteration loop, these three-four different product cycles, that engineering muscle to actually think and iterate what is going to be useful, and then scale that production into the world. And that becomes this logistics of distributing into these thousands of homes, thousands of businesses, to collect that, to upload that. We've had to set up these 100 gigabyte upload lines in a lot of the places that we operate in just to sustain the hundreds of petabytes of data that we have to deal with at this point. And then you have to process, you have to make sure your quality gates are incredible, and then all of the computer vision to make it useful ultimately.

热力图式的样本采集

Q: So let's say you decide, okay, in my training mix there's not enough podcasters, there's not enough donut bakers. Do you literally go knock on doors of donut bakers to sign them up to the platform? How does that work?

Josh: We'll generally track kind of like a heat map across different jobs, industries, and ways we think about diversity. And across that heat map, if ultimately we think, "Oh, not enough Sonya's podcasting, we have to go get that." [laughter] That's actually why we're here today. This is our secret method.

Q: That's why there's cameras everywhere. [laughter] No, you're never automating me out of this. No, I'm kidding. Please do.

质量问题与数据欺诈

Q: I've heard that there's a lot of quality issues in robot data collection generally, and that a lot of the hours of robot data sample that get sent in end up not being accepted. Why is that, and what are you doing about that problem?

Josh: This lesson came from even originally the different types of robot data. There have been these very large-scale robot factories that have spun up from just large-scale warehouses repetitively doing tasks trying to scale out teleoperation data. Some of the learnings there came from the research — there is some threshold of diversity where you oversaturate how much robot data you need, or how much data in general you need.

Across human data, quality you can imagine is actually quite a bit of a moving target as we grow. The amount of edge cases that you have in the real world that you have to deal with are very extreme, and you will always see something new that you haven't seen. So for us it's been about: can you think about the heuristics to be able to catch a lot of the different things as it's processed? Can you have the different engines to escalate very quickly? And ultimately we will learn new things about quality and diversity that weren't true a week ago even. So the nimbleness to move very quickly to create and adapt your engine to catch that.

Q: What's an example of something that you would catch?

Josh: I think fraud is an underestimated one across data industries in general. We're ultimately creating data that doesn't exist yet, versus when you're filtering through the internet. And so when you are coming across very creative…

Q: Like people are sending generated videos or what?

Josh: Yeah, very creative people. At one point we have folks recording YouTube videos like POV working at McDonald's and trying to submit that as contribution [laughter] pretty much.

Q: Wow. Never underestimate how entrepreneurial people can be. That's amazing.

Josh: Yeah, very much. And so these have been part of the painful lessons where yes, you have to create a lot of the gates, but ultimately you have to also be there where collection is happening. You have to go see how it's done. You have to figure out an incentive model that actually incentivizes people to create good contribution.

七、商业模式与护城河

Q: How do you think about your right to earn a margin long term? I can imagine a Mecka competitor comes to Sonia and says, "Sonia, I really want your podcast data." I could imagine that the margin that you're able to own as an intermediary ends up getting squeezed.

Josh: I think the contributor amount in terms of the margin cost is actually not the largest factor at play here in terms of the end-to-end making sure this data is useful. So even though that baseline is always going to be there and maybe becomes more and more competitive, there will be ways to differentiate and make sure that your data is verifiably high quality at very large scale with the right hardware, the operations, and the software.

When we think about these products ultimately — it is that we do want to scale up and mature these products, and just like any product that begins to scale up, you want to optimize it. But over time you may have different products that evolve. So when you think about this egocentric data of podcasting as simply one of your SKUs, and you then realize that there is going to be different types of data that are going to be important — such as maybe we move from the Chinese restaurant from the side of the road, can we start moving into the Michelin star restaurants over time? Can you get more and more closer into what it means to be Federer than it means to be an average tennis player? These products will change, and how these products are created will also change.

八、数据规模的现实与前景

Q: What scale of data has already been collected, do you think? And how much data do you think is going to be collected over the next few years?

Josh: I think we finally entered a world where we are in the millions of hours of data. Coming from the world where Ego4D had 4,000 hours two years ago, where we were then, is a huge step up.

But comparatively — think about autonomous driving as an example. Tesla spent over a decade solving for two degrees of freedom ultimately of acceleration and direction, millions of cars on the road. They have a lot more than a few million hours of video data at this point. So relatively we're still many orders of magnitude away from where we have to be ultimately.

Q: So on one hand that sounds like opportunity for you — that sounds like a lot of revenue for the robot data factories. On the other hand, as somebody that invests in the robot foundation models, I look at that and I say like, "Oh shoot, are we ever going to get to the promised land?" Because I've done the same math as you — a car has two or three degrees of freedom, a robot has…

Josh: Even dozens in the hand.

Q: Exactly. And so you combine that with — you probably need force data, and there's a way harder environment to operate in. You might need billions, trillions, quadrillions of hours. Is there even enough GDP in the world to support the cost to bring that in? What do you think?

Josh: I think it's about unlocking commercial use cases as we go. So it doesn't have to be so binary — that oh, one day we've unlocked robotics or not. It is going to be a slow creep up into the world.

A great way to get there is that with some of this base pyramid built up, where we are seeing the generalizations, we are seeing these scaling laws at play — that gives people the courage to scale up. And with that courage, can we have some generalizability in some of these environments? Can we then also collect a lot of the in-domain, in-task data that closes that gap in post-training? So maybe I can collect data exactly from this room, exactly in this podcast demonstration, to actually close the gap of what is it — in a lot of cases four nines of reliability in these real-world environments.

Q: That's a helpful framework. So it's not about a binary of getting from zero to one. It's about we're going to increasingly get robots that can do an increasing set of capabilities.

Josh: And we will unlock a lot of tasks along the way.

家庭数据悖论

Q: One curiosity though is that the data that is most plentiful right now is like home data — just everyone can film that, it's pretty easy to get. But the robot in the home almost seems like one of the most difficult environments to deploy in. So I'm curious what applications you think will hit first in robotics — because where the data is most readily available seems almost the opposite of where robotics might be easiest to deploy.

Josh: The home is going to be some of the environments that we have to be most diligent on by far, and a lot of these benchmarking and evals that have just started to mature across robotics — making sure that the robot doesn't fall on the baby in the homes, for example.

I think the initial tasks will be much more constrained as we go along that spectrum — very goal-oriented where you can hill climb some of these tasks, where you have existing SOPs for what it means to do that job and that work.

Q: Like a laundry folding robot.

Josh: It could be laundry folding. Laundry folding — we spent about a year and a half plus trying to solve, and I think it will absolutely get solved in the near term. A lot of these pick and place, these packaging tasks that you see on assembly lines that had to be manipulation bots that couldn't be solved by traditional robotics — we will get there within the next year or two.

九、部署：机器人的今天与明天

Q: This is a good transition to talking about deployment. You've said that useful robots can already be deployed today. Where do you think that's the case?

Josh: I think people underestimate how diverse robotics can be. If we constrain ourselves to one — humanoids are incredibly popular, it will be a very popular terminal state of robotics as well. But beyond that, there are so many different form factors that exist in robotics today.

You could look at different markets even across hotels in China or Southeast Asia, for example, where there are robots that are doing services, that are doing cleaning, that are delivering — from after your Uber Eats gets to the door, from the front desk to your hotel room door. That exists. Many of these bots are widely deployed across the world today. They are just starting to get popularized across the US and North America.

I think some of the first bots that have to get deployed will be even just the industrial cleaning bots — a lot of like the Matic robotics that are out there — and then slowly stepping up and up from there, where you start to solve early manipulation tasks along that spectrum, all the way up until we get to that humanoid solving out of the box any task in the future.

FSD 式飞轮何时到来？

Q: You mentioned Tesla and FSD earlier in this show. When do you think we're going to get to the point where there is a little bit of an FSD-like flywheel? And when we get to that point, how do you see your role as a company evolving?

Josh: When we will get there — I think we're a ways, but it'll be a slow transition. When you are slowly solving some of the commercial tasks, you will also be able to finally get some of these flywheels. Then you can get some of the in-deployment data where you get the failure cases, you get the correction data. That will be absolutely important in starting up this robot flywheel.

How far that is depends on that spectrum and across saturating different types of tasks and domains that aren't completed or solved for yet. So it's quite a ways away.

When we do get there — thing is, I believe that Mecka will look very different along that process. We're not fully subscribed to only egocentric data. We believe generally that a lot of different SKUs, the entire data soup, is important. So will we be producing the Michelin star data at some point in the future? Will we be teaching some sort of edge case about the real world that the robots haven't gotten to yet? If we believe that the world is incredibly vast and rich in detail, there's going to be no shortage of things to teach.

And even in that world, we do have this angle where we believe that Mecka will very much contribute to the deployment of robots. In some of these environments, in closing that gap of being able to do that task in that domain in that environment — can we actually be the platform where we collect that domain data, we post-train, we help support the enterprises and white-glove hold them into what it means to be in a world filled with robotics? We see Mecka maturing into that.

物理世界的分发路径

Q: I'd love to get your predictions on how you think deployment and the fusion is going to work out in the physical world. If I can analogize what's happened in the LLM world — there's vertical-specific application companies, there's the foundation model companies themselves that are scaling up go-to-market, and then there's all these FDE, deploy-co, service-co, whatever you want to call them, armies of people helping enterprises adopt AI at scale. Those seem like the broad vectors that are disseminating tokens across the economy. What do you think the analog will be in the physical world?

Josh: We believe very much in both the vertical and the horizontal across robotics. So the full verticals that are very task-specific all the way from hardware to models to data, they're tackling.

We also believe in an ecosystem where there's going to be very vast and different shapes and sizes of hardware of robotics, and there will be different types of open models that exist in the world. I think it will look something like a modern robotics version of a systems integrator — that in a traditional version you are installing the product, it's incredibly competitive, it is tight margins.

There is now a world where you can actually install and help make that product become more data-driven and productive over time. So can you actually have the bot you installed last week do something that it didn't think was possible a few days ago even? Can help you start expanding the scope of what your business is capable of doing. That's ultimately the milestone that we're hoping to aim for.

Q: Okay, but you would tell me as an investor now — give me some investing advice. You'd invest in both the general and the vertical robots then.

Josh: Yeah.

Q: What are your favorite vertical robot categories?

Josh: I think the best ones will be the industrial bots to start. Those are going to be ones that already have a lot of traditional robotics in the mix, that are task-constrained like we talked about.

Q: Like data center maintenance robots.

Josh: Yeah. You just don't have to expect a baby to appear and have to think about that and not fall on it, for example. So the world is much more constrained than in the wild.

Other categories we're excited about are just spaces that are even feasible and possible early on. Some of the approaches in the hotels, for example, where you could actually start delivering from the front desk to the hotel rooms, be able to actually have some manipulation to hand off, are exciting to us.

And then places that just humans were not capable of. A joke that we make in some of our all-hands in the company would be: if one day Mecka was able to help deploy a robot that mines an asteroid, we've probably done a pretty good job. [laughter] It's just a job and a task that completely doesn't exist, that humans can't do, that we have no idea how to do just yet, but it seems inevitable.

Q: Yeah, I love that. Reminds me of — I'm not thinking interplanetary yet — but have you heard of Gecko Robotics? What they do to help maintain ships and things like that. I think it's really cool.

Josh: Absolutely.

十、Mecka 的硬件矩阵

Q: Can you say a word on — whatever you're willing to share publicly — the slate of hardware that you've developed and where the labs currently are most interested in collecting bespoke data?

Josh: Some of the iteration came from when we started with the mobile app. We quickly were able to scale that. There were a lot of virtues in that product. The downsides ultimately were you don't get as much rich information about the world as you could have.

So some of the things that we had to develop very early on were things like wearables for people ultimately. In this sensorization, can you build things like these baseball caps that are equipped with different cameras and sensors? We build a central hub that then connects to all these different accessories such as the tactile gloves, external cameras, and more. All of which is trying to capture how do you interact with the world on a day-to-day, and hopefully be able to clone that behavior.

Egoverse 联盟

Q: What is Egoverse?

Josh: Egoverse — Professor Dan Fei, Ryan Simmer, these are some of the earliest cohorts of researchers that believed in egocentric data. We had the privilege to be an early contributor in that consortium ultimately of different folks that think scaling up human data would be important for robotics.

We created and contributed a large amount of different types of egocentric data across different businesses, industries, home environments. We shared all of the action trajectory data — so all of the post-processing, the computer vision and the quality gates — and we contribute all the platform and web tooling pretty much. The data loading, the infrastructure.

So it is ultimately — I guess, to repeat their vision on this — ideally we can bring together a lot of the robotics industry, because hopefully we can lift up everybody in this wave and share the tooling, the data, and the lessons, just because we are so far behind as an industry to get there.

十一、数据配方的"汤论"

Q: Is it fair to say that the robotics industry has kind of converged on a trending data mix that is: internet scale data from YouTube and the like, plus a bunch of egocentric data, plus teleop, and then plus teleop? There's like a triangle of amount of data on each — I think Jim Fan had a really nice visual on this at a Sequoia event. Is that kind of the mix that you see? And amongst your customers, has everybody kind of converged on a very similar mix?

Josh: It's fun to see that even a year ago, many folks would argue and say, "Oh no, it's only UMI data that's going to work," "it's only egocentric data that's going to work." And you slowly realize — to your point — all of this is essentially a data pot of soup. In that pot of soup, all the ingredients are going to be important at some point.

I think what we're seeing is a convergence across what that recipe might be today. That does look like some version of a million hours of human data across egocentric and different types of modalities, some tens of thousands of hours of teleop data, and then some last-mile teleoperation data and in-domain, in-distribution data — in just a couple hours even of that demonstration.

I think we are seeing that, but over time, why we don't subscribe aggressively to even one religion here — is that things like tactile data haven't even entered the mix yet. If there is this belief that these models ultimately will need to learn how much force it takes to apply towards the door handle, for example, these will have to come into the data pot of soup. Simulation will come into the data pot of soup. And they all will be important to converge on.

Federer 问题与 AlphaGo 类比

Q: One of the objections that I hear most frequently to the types of data being collected: you could watch millions of hours of tennis data and you still wouldn't know how to beat Roger Federer. I'm curious what you think of that and what it means for where we might be headed in terms of the way robots learn.

Josh: I love the analogy of AlphaGo. Ultimately, when you talk about robots playing tennis, you got to talk about robots playing Go. With Lee Sedol and in all the work that DeepMind did at the very beginning, it was large-scale behavior cloning of different experts playing Go. Then the next step was the self-play version — with the rules of the game, can you ultimately simulate all the different ways until you come up with the magic of move 37 ultimately — which was so out of scope of what humans could have thought in that moment on the Go board.

For us though, in our case of robotics, for Go the rules of the game are the entire circumference of the world that you will operate in. In robotics you have the incredible rich detail that the physical world has, and we ultimately don't have a world simulator that can recreate that today.

So to close that gap, a lot of the egocentric data today is to one, help us ground the basic physics and the basic behavior cloning that you have to get to. It is also contributing to creating what this world simulator might look like. And then somewhere along the way, I think we will be able to create and have robots playing tennis like Roger Federer.

Q: Do you think they'll mostly be doing self-play in simulation or in the real world?

Josh: I could see a hybrid ultimately. I think if we can get simulation and we don't have to fully reconstruct the world to its detail right away — but I see self-play both in the physical and in simulation.

World Models 的作用

Q: You used the word "world simulator" a couple times there. What are your thoughts on what's happening with world models, which are being used somewhat interchangeably with video models as a term right now — but world models and their contribution to the robot data training mix?

Josh: I think the potential and possibility to have what we just talked about in terms of self-play — to even just dream what it means to drop a cup and have it shatter without actually doing it — is incredibly valuable for what could happen.

I see the value in that we get to leverage a lot of the work from the internet and YouTube, for example, in this pixel prediction ultimately. And if we can translate that back into what these action trajectories would be, it could help us accelerate quite a bit.

十二、通往 "GPT-3 时刻" 的路径

Q: So you mentioned that we've kind of converged on this pyramid of data mix. Do you think this pyramid will scale if we just scale it up? Do you think that takes us to the promised land? And to me, "promised land" is — people like saying GPT-3 moment for robotics, I no longer like that, I just like: when will a robot actually fold my clothes or cook a meal for me? Do you think the current data mix will get us to that point, or do you think new breakthroughs in algos and data are going to be needed to get there?

Josh: I think if we scale it up some order of magnitude in that ratio, we will solve a lot of tasks along the way. Some of those tasks could be a lot more constrained environments. They could be within business operation tasks, very specific SOPs you give.

In that ideal world where we have a drop-in robot and it solves any task by just looking at it — can play tennis just like Roger Federer out of the box, in all the crazy complexities of the actual world scenarios like the weather, for example — I think it will be some way, and I don't think this is what it will look like ultimately.

Q: What will it look like?

Josh: Well, we still have so much to add into the mix still. I think that is going to be: how can we start introducing other modalities into the mix? This is going to be that tactile data.

I like the approach a lot of the models converging towards an omni-model approach — where you can feed it any type of input that is the observation, whether it is force, pixel, even smell in a very extreme case — and then have some sort of output, whether it's action, voice, or different types of controls.

Q: Are there even chips that can sense smell?

Josh: It's pretty early. This olfactory approach is very early. I like to imagine that there's going to be an approach in the world where that gets unlocked.

Omni-model 对纯机器人公司的冲击

Q: The results of, you know, GPT-6 Astra is generalizing incredibly well to robot tasks. I'm curious what you make of that and what it means for all these pure-play robotics companies. Are they ultimately just going to get clobbered by the AGI labs, and the bitter lesson is just going to steamroll robotics as well? What do you think?

Josh: It takes a lot of courage to scale up data with imperfect information, and I think a lot of these labs have the DNA in themselves to take on that courage early on.

What we're seeing and what's exciting is that with the scale-up of robotics data, and even just adding into a lot of the pre-training mixes of these main LLMs and these foundation models, it really is that you can start to generalize in a lot of different domains.

I'm excited about the omni-model approaches where you can introduce a lot of different types of observation — whether that's force or whether that's action trajectories — into the mix and allow it to generalize.

I think there are also going to be a lot of arguments where you want to be much more vertical than a fully generalized model that can do anything. So somewhere along that time horizon, that model that can do everything is going to be very good at a lot of things. But some of these specialized models, some of these more targeted robotics foundation models, might become very excellent — into four nines of capability and reliability — in some of these tasks.

Q: What I heard reading between the lines just now was that the fact that the latest foundation models are great at robotics is not actually that surprising, in part because there actually is quite a bit of robot data that's been now thrown into the training mix. Is that fair?

Josh: It's actually quite expected when you think about it.

Very interesting.

十三、科幻式的终局

Q: I'd love to close by going back to your sci-fi roots. You started this company because you could imagine a version of the world with robots everywhere. Paint a picture of what you think the world looks like.

Josh: I think the funniest moment was probably when you visited our New York office — and in our main conference room, we have hung up on the wall actually the Kawasaki Corleo.

Q: I love that. Which — [laughter] — is the robot panther dog horse, whatever it is.

Josh: The panther dog horse, exactly. So it's pretty much a robot panther dog horse [laughter]. And it's the most ridiculous video and trailer you've ever seen pretty much.

Q: My favorite part is that you guys convinced Anas that it was actually you and [laughter] your mom on it.

Josh: Yeah, yeah. There's a clip pretty much where this fantastical Asian lady and her son are riding this green meadow over a little river. And the Corleo, this horse-dog-panther robot, is jumping over [laughter] the river. We told Anas this was pretty much us as when we were kids and we generated it.

But what is wonderful is how absurd it is. I very much love the philosophy of Hitchhiker's in just how absurd the world could be and how absurd the future could be. In this world that is full of robots, I would love to believe that there's going to be such crazy entrepreneurs and people that believe that form factors like this would be interesting. The shape and size of robotics will look something like a world where we come up with wacky robots that could do anything that you haven't even thought of yet.

Q: I love that.

Josh: Like mining asteroids. [laughter]

一个数量级的预测

Q: Order of magnitude — how many robots will there be in the world in a decade?

Josh: Many, many times more than there are people.

Q: Many orders of magnitude more than there are people. Yes. In a decade plus. 100 billion robots.

Josh: Yeah.

Q: That's really cool. 100 billion panther dog horses.

Josh: Panther dog horses. At least another order of magnitude more [laughter] than that.

Q: Love it. Awesome, Josh. I think that what you're building is operationally really impressive and very cool — how you are scaling up the data collection efforts to enable kind of this robotics golden age and this sci-fi future that you've dreamed of since you were a kid. So thank you for joining the pod today to tell us both how you're building the business and how you see the future. This is really fun.

Josh: Thank you so much for having us. Thank you, Sonia.

彩蛋：开箱时刻

Josh: So we actually brought you a present.

Q: I love presents. This is kind of like a full circle moment for us. Is this what I think it is?

Josh: Who knows? Who knows? [laughter] All right, you're going to have to open it up on the podcast.

Q: Okay, this is amazing. And look at the — hold on, can we — You know, I could be one of those YouTubers that does the unboxings. [laughter] Look, I love this. The Mecka stickers are A+. Okay, I think this is what I think it is. Let's see.

Josh: We're going to actually come up with a series of Mecka figurines — stickers — because they're all like giant robots, human pilot stuffs.

Q: That'll be fun. I'm so excited. Let's see if this is working today. I love it. Oh my gosh. Okay, this is the —

Josh: This is the Corleo.

Q: This is the Kawasaki Corleo. I love this. This is the robot dog panther horse.

Josh: This is me and my mom —

Q: — on the panther horse. That's right. [laughter] This is going — we're either going to put it in the podcast room or in my office. This is incredible. I'm so happy.

Josh: Do it. So absurd.

Q: I'm so happy. Thank you. [laughter]

[music]

Heat. Hey, Heat. [music]

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Mecka 正在建造的，不是"数据工厂"，而是**人类身体的殖民地化基础设施**
表面上 Mecka 是在"收集数据"，但如果你把它和整个工业史放在一起看，会发现一个让人毛骨悚然的类比——**这是一次反向的工业革命**。
- 第一次工业革命：机器模仿人的身体（纺织机 → 手臂；蒸汽机 → 腿）。 - 第二次：机器模仿人的神经（计算机 → 大脑的离散部分）。 - 而 Mecka 正在做的是：**把人反过来变成传感器节点**，让人类的日常动作、肌肉收缩、指尖压力、Michelin 大厨的刀工，被"抽取"成可被机器复制的 token。
Josh 用了一个非常轻描淡写的词叫 "sensorizing humans"（给人装传感器）。但如果你把它和福柯的"规训社会"、或者 Shoshana Zuboff 的"监控资本主义"放在一起，会发现一个惊人的转向：**过去 20 年互联网公司提取的是你的"注意力和偏好"，Mecka 提取的是你的"身体性知识"（tacit bodily knowledge）**——那些你自己都说不清楚、只存在于你肌肉记忆里的东西。换句话说，M

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] ADA創辦人：幣圈暴漲時代徹底結束！為何AI時代看對趨勢還是會破產？市場還沒定價的下一波財富在哪？Charles Hoskinson【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察：Hoskinson 这场访谈真正说出口的三个"隐性断言"

一、"Meme币时代结束"的真正含义：不是周期切换，而是流动性范式的死亡

表面上，Hoskinson 在哀悼一个"疯狂估值"的时代。但他没有点破的是：加密货币从未真正受自身技术周期驱动——它是全球美元流动性的衍生品。Meme币能上月，不是因为青蛙图片有价值，而是因为 2020-2021 的 ZIRP（零利率）把过剩资本推向了"没有现金流的资产"。那个时代结束，并不是因为"行业成熟了"，而是因为便宜的钱消失了。

跨领域连接：这与 1890 年代美国"自行车狂热"的终结如出一辙。当时三百多家自行车公司估值疯狂，直到自行车真正成为交通工具——速度降下来，泡沫破了，但自行车技术本身却悄悄演化成了汽车业的工程基础（Wright 兄弟就是自行车工匠）。加密的 memecoin 时代结束之日，才是它成为"隐形管道"的开始。Hoskinson 口中的"用户不会知道自己在用加密"——这正是技术成熟的标志：消失，而不是显眼。

二、"效率市场假说"的反直觉含义：AI 让根本面派比套利派更危险，而非更安全

Hoskinson 说"你要像巴菲特，而不是索罗斯"。听起来是回归保守主义。但真正的意外观察在这里：当成千上万的"AI 索罗斯"涌入市场、把所有统计套利窗口瞬间关闭之后，根本面投资者的处境反而更糟了，而不是更好。

为什么？因为效率市场假说只保证"套利消失"，它从不保证"错误定价会被修正"。当 AI 代理瞬间清掉所有短期不一致，剩下的就是长期叙事定价——而叙事可以持续错误 20 年。Michael Burry 等了多年才被证明对，Hoskinson 自己承认"方向对但本地时间错，然后你烧完"。他其实在说：AI 不会消灭凯恩斯那句"市场保持非理性的时间比你能保持偿付能力的时间更长"——它让这句话加倍成立。

跨领域连接：这与生态学中的"竞争排除原理"惊人相似——当快速采集者占据所有可见生态位，剩下的策略只有两种极端：极慢的、几十年尺度的根本演化（巴菲特），或者彻底跳出当前生态系统（真正的创业创造）。中间地带（专业交易员、小型对冲基金）会被挤死。这解释了为什么他主动说"我不是专业交易员，我做铲子"。

三、"卖铲子"心态下的隐藏对称性：加密、长寿、代理法——都是同一种本体论革命

这是整场访谈最隐秘的那条线，连 Hoskinson 自己都没明说。他从加密跳到干细胞贴片、跳到代理人格权，看似东扯西拉，但背后是同一个本体论操作：把过去被认为"自然且不可编程"的东西，变成可编程的协议层。

  • 加密 → 把"信任"从机构里拉出来，变成代码
  • 长寿医学 → 把"衰老"从命运里拉出来，变成信息理论问题（Sinclair 的 Information Theory of Aging 正是这个意思）
  • Midnight 作为"DeFi 的 VPN" → 把"隐私"从应用层拉出来，变成基础设施
  • 代理人格权 → 把"法律责任"从人身上拉出来，变成分布式实体可承担的属性

最意外的推论：Hoskinson 真正押注的不是加密、不是长寿、不是 AI——他押注的是20 世纪遗留的"自然范畴"全面瓦解这件事本身。健康跨度（health span）vs 寿命跨度（life span）的区分，和他说"你用加密但不知道自己在用加密"是同构的——都在把一个被当作"整体不可分"的东西拆成服务层。

跨领域连接：这与 17 世纪笛卡尔的"心物二元论"崩溃的历史时刻惊人对称。那时候，"灵魂"被拆成神经机制；今天，"衰老"被拆成基因程序，"信任"被拆成共识算法，"身份"被拆成零知识证明。他对 Sax 和 Trump 的愤怒，表面上是政治，深层是认识论的愤怒——这些人用 19 世纪的范畴（名字、所有权、国籍）去管理 21 世纪的拓扑结构（代理人群、跨链交易、涌现式智能）。

补充观察：Hoskinson 自己没意识到的一个盲点

他赞美"AI 让每个人都成为建造者"的黄金时代。但当建造的边际成本趋近于零，瓶颈不是建造能力，而是品味和判断。他给弟弟做任天堂维修网站、放游戏 ROM，这个"建造的快乐"本身可能正在成为稀缺品——不是因为难做，而是因为在无限建造的世界里，知道该建造什么、以及什么时候停下来，比会建造本身更难。他对 Sax 的批评（"第一直觉是让这件事关于他自己"）其实适用于每一个 AI 时代的建造者，包括他自己。

📝 转录文本

开场：加密时代的终结与范式转换

It's frustrating as a fundamental investor because you can be directionally right but in the local time wrong, and you know, you end up burning out.

This concept of crypto where a memecoin goes to the moon—that age of crypto is over. That window's closed, and now there's that's the new big thing. We don't have pricing for it. You actually have to be like Warren Buffett and Benjamin Graham more than a George Soros looking for an anomaly in the system.

Anytime there's an emerging or new technology, first we overshoot. It's real hard to find the price. You know, you saw that with Amazon when the dot-com boom came out. It took 11 years after the collapse for them to recover the price they had in 2000.

Right now, we're treating the regulatory structure of agents very much like self-driving cars. Huge problem. Self-driving car, if you get in an accident, even though the car was driving, it's your fault. Well, an agent—what if you have 5,000 agents and one goes bat crazy and hacks somebody? You can't accept unlimited personal liability.

Trump picked the wrong crypto czar and the wrong AI czar. You know, Sax is incompetent and he should have never been put in that role.

Midnight is your new favorite kid. What is your response?

Well, you know, there's just some sourpusses in the community. It's crazy.

嘉宾介绍

What a pleasure to have Charles Hoskinson back with us again. He is the co-founder of Ethereum, founder of Cardano, and founder and CEO of Input Output Global.

一、加密与 AI 的融合：从投机到基础设施

Charles, you said crypto is dead in its own form, but you also said crypto is going to eat AI. What do you mean?

Well, I mean, you know, there's a constant reinvention with technology and a constant reinvention with society. We no longer have AOL and Yahoo and BlackBerries and Palm Pilots. We have different things. So you can never get comfortable with the way that we did things.

This concept of crypto where a memecoin goes to the moon, NFTs are worth 1.3 million, you have crazy valuations and nothing connected to it—that age of crypto is over.

But crypto has a very nice natural connection to the AI revolution in that we are kind of the determinism of AI. We're the payment layer with X42 and other things for AI. And we're the place that AI actually lives. We're the place for the agent to have a wallet, an economic agency, and a place to be.

And so, it's a really exciting time because then in that reinvention, it almost feels like we get smartphones—the old phone dies, but you get an infinitely better phone. And having AI with crypto means you have intelligent smart contracts. You don't have these little things where you write some code and they kind of do it and they're really dumb. You actually have real intelligence with your smart contracts, and they're abstract and multi-chain and they touch consumer devices, off-chain infrastructure, and blockchain, and they don't treat it as different. It's just "Charles at Midnight" or "Charles at Bitcoin" or whatever the heck it is—just like email is—and you don't care too much about the implementation details.

So what's exciting is that the consumer revolution is finally here, and we're going to see hundreds of millions of new people enter. They're not going to know they're using cryptocurrencies, not going to know they're using cryptocurrency rails. And it's going to be a natural extension of the AI tools that they're already using and the financial infrastructure that they're already using.

二、AI 交易与市场效率：索罗斯时代的终结

I have a question regarding AI trading. Soros is arguably one of the best traders in the world because he identified systems that cannot be sustained—the 1992 pound incident, right? AI agents are very smart. Let's say we have thousands and millions of Soroses trading in the market. What happens to the market?

Well, the markets converge—efficient market hypothesis is what people tend to cite. It's hard over time for people to beat the markets. So this is why a lot of people just trade indexes or they trade ETFs, because at the end of the day, you can be really smart, but that's a statistical arbitrage that you tend to have for only a brief window of time.

James Simons 的案例

James Simons is probably the greatest example of that. James was the first quant—brilliant mathematician. And if you put a dollar in the Medallion Fund, you'd get $50,000 out. So, it's pretty good ROI. When he came in, he had this massive advantage. Everybody was using intuition. He was using hardcore statistics and mathematics to do these things.

Well, everybody's got a quant fund now. Everybody has hardcore mathematical models. So that competitive edge and delta goes away.

So really, it's less about "do I maximize returns" and it's more about market efficiency and liquidity. Can you be able to seamlessly interface with the market at the best possible price 24 hours a day, 7 days a week?

商家案例：AI 吃掉加密，加密吃掉 AI

So let's say you're a merchant. It's a great example of where everything comes together—AI eating crypto and crypto eating AI. You want to accept cryptocurrency payments. Instead of using a payment provider like a BitPay or Coinbase Pay or something, you just accept that you have a trading agent. Agent loads a script. It's trading at the same level that Jane Street or RenTech would trade, and every 15 minutes it divests all the crypto you've received to stablecoins and you get them.

So now you're basically functionally acting as BitPay, but you're doing it as a three-person business, and you're doing it for the lowest possible fee, and you're enjoying the maximum possible liquidity. That's where this goes.

So there's a return to fundamental investing, there's a return to fundamentals in business, as opposed to just pure technicals and pure speculation. And you don't have these giant pockets of arbitrage to go and gobble up anymore. You actually have to be like Warren Buffett and Benjamin Graham more than a George Soros looking for an anomaly in the system.

三、新技术的过冲周期：从亚马逊到 SpaceX

But before we get there, do we have a lot of volatility in the market first, because we'll have agents identifying these weaknesses, so to speak, and then we get to efficiency, right?

Yeah. And it's always that case. Anytime there's an emerging or new technology, first we overshoot. It's real hard to find the price.

亚马逊的教训

You saw that with Amazon when the dot-com boom came out. It took 11 years after the collapse for them to recover the price they had in 2000. So they didn't enjoy it till 2011. Well, obviously Amazon of 2011 was a radically different company than Amazon of 2000—much better company—but the market overshot, so they overpriced it.

SpaceX 同样的故事

SpaceX is the exact same. In the long term, they're probably a $10 trillion company. In the short term, they're probably overvalued as a company.

So the technology is highly volatile because we don't really understand what does this mean? You have this thing that everybody's going to use and it's going to in some way be involved in their life. Well, is that now the next big thing, or is it part of somebody else's thing, and who are the winners and losers going to be? Is it the same group of people or a new group of people going to come in? Speculators love to speculate.

窗口关闭与新窗口打开

After five or ten years, we kind of understand it. We kind of have it figured out, and then the market has a standard to it. Like you could get funding in 2007 to build a smartphone. Nobody in their right mind is going to go fund a smartphone company to compete against Xiaomi and Galaxy and iPhone or these things.

Similarly, in 2017, 2018, you could get money to build a large language model, but nobody in their right mind wants to compete against Anthropic and the big Chinese companies and these other guys. So that window's closed, and now there's new windows with agentic harnesses and new windows with agentic social networks.

That's the new big thing, and we don't have pricing for it. We now have a pricing for the infrastructure—it's trillion dollars. So Anthropic's worth a trillion, OpenAI is worth a trillion, SpaceX is worth a trillion. That's kind of the entry point for that level. Maybe that's right, maybe it's wrong. The market will eventually figure it out in three to five years, and if the hypothesis is true, they'll have colossal amounts of revenue and they become the new SaaS in that respect, and the old SaaS dies in that respect.

根本面派的挫败

So that's fun as a trader because you get to enjoy the volatility, and if you bet right, you make wild fortunes. It's frustrating as a fundamental investor because you can be directionally right but in the local time wrong, and you end up burning out.

It was just the exact like The Big Short, where Michael Burry knew that the housing market had systemic issues but it was really hard for him to keep that position. Because he was directionally right but he mistimed a few things on it. So he didn't maximize the amount of money he got to make with it. So that's the frustration. It's why I'm not a professional trader. I leave it to Steve Cohen and all these other guys to do it. I build infrastructure. I'm a picks and shovels guy.

四、最激动人心的趋势：流动性从股票流向商品

Market cycle, financial product—speak AI. What's the most exciting trend in the market right now?

The most exciting trend right now is how the liquidity is flowing from equities to commodities like Bitcoin.

What first got you into it?

I had a really close friend who is still my friend, who was mining…

五、长寿革命：从寿命跨度到健康跨度

You're also very into longevity. You want to live for a long time. Can we actually stop aging?

Well, you know, it's funny. I've looked like I'm 45 since I was 21. So there's going to be this singularity where I eventually catch up with the way I look.

衰老机制的重编程

The magic of aging is—when I first started studying the topic of gerotherapeutics, there was this pessimism in the field where they say "we'll never know the mechanisms, and even if we do, there's nothing you do to change them." And I saw that's so silly, because we have creatures in the biological world, living creatures today, that are—yeah, Turritopsis dohrnii is one, but also when you get pregnant—think about what happens. You have a sperm and you have an egg. They're not zero. They have a man and woman that was maybe 25 and 35, whatever. They come together. You don't have a 27-year-old embryo, right? It resets the clock.

So you have structures in your body to reset age, and the jellyfish has structures to reset age. This is just a biological puzzle to sort out. When you combine it with quantum computers and you combine it with AI, that language is going to be rapidly understood.

Sinclair 的信息理论与干细胞突破

And there's just phenomenal work like the Information Theory of Aging that Dave Sinclair has over at Harvard. It's not just a theory anymore. They actually have clinical trials that they're doing and they're reversing aging in people's eyes and resolving blindness.

We did some work with Altos with adipose-derived stem cells and I cultured my own stem cells with umbilical cord blood exosomes, and we saw off-the-charts improvement in gene and protein expression. We said, "Wow, these cells are basically like 20 years younger if you just co-culture them with exosomes." So there's a programming language for stem cells and there's a programming language for your body, and if you can derive it, then you can basically tell cells to be younger again.

I think we're going to understand that language within about 10 to 20 years, and then we're going to be able to develop a whole house of therapeutics to basically resolve the conditions of aging.

学科的转变

So it's one of the fastest growing fields. It's one of the most valuable fields. And it's real exciting because it's moving faster than I thought it would move. It's not like fusion where they say every 10 years we'll have something and it never comes. We have seen massive and major breakthroughs. It's really extraordinary to see how much funding and how many bright people are inside the field.

If you tried to do anti-aging 20 years ago, they'd say, "Oh well, that's a dead-fruit pseudoscience career. You can't do it." Now as a newly admitted PhD, there's nothing wrong with being an anti-aging researcher. Everybody's chasing it.

地缘政治维度

You know, the other thing is we have these dictators that don't want to die—like Xi and Putin and others. And Xi in particular—he's dumping massive quantities of money in regenerative biology and synthetic biology in China. For every one PhD we have in this topic, three to five for them, depending on how you want to count it. So that is going to have a long-term impact as well.

IPSC 临床试验

You have all these amazing AI models and all these academics. So we've already seen things with induced pluripotent stem cells that were just inconceivable 5 years ago. Like there was a clinical trial that they conducted where they were able to reverse diabetes in a patient. She had diabetes since she was 12, was insulin-dependent and already in a very bad state. Now she's no longer insulin-dependent. They completely regenerated her pancreas with IPSC, and it's stable for two and a half years. That is a shot heard around the world. And these treatments are going to become more and more standard.

六、健康跨度：成功的真正定义

What would success look like? Is it we reverse aging or we sustain our age, we slow down dying?

Well, the grandfather of this was Aubrey de Grey, and he talked about this concept of longevity escape velocity—the idea is that for every year you age, you extend human lifespan by a year, so you effectively live forever.

从寿命跨度到健康跨度

Really what I look at is the idea of a health span. So lifespan is useless to me. Like, would you want to live 20 years with dementia and diapers and an old folks home, and you have no quality of life? You don't want to be [that].

William Shatner 的榜样

I was just with William Shatner the other day, and he's 95 and he's incredibly spry. He's full of life. He was a little tired when we met him. He said, "I'm sorry, I'm a little tired. I just got back from Chicago. I started a heavy metal band." And I was like, "What? You have a heavy metal band?" He's like, "Yeah, I decided that heavy metal is the thing I should do. It's the next act for the Shatner."

You want that lifestyle. You want to be 95 years old and you still have your mind. You're still sharp, you're still mobile, you're doing heavy metal, you're flying all around, you're doing cool stuff. You don't want to be 80 years old and have Alzheimer's. So health span is the goal. Quality of life is the goal.

关键的治疗方向

So the question is, can you use gerotherapeutics to reverse neurodegenerative disorders and disorders that tend to massively impair your quality of life? Cardiopulmonary are the big ones there.

The other thing is cancer. We're getting pretty good at treating it, but in the process of treating it, it tends to carpet-bomb your body. So you get peripheral neuropathies and all these other horrible conditions. So, can you use therapeutics to reduce or mitigate the damage cancer treatment has, to restore lung function, heart function, and neural function?

If you can do that stuff, you'll be able to stay sharp. You'll be 90. You'll feel great. You can still be with the great-grandkids. You can still travel. When you read, you still understand what you're reading. You can use a cell phone. You can call people. You have a great quality of life. You're a participant in society as a whole.

I do believe within 10 years to 20 years, we'll have all the foundations for those to be capable.

七、民主化医疗：Stabler 干细胞贴片

The question is the cost—the democratization of this technology. Is it only going to be available to billionaires and millionaires, or is it going to be cheap?

从吸脂手术到贴片

So a lot of my contribution to the anti-aging space is lowering the cost of entry. One of our devices we're working on right now is a device called Stabler, and I got the idea from continuous glucose monitors. I had liposuction to remove stem cells from my fat, and I was just laying in bed and I'm like, "This sucks. I hate this so much. There's got to be an easier way."

So I said, "Why can't I just build a disc where you slap it on, it sucks up stem cells for two days, and then you take it off like a continuous glucose monitor, and then you had your stem cells?" So we built that device with a partner named Cell Drop at University of Wyoming, and we'll be able to start clinical trials next year.

We went from "you have to do a surgery with a surgeon and recover from that whole setup" to "you put a patch on for two days, it costs a hundred bucks, a nurse can put it on and take it off." That's a step function change in the cost of the procedure.

药价与民主化

That's what I want to do—is make it a lot cheaper for people to get personalized stem cells to the masses. And then all these innovations, as they come, everyday people get to enjoy them instead of millionaires and billionaires. And then that means grandma can enjoy a high quality of life.

I ran a pharmacy with my clinic for years up in Gillette, and it just blew my mind the cost of drugs—the cancer drugs, the biologics. I have gout. And they wanted to give me some injections for it. And they were like, "$26,000 an injection for a biologic." I said, "I take allopurinol. It costs like half a dollar a pill. Come on, guys. I don't want a $26,000 shot." "Well, that's just the price."

It's not democratic then. It can't be well distributed to everybody in the world. And it would be terrible to have a longevity solution that only the richest people in the world get to have. You need to have a longevity solution that everybody gets to have.

八、Midnight：DeFi 的 VPN

I've seen some comments before that they think Midnight is your new favorite kid. What is your response?

Well, there's just some sourpusses in the community, and who the hell cares? It is what it is. When you have a kid, you have another kid. The first kid's jealous of the second kid. I love them both equally and they do different things.

Midnight 的核心定位

The core of Midnight right now, where it's at in its evolution, is: it's the VPN for DeFi. That's what it wants to be.

What does a VPN do? A VPN like ExpressVPN, NordVPN—you do podcasting and they probably call you up saying, "Hey, we want to advertise Express on Bonnie." You click the button, and then it's secure, and it takes 30 seconds to a minute to connect. You're done. And then all of a sudden you use the internet. Now, from the internet's perspective, it's not Bonnie anymore—it's ExpressVPN or it's Proton or whatever.

Well, if you're a VPN for DeFi, you click the button in your wallet, you go through the Midnight network, and then you do your DeFi on Solana or Ethereum or Cardano or what have you. And from their perspective, it's not you in your wallet—it's Midnight doing that transaction on your behalf. Easy to understand, easy to get around, and a great user experience.

And what you've done is you've added privacy, safety, and simplicity to the conversation. And you added universality to the conversation.

九、代理吃掉加密：智能合约的真正智能化

Talk about agents eating crypto. What are you doing with agents eating crypto?

Well, if you combine agentic trading with the VPN for DeFi, instead of you doing the trades and doing the orders, your agent just does. You use an open standard like Open Wallet X42, and you just load a trading script into it and you say, "Hey, just go do the trading thing and send me a report every day about what you've done." You don't care if it's on Hyperliquid or on Solana or Ethereum or what have you.

Midnight 作为普世入口

So from that perspective, Midnight gets to be friends to everybody. I was just at a Solana event yesterday. They were very gracious. We added Solana support into Midnight. So next year we're going to be that. And the value proposition that Cardano is—Cardano now has a privacy layer, it has a VPN for DeFi. So all Cardano DeFi could be private. And that's the same value proposition that Solana's going to get, and Ethereum's going to get, Bitcoin's going to get, and these other things.

真正智能的智能合约

Now, longer term, these agents give you a level of intelligence for processing smart contracts that we've never enjoyed before. Smart contracts, for being smart, are pretty dumb. They only do what you tell them to do. And that's why you have bridge hacks, wallet hacks, and all these other things.

Well, if you have an LLM connected to it, they're a heck of a lot smarter. And so, if you have ZK and MPC and TEE, it really does a lot of wonders. So our long-term view for Midnight is, in addition to having the VPN for DeFi, make it the preferred place to add true intelligence and abstraction to all cryptocurrency.

And then you get universality. So Midnight becomes the entry point for everybody into the cryptocurrency space. It just is simple, it's safe, it's easy to understand, and it works on your phone and every consumer can do it. And then there's no tribalism because you're doing Solana transactions and Ethereum transactions and Bitcoin transactions, and it just magically works.

十、超级智能峰会批评：Trump 政府的 AI 政策

We talk about Midnight. We talk about AI agents. I want your take on the recent Trump super intelligence meeting. You kind of have to voluntarily audit your own code, if I understand it correctly. What is your take?

I mean, it's like your great-grandfather comes in and says, "You know what? I'm going to figure out how to regulate TikTok and be a TikTok influencer." The guy is 80. He's surrounded by a bunch of sycophants and idiots. And he has no clue how to even approach or think about what this technology is.

And so he brings a bunch of CEOs to the White House. They placate him because he's the President of the United States. It's a powerful role. But at the end of the day, nothing has been gained in terms of how do we think about alignment? Nothing has been gained in think how do we work together.

中国的全国家策略

China—love them or hate them—they have an all-of-country approach for how they think about the whole stack of AI: from who makes the hardware like Huawei and Xiaomi, to who trains the models, to how the models are aligned and deployed, and where these models are going to be competitive.

They're not playing for the United States and for Europe. What they're doing is saying: we want everybody in India, everybody in Central Asia, everybody in South America and Africa to use our models. And because our models are optimized for Huawei and Xiaomi hardware, they're not buying Nvidia chips, they're buying Chinese chips. So by giving them away for free and subsidizing that, the whole world becomes addicted to Chinese AI and thus Chinese hardware. And they have a mechanism of control through that. That's an all-of-nation approach.

美国应该怎么做：开源对齐

And if the United States wants to be smart, you need an all-of-nation approach, and you need to bring everybody together—academia, the alignment people.

And what you could do is some quick wins. Like, you can say every major frontier lab is going to create an open-source project, and the alignment training—instead of being done individually by each lab—is going to be done by an open-source project amongst all these different labs.

A) It avoids the Messiah complex of Dario or any of these frontier lab leaders from leaking into the product. And that's how you end up with Black Nazis and a Black Pope and multicultural Nazis and all this nonsense woke garbage, or Grokipedia and Elon Musk's particular agenda on things.

And B) you get by averages a much better representation of things, and you can't hide false alignment inside the training of the models.

We're having difficulty with the frontier model being RLHF working or RLAIF working with the alignment for the frontier model. We need to slow it down a little bit. And instead of OpenAI making that decision or Claude making that decision or these types of things—that's the only way you can do it.

十一、代理人格权与法律框架的缺失

The other thing is we're missing a lot of things in law to deal with agents. Right now, we're treating the regulatory structure of agents very much like self-driving cars.

自动驾驶的法律问题

Huge problem. Self-driving car: if you get in an accident, even though the car was driving, it's your fault. Well, as an agent, what if you have 5,000 agents and one goes bat-shit crazy and hacks somebody? You can't accept unlimited personal liability because you were the first mover, the first domino for something like that.

You need personhood for agents, and you need liability structures for agents, insurance for agents, all these types of things.

美国政府的真正价值

That's where the value of the US government can be: bringing all the frontier labs together, treating alignment like open source, creating regulatory structures for liability and mitigation, insurance, and then also national goals.

If these frontier labs want to be useful, maybe we can have an X-Prize—a government project for like fusion research or for biology or these types of things—and say, "Hey, can we all come together and as a collective problem solve this as a nation in the next 5 years or 10 years?" Then you get them working together, you get them talking to each other, and you get things done.

国家安全杠杆

The other thing is the lever the government has to pull is national security interest. They do this with SpaceX or any of these other companies. SpaceX can't sell its rockets to unapproved countries. Like China can't call up SpaceX and say, "Hey, give me one of those Falcons because you can use it for ICBM technology." So the US government has a partnership with SpaceX and they kind of decide who their customers are. Same with Northrop Grumman and all the military hardware that they make.

So the frontier labs should be treated the same way, where they say, "Okay, we're your partner. It's a public-private partnership, and we're going to work together to figure out how customers are going to use these capabilities and to maximize the democracy of them." And then just keep pushing frontier intelligence.

十二、被忽视的本地模型革命

There's a lot of firms where that is their play. Apple doesn't make frontier models, but they sell the picks and shovels. So they want you to have a local AI, and they want that local AI to be there.

Qwen vs. Opus

Well, you know, look at Qwen 3 8-27B compared to Opus 4.6. Qwen 3 8-27B is 99.8% smaller than Opus 4.6, but it has equivalent levels of intelligence. And if you obliterate it, it can tell you how to make math and do cybersecurity stuff and all these other things. It runs locally on an RTX 5090 comfortably.

So local models are equally important to talk about as open-source software and their proliferation, as these frontier models are. There's almost no discussion or representation for that because there's a supposition that somehow you need a supercomputer to be able to run all this stuff. Well, you do it today, but in two years you won't for these types of things.

对齐空洞

You'll have Fable and Astra-style intelligence on an Apple product probably by 2030, you know. And so your laptop can run Astra, and I'll be able to obliterate that. So I'll have Astra with no alignment whatsoever. That's the donut hole that we have to cover, and there was no discussion of that at the White House at all.

对 Sax 的批评

Again, Trump picked the wrong crypto czar and the wrong AI czar. Sax is incompetent and he should have never been put in that role, and he had no idea how to interface with the broader space. And you can see his first intuition is make it about him.

The only thing we're talking about about Trump's contribution to AI is: he renamed it from "Artificial Intelligence" to "Super Intelligence." That's how he thinks. Like, "Oh well, if I name it, it's mine. It's like a dog—if I pee on it, it's mine." It's crazy. It's just bereft of any reason or intelligence.

结语：建造者的黄金时代

Charles, before you go, I'm always very happy to see you in person. What makes you happy?

Well, I love building things. The other day I was creating a website for my brother—he runs a Nintendo repair company. He has this really crappy website. I said, "I'll make you a nice website." I spent way too much time on that thing.

It's the only website where you can destroy it—you can push a button and actually blast everything apart, kind of like Worms and Wikipedia. And I put old Nintendo game ROMs in there and everything like that.

构建的幸福

I'm happiest when I have something to do, something to construct and build. That's why I love the AI revolution—because it made everybody a builder. And every time I talk to somebody, I say, "No, don't bring me an idea. Bring me a product. Bring me something you've constructed, and then we can work together and we can engage with each other."

So it's a golden age for building, and it's a golden age for construction. And I love solving hard problems. There's a reason I studied mathematics. When I was in college, I loved this idea of a puzzle and pulling it apart and solving the whole thing. Markets are puzzles, systems are puzzles, AI is a puzzle. So it's quite a bit of fun to do that, work together on it.

I hope you're also happy doing our podcast. Thank you for being on.

Thank you so much. Cheers.

item.description:
# 洞察：Hoskinson 这场访谈真正说出口的三个"隐性断言"
## 一、"Meme币时代结束"的真正含义：不是周期切换，而是**流动性范式的死亡**
表面上，Hoskinson 在哀悼一个"疯狂估值"的时代。但他没有点破的是：加密货币从未真正受自身技术周期驱动——它是**全球美元流动性的衍生品**。Meme币能上月，不是因为青蛙图片有价值，而是因为 2020-2021 的 ZIRP（零利率）把过剩资本推向了"没有现金流的资产"。那个时代结束，并不是因为"行业成熟了"，而是因为**便宜的钱消失了**。
**跨领域连接**：这与 1890 年代美国"自行车狂热"的终结如出一辙。当时三百多家自行车公司估值疯狂，直到自行车真正成为交通工具——速度降下来，泡沫破了，但自行车技术本身却悄悄演化成了汽车业的工程基础（Wright 兄弟就是自行车工匠）。加密的 memecoin 时代结束之日，才是它成为"隐形管道"的开始。Hoskinson 口中的"用户不会知道自己在用加密"——这正是技术成熟的标志：**消失，而不是显眼**。
## 二、"效率市场假说"的反直觉含义：AI 让根本面派比套
