item.title: [Alan Chen加州生活号] AI股还要跌多深？财报前，我们如何加仓、对冲、留后手
item.dc:creator: Alan Chen加州生活号
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反常识的观察：这波下跌的"受害者结构"揭示了AI叙事的真正脆弱点

视频里提到"VIX在14-15的低位、财报季前、中期选举前"——这三件事放在一起，构成了一个心理学上的"安全幻觉三角"。真正值得警惕的不是AI基本面，而是市场在高度集中赌注的同时集体购买了"低价保险"。这与2007年次贷危机前"CDS利差异常收窄"的结构惊人相似：不是风险消失了，而是风险的定价失灵了。

更出人意料的是：Alan反复强调"Hedge是运营成本，不是利润点"——这句话看似理财常识，但它其实揭示了一个认知层级的分水岭。大多数散户把对冲视为"预测工具"（赌对了赚钱），而机构把对冲视为"摩擦成本"（像电费一样）。能否接受"花钱买确定性"而非"花钱买方向"，决定了你在这种结构性波动中会被震出还是能加仓。

二、跨领域连接：Vera AI基金爆仓 × 工业革命中的"信徒筛选机制"

视频里一笔带过的"Vera AI基金在周五爆仓"是个被低估的信号。回看历史，1840年代英国铁路泡沫中，第一批爆掉的不是铁路公司本身，而是用铁路股做抵押的高杠杆投机基金。真正的产业革命从不被单一事件证伪，但依附于革命的金融结构却极度脆弱。

这就带来一个反直觉的推论：AI叙事越真实，杠杆产品的爆仓就越频繁。原因在于——如果AI是伪命题，没人敢加杠杆；正因为所有人都相信它是真的，杠杆才能堆得这么高。所以每一次"AI基金爆仓"的新闻，恰恰是AI真实性的反向证据，而非证伪。

这与科学哲学中Lakatos的"研究纲领"理论形成有趣映射：一个强大的研究纲领的边缘假设可以不断被证伪，但硬核假设反而更稳固。AI的硬核假设（Token消耗、Agent流量、算力需求）仍在25倍/50倍的指数增长，被证伪的只是周边的估值透镜。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Alan没点破的"马斯克-黄仁勋耦合"

视频里有个一闪而过的洞察："如果你认为老马是傻子，那他现在做的事就是蠢的"——Alan用这个作为worldview的分水岭。但这里有个更深的系统性结构他没有展开：

马斯克的xAI、OpenAI的Stargate、Meta的超算集群、谷歌TPU扩张——这四条路径都把Nvidia 17.7倍PE的估值"锚定"在了一个博弈均衡上。只要四家中有一家不敢停，其他三家就不敢停。这是经典的军备竞赛纳什均衡——每个玩家单独退出都是亏的，集体退出又无法协调。

所以市场现在真正在定价的，不是"AI是否有需求"，而是"这个纳什均衡何时破裂"。而历史上这种均衡的破裂点，往往不是技术失败，而是某个玩家的现金流断裂（这就是Alan反复提到"Coreweave的债务不要忽视"的深层原因——它可能是均衡的第一个薄弱节点）。

真正该追踪的不是QQQ的50日均线，而是数据中心公司的债务利率曲线。 当CoreWeave、Oracle等"算力租赁层"的融资成本超过某个阈值时，纳什均衡才会出现第一道裂缝——而那时QQQ的技术支撑位将毫无意义。

一个送给你的"啊哈时刻"：在工业革命中，蒸汽机不会死，但卖铲子给矿工的高利贷会死；AI不会死，但给算力租赁商放贷的结构性产品可能先死。看懂这一层，就能理解为什么Alan加仓的是"高质量"而不是"便宜"——因为便宜的那些，可能正是债务链上的脆弱节点。

item.description:
## 一、最反常识的观察：这波下跌的"受害者结构"揭示了AI叙事的真正脆弱点
视频里提到"VIX在14-15的低位、财报季前、中期选举前"——这三件事放在一起，构成了一个**心理学上的"安全幻觉三角"**。真正值得警惕的不是AI基本面，而是**市场在高度集中赌注的同时集体购买了"低价保险"**。这与2007年次贷危机前"CDS利差异常收窄"的结构惊人相似：**不是风险消失了，而是风险的定价失灵了**。
更出人意料的是：Alan反复强调"Hedge是运营成本，不是利润点"——这句话看似理财常识，但它其实揭示了一个**认知层级的分水岭**。大多数散户把对冲视为"预测工具"（赌对了赚钱），而机构把对冲视为"摩擦成本"（像电费一样）。能否接受"花钱买确定性"而非"花钱买方向"，决定了你在这种结构性波动中会被震出还是能加仓。
## 二、跨领域连接：Vera AI基金爆仓 × 工业革命中的"信徒筛选机制"
视频里一笔带过的"Vera AI基金在周五爆仓"是个被低估的信号。回看历史，**1840年代英国铁路泡沫**中，第一批爆掉的不是铁路公司本身，而是**用铁路股做抵押的高杠杆投机基金**。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Jensen Huang on growing up in Taiwan | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外的观察：那把刀，才是黄仁勋真正的"第一款芯片"

大多数人读这段访谈，会看到"温情"、"乡愁"、"台湾人情味"。但真正值得驻足的，是他五岁时那把贴着脸颊划过的厨刀——以及他本应对夜市产生终生恐惧的那一刻，他却说："我从那以后更爱夜市了。"

这不是一个被创伤塑造的人。这是一个在创伤现场完成情绪重写的人。

黄仁勋没有把那把刀记成"刀"，他记成了"去夜市的理由"。一个五岁孩子，在血还没干的时候，就已经悄悄完成了一次语义重标注（semantic re-labeling）——把疼痛归档到"归属感"的目录下，而不是"威胁"的目录下。

这与他后来三十年如一日押注 CUDA 的方式在底层算法上是同一个： - 别人看到的是失败的季度、崩塌的股价、嘲讽的分析师； - 他把这些重标注成"证据——我们还没到"。

他不是乐观主义者。他是一个天生的损失函数定义者。 他能决定什么算"坏事"。

二、跨领域连接：夜市经济学 × 芯片堆栈的拓扑同构

注意他讲食物的方式——他不是在讲一道菜，他是在讲一个层级结构：

"外面是一点鱼糕……里面是猪肉……那个嚼劲是鱼糕给的……"

他下意识地在解剖 stack。鱼糕是外壳、肉是内核、嚼劲是接口层。这跟他讲 GPU 架构时的口吻完全是同一个人：底层 CUDA、中层 cuDNN、上层框架、再上层应用——每一层都"给另一层一点什么"。

更有意思的是他对夜市摊主的描述：

"他们一天的利润大概只有一毛钱……他们把全部利润都给了我。"

这是一个关于极薄利润率下的慷慨的观察。而 Nvidia 作为公司，恰恰是反向的同一个结构——极高利润率下的慷慨：疯狂把钱砸进研究者、开源生态、免费教程、给学术界的 GPU。摊主的一毛钱和 Nvidia 的几百亿美金，在动作上是同构的：都是用超出理性经济学的方式送出东西，为的是建立一个你无法用交易买到的关系网络。

他五岁时在摊位边收到的那颗猪肉肠，可能是他商业哲学的第一堂课——只是他当时不知道，摊主也不知道。

三、更深一层：他为什么反复讲"手艺"？

这段里他提到 Jiro Dreams of Sushi，然后说"夜市里有一堆 Jiro"。

这句话被访谈的温情氛围掩盖了，但它其实很反主流。

硅谷文化推崇的是什么？scale（规模化）、disruption（颠覆）、10x（十倍好）。一个一辈子做同一碗面的人，在硅谷叙事里是失败者——没有扩张、没有退出、没有估值。

但黄仁勋把他们和 Jiro 并列，而且他这辈子最骄傲的事之一，是他本人也做了三十年同一件事：造加速计算的芯片。他拒绝横向扩张进消费电子、拒绝做手机、拒绝做自动驾驶整车——他就守着那一个摊位，熬那一锅汤。

夜市摊主是他的镜像，不是他的乡愁。 他回去看的不是童年，是一种被硅谷主流叙事排挤掉的时间观：复利不是来自扩张，是来自在同一个点上重复到可笑的程度。

这也解释了一个你可能没留意的细节——他讲每一道菜时都在笑，但他没有一次说"我想念"。他不是在怀旧。他是在反复确认一个仍在运行的操作系统。

📝 转录文本

童年的夜市与那把刀

My mom and dad loved that. And we would come to the night market. And that's kind of, you know, when we go out to dinner, that's the definition of going out to eat. You don't go to a restaurant, you know, we didn't have money like that. And so, we just go to night market. You sit at these tables.

And I I was looking for a restroom, so I wandered off. And I walked up to this guy, this cook, and I was about to ask him, you know, if there was a restroom somewhere. And he was cleaning his knife, and my my face was right next to his knife. Cut me right through right across my face. I was five. I was I was fine. So, my dad picked me up, ran me to the hospital.

[sighs]

I always loved the night market after that.

[laughter]

It was always had a fun memory.

Yeah, sometimes the pain solidifies the happiness right?

Yeah. It's just, you know, it was a reason why I went. The food was so good. I loved the place.

仍是那个孩子——台湾式的慷慨

You still You still feel like that kid to some degree?

Yeah. I mean, you could, you know, I loved everything. I loved all the people. Everybody's working hard for a living, and they're working so hard, and they still want to share a little something with you, you know? They don't have that much money. Their profit margin in that day must be a dime each, you know? They gave me all their profit. Right?

Right.

Just to be kind. It's the Taiwanese way. And it's nice to watch, you know, these people their craft.

Mhm.

And many of them have been doing it for years. That's saying I mean, you know, there's a famous documentary, Jiro Dreams of Sushi, but there's a bunch of Jiros over there.

Exactly.

They've been doing the same meal at the night market.

一桌子的回忆：那些永远记得的味道

That pork sausage was so good.

[laughter]

That was so good. And that bun was good.

Yeah, that bun was good.

Yeah. The fried potato balls.

Mhm. Amazing. I don't know how they do it.

And that fluffy rice cake with the brown sugar on top.

If somebody just handed you it and it turned out to be magic.

And that noodle.

Oh, yeah.

Oh, come on. That noodle. That That hot sauce.

Uh-huh.

[laughter]

That ball with that white ball.

Mhm.

It's It's a little bit of a fish cake on the outside and since pork on the inside. Man, oh man.

Yeah, the layers. You're right. It's a little bit of fish cake.

Yeah. That's gives it that little chew chew.

Yeah.

[laughter]

We ate like 10 things. That noodle was good. That was my first time with that noodle. Wow.

Mhm.

Dang.

## 一、意外的观察：那把刀，才是黄仁勋真正的"第一款芯片"
大多数人读这段访谈，会看到"温情"、"乡愁"、"台湾人情味"。但真正值得驻足的，是他五岁时那把贴着脸颊划过的厨刀——以及他**本应**对夜市产生终生恐惧的那一刻，他却说："我从那以后更爱夜市了。"
这不是一个被创伤塑造的人。这是一个**在创伤现场完成情绪重写**的人。
黄仁勋没有把那把刀记成"刀"，他记成了"去夜市的理由"。一个五岁孩子，在血还没干的时候，就已经悄悄完成了一次语义重标注（semantic re-labeling）——把疼痛归档到"归属感"的目录下，而不是"威胁"的目录下。
这与他后来三十年如一日押注 CUDA 的方式**在底层算法上是同一个**： - 别人看到的是失败的季度、崩塌的股价、嘲讽的分析师； - 他把这些重标注成"证据——我们还没到"。
**他不是乐观主义者。他是一个天生的损失函数定义者。** 他能决定什么算"坏事"。
---
## 二、跨领域连接：夜市经济学 × 芯片堆栈的拓扑同构
注意他讲食物的方式——他不是在讲一道菜，他是在讲一个**层级结构**：
> "外面是一点鱼糕……里

item.title: [Lex Clips] Jensen Huang on China's AI labs | Lex Fridman in Taiwan
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、刀疤里的"反向因果"：疼痛不是记忆的敌人，而是情感的放大器

黄仁勋五岁时在夜市被厨师的刀划破脸，但他后来说："我总是喜欢夜市之后。"——这是整段对话里最反直觉的一句。

常识告诉我们，创伤会让人回避场所。但他的大脑做了相反的运算：把"疼痛 + 父亲抱起他狂奔"的强烈生理激活，和"食物香气 + 母亲温度 + 夜市人声"共同编码成同一段记忆。神经科学上，这叫做杏仁核标记的情景整合——高唤醒事件会把周围的所有感官细节一起"焊死"。

这件事其实揭示了黄仁勋的一种底层操作系统：他天然把"痛苦与价值"绑定存储，而不是分离存储。这或许能解释为什么 NVIDIA 在 CUDA 上烧了十几年没人用、2008 年股价崩掉八成的时候他没走——对他来说，疼痛不是信号去离开，而是信号去确认"这里值得"。

二、"算力饥饿"的悖论：中国 AI 公司正在被 GPU 短缺"喂养"

黄仁勋对中国 AI 公司（MiniMax、Unitree 等）的描述里，藏着一个 NVIDIA CEO 几乎不该说的话——"他们算力严重匮乏……但正是这个逼他们搞出了那些难以置信的、极其高效的架构。"

这是卖铲人在公开承认：铲子不够用的矿工，挖得反而更深。

这里有个跨领域的类比： - 日本汽车工业在 1970 年代石油危机下的燃油限制里，被迫发明了精益生产和小排量高效引擎，二十年后反杀底特律； - 苏联在冷战期间的计算机硬件落后，逼出了世界顶级的算法数学家（柯尔莫哥洛夫学派）； - 印度航天用美国项目十分之一的预算把探测器送到了火星。

规律非常清晰：资源丰裕催生工程惯性，资源稀缺催生架构创新。黄仁勋话里真正的潜台词可能是——如果出口管制继续，未来十年最优雅的 AI 架构可能都带着中文注释，而 NVIDIA 的"硬件暴力美学"反而会变成一种战略脆弱性。

三、夜市与数据中心是同一种拓扑结构

这是最容易被忽略的一层：Lex 问他是否"还感觉像那个孩子"，黄仁勋回答时谈的不是童年，而是——夜市摊主的利润率只有一毛钱，却把全部利润都给了他。

然后他紧接着飞到杭州看机器人、去上海见 AI 公司，用的是同一个词："humility"（谦卑）。

把这两个场景叠起来看，你会发现黄仁勋判断一个生态健康与否的真正指标，不是技术、不是估值、不是算力，而是从业者的"低边际利润 + 高分享意愿"的组合。夜市小贩和 Unitree 工程师，在他的识别系统里属于同一类人。

这暗示了一个反主流的商业哲学：最值得下注的生态，是那些"又穷又慷慨"的生态——因为穷意味着他们还没学会贪婪，慷慨意味着他们的知识流动摩擦系数低，而这两者加起来就是真正的复合增长条件。硅谷正在失去第一个，台北夜市从来没失去过第二个，而杭州的机器人圈子，可能两个都还有。

这也许能解释，为什么全世界最有权力的半导体 CEO，愿意飞到他本可以用 Zoom 搞定的地方——他在为自己的下一个十年，采样生态系统的"羞怯度"。

📝 转录文本

夜市与那道刀疤

That oyster pancake. — Oh yeah, yeah. Perfect. — Wow. Perfect. Wow. — That's the reason it's famous.

My mom and dad love that. And we would come to the night market. And that's kind of, you know, when we go out to dinner, that's the definition of going to — you don't go to one restaurant, you know, we didn't have money like that. And so we just go to night market. We sit at these tables.

And I [sighs] was looking for a restroom, so wandered off. And I walked up to this guy, this cook. And I was about to ask him, you know, if there was a restroom somewhere. And he was cleaning his knife. And my face was right next to his knife. Cut me right through — right across my face. I was five. I was almost five.

So my dad picked me up, ran me to the hospital. I always loved the night market after that. — [laughter] — I always had a fun memory. — Yeah, sometimes the pain solidifies the happiness, right? — Yeah. Yes, you know, it was the reason why I went. The food was so good. I love the place.

台湾人的方式

— Do you still — do you still feel like that kid to some degree? — Yeah. I mean, you could, you know, I loved everything. I loved all the people. Everybody's working hard for a living. And they're working so hard, and they still want to share a little something with you, you know? They don't have that much money. Their profit margin on that thing must be a dime each, you know? They gave me all their profit. Right? — Right. — Just to be kind. It's the Taiwanese way. And it's nice to watch, you know, these people — their craft. — Mhm. And many of them have been doing it for years. That's saying — I mean, you know, there's a famous documentary Jiro Dreams of Sushi, but there's a bunch of Jiros over there. — Exactly. — They've been doing the same meal in the night market.

一桌子的记忆

— Dang. That pork sausage was so good. — [laughter] — That was so good. And that bun was good. — Yeah, that bun was good. — Yeah. The fried potato balls. — Mhm. Amazing. I don't know how they do it. — And that fluffy rice cake with the brown sugar on top. — Somebody just handed a Jiro and it turned out [laughter] to be magic. — And that noodle. — Oh, yeah. — Oh, come on. That noodle. The hot sauce. — Uh-huh. — [laughter] — That ball with the white ball. — Mhm. — It's a little bit of a fish cake on the outside and since pork on the inside. Man, oh man. — Yeah, the layers. You're right. It's a little bit of fish cake. — Yeah. That's — gives it that little Q Q. — Yeah. — [laughter] — We ate like 10 things. — That noodle was good. — That was my first time with that noodle. — Wow. — Mhm. Dang.

上海、杭州与"算力饥饿"

— Did you go to Shanghai? — Yeah, for some of the MiniMax, some of the AI companies. — Okay, yeah. — Boy, those companies are good. And then went to Hangzhou for Unitree. And those — the robotics folks — full of humility. There's a lot of robotics companies.

And you know what all the AI companies are saying? They're compute starved. — Yeah. — More compute. — Yeah, but somehow — somehow, you know, while they're compute starved, it forces them to come up with these incredible architectures. They're so efficient. — Yeah. Yeah, constraints is the kind of mother of invention. — Right. — Scarcity. — Yeah. They're severely, severely constrained. And they're still — they're getting funded. They're still, right? — Mhm. Yeah. Many IPOs. — Yeah. They're still getting it done. I guess some of them are good. — [laughter]

收尾

— All right, Jesse. Thank you for an experience of a lifetime. That was — that was delicious. — Thank you. That was fun. That was incredible. — Was awesome. — All right, we got the data box. — Still going.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Jensen Huang reflects on huge crowds greeting him in Taiwan | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

当"芯片之神"递出便当：一场被忽略的系统性信号

大多数人看到黄仁勋在台湾给记者分发食物时，关注的是"亲民"或"接地气"。但这里藏着一个真正值得玩味的系统性现象：全球最昂贵算力的掌舵人，正在用最低带宽的物理动作——递便当——完成他最高带宽的信息广播。这不是作秀，这是一种"反摩尔定律"的沟通策略。当芯片越来越快、信号越来越稀薄时，领导力的稀缺品反而是"面对面的热量"。你能用GPU复制一切，唯独不能复制一个CEO弯腰递食物的那三秒钟。

冷气机旁的隐藏隐喻：供应链的本质不是效率，是"愿意站在热气里"

视频里有一个几乎被人忽略的瞬间——众人发现冰箱旁边有一股凉气，于是停下脚步享受那片刻清凉。这个画面是整个台湾科技生态的完美缩影：全世界都来这里"蹭凉"，但真正托起这个生态的人，是17年如一日站在热气里的那位记者、那位工程师、那位半导体操作员。黄仁勋把这件事说破了——"capacity for generosity"加上"super hard work"。跨领域连接一下：这其实和京都百年老铺、瑞士钟表山谷、意大利小提琴作坊是同一种结构——不是技术护城河，是"愿意长期不舒服"的文化护城河。技术可以迁移，意愿不能。所以台积电搬到亚利桑那遇到的真正阻力，从来不是设备，是那股"甘愿站在热气里"的意愿密度。

真正令人意外的观察：欢呼声是"滞后指标"，不是"同步指标"

视频里黄仁勋说了一句很容易被略过的话——"all that cheer is after many, many hours of doing another booth tour"。这句话里埋着一个反直觉的系统性真相：公众的热情从来不是对"当下魅力"的反应，而是对"过去持续性"的滞后计价。人们以为自己在为黄仁勋的现场气场欢呼，其实是在为他过去30年的"没有停下来"结账。这和股市估值、婚姻信任、学术声誉是同一种机制——都是delayed compounding被瞬间兑现。更有趣的"啊哈时刻"是：那几千人在街角爆发的尖叫，在数学结构上，和NVIDIA股价曲线从2016年到今天的指数段，是同一条曲线的两种显现方式——一个在K线图上，一个在人群的声波里。市场和人群，最终用同一种语言给"长期主义"定价。

📝 转录文本

幕后花絮：Jensen 亲自给记者递食物

Jensen is literally feeding the press.

Okay. So, what do you guys think? Just handing out food to the press. It's awesome. It's hot out here. It's dinner time. They're working around the clock. They need love, too. Yeah, Lex Fridman. OH, LEX FRIDMAN. He just met the goat. The OG. [laughter] Lex Fridman. Look at that. Such a sweetheart. Cheers.

欢呼背后：几个小时的 booth tour

What people need to realize, all that cheer is after many, many hours of doing another booth tour today.

Did you see what happened today? I I heard it got nuts. There were several thousand people were lined up. I came around the corner, I looked down, and my mind just went, I have no idea what to do. I have no idea what to do. It blew my mind. And then we're all screaming and cheering and It's all love. Oh, man, it's incredible.

台湾生态的底层：慷慨与苦干

Their capacity, their capacity for generosity and kindness and be helpful to other people. It is the reason why this island, all these companies here, are at the center of the ecosystem. It's because of that fundamental generosity and the capacity to help other people. It's the reason why they're the supply chain for the world. And it's from that.

Willingness to work very hard. Super hard. Super hard. It's the combination of the two. Super hard.

冷气机旁的小插曲

Lex, I don't know what's going on here, but there's air conditioning. This spot in Taiwan,

there is air conditioning. There's a There's a specific spot in this place in time. Right here. Right here. The universe just says you need a little break. How long you've been working at video? 17 years. 17 years, there we go. Look at this. He's taking selfies. Yeah, that's right. Something is happening right here. This all the time one is hot. It's true. It's right here. This is the truth. This is that's the cool air Is that I think it's the cool air from there. Oh, from the refrigerator. Is it because of that? Yeah, I'll stand here. This is literally [laughter] air conditioner. It's a refrigerator.

结尾：一口酱汁的温度

[music] What's that? It's good. It's not [music] The The sauce makes it. With a bit of that corn sauce amazing. [music] Hey, thank you. Thank you.

item.title: [Lex Clips] The best street food in Taiwan with Jensen Huang | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、整条视频里被食物盖过去的那句话

Jensen 在吞下蚵仔煎的间隙说了一句被完全忽略的话："我们要盖一栋 4000 人的楼，几乎是你刚才去的那栋的复制品。"

这句话用蚵仔煎的油香做了掩护，但它才是整段视频里真正的新闻。请注意他的用词——不是"更大的"、不是"升级版"，而是 "almost a replica"。NVIDIA 的组织扩张哲学与它自己的 GPU 架构是同构的：GPU 之所以能战胜 CPU，不是因为单个核心更强，而是因为把同一个计算单元克隆上万次，让并行吞噬一切。Jensen 现在把这套哲学用在了组织上——不升级，而是复制粘贴整栋楼。

这里的隐藏启示是：当一家公司开始用自家产品的底层逻辑来复制自己的组织时，它已经不只是在卖产品，而是在把自己变成产品的一个巨型实例。

二、夜市摊贩的回归 = NVIDIA 在供应链里的镜像位置

Lex 轻描淡写地说了一句："这些摊贩很多是因为 Jensen 两天前来过才回来的。" 这是一句被当作花絮的台词，但你把它翻译一下就会毛骨悚然——摊贩不是在摆摊，他们在等待下一次信号脉冲。他们形成了一个围绕 Jensen 的"小型供应生态"，用自己的时间和库存去押注他的出现概率。

而这恰好就是台积电、广达、鸿海、SK 海力士、三星和整个全球 AI 基建产业现在在做的事情——他们都在等 Jensen 的下一次信号，调整产能、备货、人力。士林夜市只是把这个全球图景微缩成了一个夜市街区。

跨领域的连接在这里浮现：夜市经济和 AI 基础设施经济在底层是同一种"注意力—生产"的耦合系统。Jensen 的身体在哪里，产能就在哪里重新分配。他不是消费者，他是信号源。

三、"People tried to explain it to me. Not even close."

Jensen 对夜市体验说的这句话，是整段视频里最哲学的句子，而且他本人没意识到自己在说什么。

"有人试图跟我解释，但差得远了。" ——这正是 AI 从业者面对外行的所有困境的根源。你没法用 PPT 把 ChatGPT 解释给没用过的人，就像你没法用文字把烤番薯爆开的瞬间描述给没咬过的人。体验先于理解，且无法被压缩成信息。

这解释了一个意外的事实：Jensen 做芯片战略决策的方式，和他吃夜市的方式是一样的——不是读报告，而是亲身去咬一口。他亲自跑客户、亲自试产品、亲自站在产线旁。他知道有些信息只能通过身体传递，而不是通过幻灯片。整个硅谷的 CEO 里，这种"用身体做决策"的习惯几乎绝迹了，而这可能才是 NVIDIA 真正的护城河——决策者还有舌头、牙齿和胃。

四、顺便一个让人不舒服的观察

视频里有个瞬间：摊主主动塞给他们一杯菠萝番石榴汁，Lex 还天真地说："They wanted you to try something new. Expand the market."

他们没意识到——他们自己在那一刻就是产品发布渠道。摊主在用全球最顶级的 KOL 做新品种水果的 A/B test。整个 YouTube 片段，从摊贩的角度看，是一次完美执行的开发者关系运营（DevRel）。这种能力不是硅谷教给台湾的，是台湾夜市经济在三十年前就在做的。NVIDIA 的开发者生态做得好，不是因为学了 Apple，而是因为 Jensen 的童年和味觉就浸泡在这种"让客户先尝一口再说"的本能里。

📝 转录文本

开场：忍不住要来夜市

Couldn't help it. Had to. Jensen loves the night market way too much not to do it.

This is so good. Oh, they love Jensen. This is incredible. All right, I officially can't wait to eat this. This is nuts. Don't lose the white kid.

西瓜 / 神秘球

Watermelon. It's like hamburger.

item.description:
## 一、整条视频里被食物盖过去的那句话
Jensen 在吞下蚵仔煎的间隙说了一句被完全忽略的话：**"我们要盖一栋 4000 人的楼，几乎是你刚才去的那栋的复制品。"**
这句话用蚵仔煎的油香做了掩护，但它才是整段视频里**真正的新闻**。请注意他的用词——不是"更大的"、不是"升级版"，而是 **"almost a replica"**。NVIDIA 的组织扩张哲学与它自己的 GPU 架构是**同构的**：GPU 之所以能战胜 CPU，不是因为单个核心更强，而是因为把**同一个计算单元克隆上万次**，让并行吞噬一切。Jensen 现在把这套哲学用在了组织上——不升级，而是**复制粘贴整栋楼**。
这里的隐藏启示是：当一家公司开始用自家产品的底层逻辑来复制自己的组织时，它已经不只是在卖产品，而是在**把自己变成产品的一个巨型实例**。
## 二、夜市摊贩的回归 = NVIDIA 在供应链里的镜像位置
Lex 轻描淡写地说了一句："这些摊贩很多是因为 Jensen 两天前来过才回来的。" 这是一句被当作花絮的台词，但你把它翻译一下就会毛骨悚然——**摊贩不是在摆摊，他们在等待

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"善意不是零和游戏"——黄仁勋无意间揭示了半导体产业的拓扑秘密

黄仁勋说"goodwill is not a zero-sum game, it's not limited by physics"，这句话看似鸡汤，但如果你把它放回半导体产业的物理语境里看，会发现一个令人不寒而栗的对称性：芯片产业本身恰恰是被物理定律所限制的——摩尔定律的终结、光刻的衍射极限、散热的热力学墙。而黄仁勋能从一个物理极限领域的掌门人口中说出"善意不受物理约束"，这不是哲学宣言，而是他找到的那条绕过物理极限的捷径。

当硅本身越来越难突破时，Nvidia 的护城河早已不在晶体管里，而在CUDA 生态、开发者友谊、客户信任——这些反熵的社会结构。他本能地意识到：当硬件触顶，软关系就成了唯一还能指数增长的变量。所以他谈的不是道德，是一种被逼出来的新物理学。

二、出口管制争论里，藏着一个"量子力学式"的悖论

黄仁勋对出口管制的论述表面是经济学，但其底层逻辑与量子观察者效应惊人地同构：你观察（限制）一个系统的那一刻，你就改变了它的状态。

美国限制中国获得芯片——这个动作本身催生了华为昇腾、寒武纪、中芯国际的加速进化。换句话说，禁运不是在"冻结"对手，而是在激发对手——这和试图通过观测来定住一个粒子，却把它弹到了另一个本征态，是同一回事。

更出人意料的跨领域连接：这与生物学里的抗生素滥用悖论完全同构。你以为在消灭细菌，实际上你在筛选超级细菌。你以为出口管制在削弱对手，实际上你在为对手的国产替代链路清场——把所有竞争者（Nvidia）赶出赛道，让中国本土玩家独占一个 14 亿人的测试市场。黄仁勋嘴上没说，但他比谁都清楚这个"抗生素悖论"。

三、"英语是真正的护城河"——这是整段访谈里最被低估的一句话

黄仁勋轻描淡写地提到："the vast majority of the world responds to English"，然后把它当成一个"顺带的优势"。但这其实是整个美国 AI 霸权最深的那一层地基，深到连他自己都几乎没意识到自己在说什么。

想想看： - Transformer 架构的训练语料 70%+ 是英语。 - GitHub 代码注释、API 文档、Stack Overflow 的默认语言是英语。 - 论文、arXiv、会议 的通用语是英语。 - 提示词工程（prompt engineering） 本质上是用英语思维来操控模型。

这意味着：AI 模型天然"更懂"英语使用者的意图，不是因为模型偏见，而是因为模型的"潜意识"就是英文的。当一个中文使用者在用中文 prompt 时，他是在翻译后的二阶空间里操作。

跨领域连接：这完全复刻了 19 世纪大英帝国的"海图垄断"。英国人并不比别人更会航海，但全世界的航线图、港口深度图、潮汐表都是英文的，所以无论你是哪国船长，你一打开地图，就已经在"英国的世界观"里航行了。今天的 AI 模型，就是 21 世纪的海图。

真正的意外在这里：黄仁勋自己是台裔美国人、母语不是英语，但他运营着全球最依赖英语生态的公司。他深知这个优势，却也隐隐知道——如果中文大模型（DeepSeek、通义、Kimi）能把"中文母语的 AI 本能"做到位，这个三百年的海图垄断第一次有可能被改写。这才是他真正在意的"flywheel"脆弱性，比出口管制重要一万倍。

📝 转录文本

开场：关于责任与善意

[cheering]

Lex Fridman: Beatles in the 60s. Through all of that, maintaining humility. What a life, Jensen. Does that weight ever get heavy, that you have this responsibility, millions of people looking up to you?

Jensen Huang: It doesn't, you know, because I don't take it like that. You know, people have always been nice to me.

Lex: Even when you had nothing?

Jensen: Yeah. And I was always nice to other people. You know? And I was always polite. And I always wanted people to succeed. I wanted them to be happy. When I was going through school, I was always hoping that all the other kids would do well in school. And I was happy to share my homework with everybody. I like seeing other people succeed, even my colleagues in other companies.

Lex: It's a funny thing how the world works. If you just celebrate others and you want them to succeed, somehow you succeed.

Jensen: Well, for example, 43,000 employees at Nvidia want me to succeed. Literally. You know what I'm saying?

Lex: And you want each of them to succeed.

Jensen: Exactly.

Lex: And I mean, I've seen you. You want people at other companies to succeed. [snorts]

Jensen: And they want me to succeed.

Lex: And there's a ripple effect to the whole thing.

Jensen: Yeah. Exactly. There's that... You know, goodwill is not a zero-sum game. It's not limited by physics.

出口管制：两面论证

[clears throat]

Lex: Can you talk through your export controls view? You've had strong opinions that export controls is not the way America should win. Can you steel-man the case for that and against it?

Jensen: The case against it is simple. If there's something that is valuable, something that's useful, something that is a force multiplier — so, for example, rare earth is a force multiplier, computer technology is a force multiplier. You know, technology in general is a force multiplier. You could argue that knowledge is a force multiplier. And intellectual property is a force multiplier.

And so if we have assets like that, then depriving other people of it enhances our position. Deprives them of theirs.

Lex: It's a way to gain a competitive edge. By hoarding that particular resource.

Jensen: Right. Keep it out of the hands of others. And that's not completely untrue with respect to the physical things. Like for example, it is not untrue with respect to refined rare earth. It's not untrue when it relates to bullets, bombs. I think that's generally not untrue. To the extent that the opposition and other parties can therefore create their own, it is generally not untrue.

另一面：繁荣即安全

Jensen: The other side of the argument is that if our goal is to optimize for long-term national security, long-term domestic tranquility and harmony, then prosperity is the best way to do that.

The safest countries in the world are the richest countries. The reason why the United States is so powerful militarily is because we have extraordinary wealth. And that extraordinary wealth came along with extraordinary technology, and that technology and wealth becomes a flywheel. And that flywheel is ultimately what you're optimizing for.

So the question is: are you optimizing for someone else not having access to this technology, or are you optimizing for a flywheel? And I suggest that a more sophisticated long-term strategy is to optimize for a flywheel.

Flywheel 理论：技术与财富的正反馈

Jensen: In order to optimize for that flywheel, you have to have both simultaneously — technology leadership and wealth. That flywheel is really important.

This is no different than a lot of computing technologies and platform technologies. The concept of wealth is basically customer engagement and installed base, and that installed base and customer usage drives more consumption of your technology, which then drives more wealth, which allows you to scale your technology faster than anyone.

So this concept of flywheel — which comes along with technology leadership, economic leadership, which fuels technology leadership, which drives more economic leadership — and that flywheel's cog is what causes companies and countries to stay ahead.

That's what I would suggest: instead of finite things that are concrete and have no positive feedback system, I would advocate that the better strategy is to be quite extremely selective — extremely selective — about access to certain technologies. But aside from that, balance that with optimizing for that technology and economic flywheel. So there's a balance.

关键追问：这个 Flywheel 包含中国吗？

Lex: I think the question is: does America flourish if that flywheel includes China or doesn't include China? That's the open question for America and the open question for humanity.

There's a line that's crossed when two nations are competing — as you can even say geopolitically friends competing versus becoming enemies competing. And there's a line, and once you cross that line, you have the potential to destroy everybody's flywheel.

Jensen: That's right. I would say that we should do everything we can to avoid conflict. We should compete — that we can't do without. But we should do everything we can to avoid conflict.

And so the question is: if you have relationships that are competitive, there are strategies that cause that relationship to lead towards conflict, and there are strategies to avoid conflict.

相互依赖作为和平的锚

Lex: I think, to the degree there's interdependence — it's something you and I talked about — amongst, let's say, AI stacks. Everybody's using the same hardware, everyone's using the same software. Everybody's going to each other's universities, there's friendships, there's scientific collaborations. There's friendly competition amongst different companies, but nevertheless it really fundamentally is collaboration.

The more of that we have, the harder it is to actually divide the two different peoples in order to then have something like a global conflict.

Jensen: The harder it is to decouple, the harder it is to have conflict. And I agree with that.

AI 不是模型，而是一整个技术栈

Jensen: Now, one of the things that is helpful — just now the way you described it is absolutely right. In fact, AI is not a model. AI is a whole stack of technologies and they're all contributing to AI.

You can't have AI without energy. And we know that certain countries and certain regions have extraordinary leadership and capabilities in energy while others don't. And so if you keep going up and down that stack, you'll observe that depending on where you're talking about, leadership is happening in different places.

美国的真正优势：创新文化与英语平台

Lex: Jensen, as a proud American, I personally believe that America has the most innovative people. Like the craziest, wildest, out there, big, big moonshot ideas. I think America's on top of the world in doing that.

Jensen: Well, Nvidia is an American company.

Lex: Yeah.

Jensen: Anthropic, OpenAI, you know, Google. There's just so much overwhelming evidence that what you're saying is absolutely right. The compounded chemistry that leads to this innovation capability over time is overwhelming.

One of the overwhelming advantages that we have is that our flywheel is also the best. And the reason for that is because the vast majority of the world responds to English. And so if you're an American company and you build on an American tech stack using American standards, you're fairly deployable throughout the world. That's not true with China.

And so we have a global flywheel advantage. Technology without customers is useless.

Lex: Yeah, you have to use that advantage. Don't take for granted your advantage. There is a global power to English as a language. It's just the way that America's able to create an ecosystem that's used by everybody. That's a real advantage. So closing yourself off from the rest of the world for some sort of benefits you do get from isolationism — there's a real cost to that. You lose that advantage.

平衡的艺术：主权与平台覆盖

Jensen: Exactly. Which is exactly the reason why I believe that, on the one hand, we want to keep great technology to ourselves. On the other hand, we need that flywheel. We need exactly the sentence that you are applying just now — every single word of it.

And so we want to have as much platform reach as possible because it generates that flywheel, which generates the wealth, which generates our R&D capacity to continue to innovate.

Now, that flywheel is also really delicate. You could see flywheels — once it gets going, it becomes a bit of an exponential. And platform quickly seems like, overnight, after being built for a decade, two decades, in our case three decades, all of a sudden it reaches a tipping point and it's everywhere.

On the other hand, that flywheel can stop. And it could slow down very quickly.

So the question about export controls is just this balance. Every country has the right — for the technologies, the capabilities, the assets, the resources that they've created for the support of their national advantage — they have the right to decide how they want to use it. That's a sovereign right. That's a national right.

On the other hand, we also want to make sure that the national treasure of the United States — which the technology industry is part of — that national treasure has the largest possible flywheel, the largest possible platform reach, so that we can sustain that economic and technology leadership flywheel. So, that's the balance.

结语：人类共同点多于分歧

Lex: And at the end of the day, as we've been sharing a lot of food, I think we have to remember that all the humans all across the world have a lot more in common than we have as differences. And it's good to understand each other, to collaborate, to be friends with each other, to work together and compete as friends — versus dividing each other and making enemies of each other.

Jensen: And when you travel, you really get hit with that.

Lex: Especially when you hitchhike. [laughter]

Jensen: Especially when you hitchhike, you realize that so much.

Lex: Jensen, thank you so much for the delicious food. This is amazing. How was that?

Jensen: That was fun. How fun was that? And maybe some night market tonight as well.

Lex: Okay. Okay, I'm going to take you to a different one.

Jensen: Yeah. Even crazier. Even crazier. It's going to be incredible.

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] AI晶片專家：股市搖搖欲墜，台積電護城河還有幾年？Alex Lee【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：中国 AI 实验室的"GPU 禁运"可能是长期竞争优势而非劣势

Alex 轻描淡写地提到：中国实验室无法拿到最好的 GPU，但靠蒸馏（distillation）和算法优化，与前沿模型差距缩短到 3-5 个月。这里藏着一个被所有人忽略的系统性真相——约束是最被低估的创新催化剂。

这与 1970 年代日本汽车业的故事惊人相似：石油危机 + 美国市场的尺寸偏好让日本车厂被迫做小、做省、做精，结果是丰田精益生产模式反向殖民了全球制造业。中国实验室今天做的"参数-token 效率优化"，可能在 5 年后变成通用方法论——当美国实验室还在用"钞能力"堆算力时，中国实验室被迫学会了"烹饪的手艺"。有趣的是，Alex 作为 NVIDIA 2013 年的持仓者，这反而是他自己最大的做多逻辑的隐藏裂缝。他讲 TSMC 定价权时自信满满，但没意识到：定价权来自不可替代性，而不可替代性正在被约束性创新从外侧瓦解。

二、整个访谈的核心矛盾：Alex 说"AI 不能给你 alpha"，但 True North 的真正护城河恰恰是在偷偷积累 alpha

这里有个精妙的叙事结构——Alex 反复强调 "we never promise alpha"，但他真正暗埋的产品护城河叫 trader metadata：你每一笔交易、每一次情绪化的决策、每一个你不愿面对的亏损，都在 feed 一个只属于你的 trader persona。

这与 Spotify 的 "Discover Weekly" 是同一种心理锁定机制——不是算法多聪明，而是离开意味着放弃你多年沉淀的"自我画像"。再深一层，这个结构还和心理咨询的"交易日记"疗法同构：行为心理学 50 年前就发现，让赌徒把亏损写下来、面对数字，是对抗损失厌恶（loss aversion）最有效的工具。Alex 不是在造一个"更聪明的 AI"，他是在用机器完成人类从不愿对自己做的事——情绪化地面对历史证据。

最意外的点：真正的 moat 不在模型层（他明说"干不过 Anthropic"），不在执行层（谁都能接 Hyperliquid），而在用户羞耻感的客观化外包。这是一个比"量化"更贴近治疗的产品定位。

三、"核武器类比"背后的更深危险：AI 监管问题的本质不是技术，而是博弈论里的 "unraveling"

Alex 提到白宫 superintelligence 会议时类比核武器监管，但没说透的是：核武器的监管之所以勉强成立，是因为造一枚核弹需要巨大的物理资产（铀浓缩、离心机、测试场），这些东西无法藏在车库里。AI 不是——它可以在云端训练、可以通过开源权重扩散、可以在任何有 GPU 的国家复刻。

这意味着 AI 监管面临一个核不扩散条约从未面对过的问题：monitoring asymmetry（监测不对称）。借用博弈论里 Akerlof 的"柠檬市场"思路——当监管方无法区分"遵守方"和"违规方"时，守规矩的实验室会被劣币驱逐，最终所有人都 defect。这是 unraveling 均衡。

更令人意外的跨领域连接：Alex 自己构建 True North 的"信任层"（enclave、TEE、SOC 2 认证），竟然与 AI 全球治理面对的是同一个问题的两个尺度——都是在"无法直接验证内部状态"的前提下，试图通过可验证的外部签名构建信任。你信任银行是因为 FDIC，你信任 AI 代理需要的也许是某种"AI 版 FDIC"。而目前没有任何国家在做这件事——它既不是技术问题也不是政策问题，而是一个尚未被命名的制度空缺。

四、藏在"德州电费"故事里的终极反讽

Alex 讲他前老板在 Temasek 靠一本枯燥的德州电价法案赚了几千万，用来证明"AI 无法替代人类的初始假设"。但他没发现这个故事的二阶讽刺：德州电费法案能产生 alpha，恰恰是因为"没人愿意读它"。

一旦所有人都用 AI agent 去读所有枯燥文件，信息优势的来源不再是"读到"，而是"不读"——是一种刻意的、反潮流的注意力分配。这就是 Shannon 信息论的核心：信息 = 不确定性 = 稀缺性。当 AI 把每个文档的 base rate 都拉到 100%，alpha 就必须藏在 AI 拒绝去读的地方——人类的直觉、线下关系、未数字化的区域。

最终的悖论：Alex 的产品越成功，Alex 老板那种 alpha 消失得越快；而当所有 varsity 用相同 AI 时，varsity 之间的真正差异化会倒逼他们重新回到人类独有的东西——判断力、品味、反共识的勇气。AI 代理交易普及化的终局，不是机器取代人，而是人被迫进化到机器无法到达的地方。

三、中美 AI 实验室估值差距：地缘政治还是纯粹经济学？

And I think for a while — at least like 12 months ago — it has always been drawn by OpenAI and Anthropic. So they're kind of like leading the Pareto. It's very expensive — the Sonnets at that time, super expensive.

But then Chinese labs — very good at catching up. Probably did a lot of good distillation, but after that capabilities when they pick up, they're able to kind of price it at a point where they can not take too much margins but still be able to comfortably serve a mass market.

So if you look at the timeline for the past two, three quarters, probably MiniMax did the first drop, and then Kimi, and then DeepSeek. And DeepSeek still is. But it became very interesting because as of today, Claude Haiku 5.5 came out — that's like a matching ROI with Luna GP6 Luna, and that pushed the Pareto to the left again.

So leading labs, I mean, they always have the capability to cost up, but then it's a margin issue. So it's about competitiveness compared to Chinese labs, where to price, and what kind of implied margins they're looking for.

Bonnie: You don't think it's a geopolitical thing? It's just pure numbers.

Alex: I think it is geopolitical in a different aspect, as in Chinese labs do not have direct access to the best GPUs to pre-train, post-train whatever model that is the most advanced. But then again, we all kind of know with proper distillation, with good advancements of algorithms — like DeepSeek is doing right now — they are capable of reaching certain levels of parity with the leading labs. So that's why I said pricing power with ample capabilities place Chinese labs at a leading frontier here that's not lagging as much as we would have believed 12 months ago. 七、Alpha 会被稀释吗？Agent 的真正价值

Bonnie: If everybody uses your agent, who makes money?

Alex: I think what you're trying to ask is: will alpha decay or will alpha be leaked in a sense if everyone is chasing the same narrative?

I think it really depends on what type of trading you're pursuing.

If it's like short time-frame quant-like trading, like HFT, I do agree that there is never free alpha. So that's not something we promise in our product. We believe that our product is here to generally help you trade better with AI — either it's a co-pilot experience or it's fully automatic.

Short time-frame stuff: we help you in terms of overlaying the confluences to help you go about trading. Like where are the support resistances, where's the options walls, where is Polymarket bands, where are the derivatives looking at — to give you a clue to make your own discretionary judgment. So even for short time-frame trading, the same set of information or clues present very different decision boundaries. So you may look at the market differently, I may look at differently. So that in itself already kind of kills the problem of following certain directions on one front.

Longer time-frame: if you're looking at something that's a little bit longer in time frame — like you want to form a basket, you want to DCA into something, we're talking about days to weeks to month — alpha does not disappear. It's more about like where the consensus is flowing and whether your idea is something that is not priced in. So in that regard, everyone has different ideas. Everyone will inject different orthogonal issue tree components to validate or invalidate. So our AI basically helps you track that diligently.

So again, it's not handing you alpha on a free platter. It is really about helping you get the ideas that you didn't know about before. Tracking it diligently, executing it securely, and at runtime that is hosted by us.

八、安全性：Agent 钱包与"爆炸半径"控制

Bonnie: Security how?

Alex: For example, you delegate a lot of access authority to the agents. It can operate your account. So you see a lot of players these days — they have specialized agent wallets where it's like a silo. You place money. To be super honest, it's a confinement of blast radius. It's a good beginning to have the agents have only the capability to move the assets within that realm.

So we do things that are very similar on that regard, but it needs to be paired with more complex strategies. And when these complex strategies or conditions kick in, how can the agents continuously keep track of it while executing in an enclave or like a TEE environment that does not send your credentials going wild? I think that's how it will get secure.

Bonnie: There will be people watching and asking: if your strategy and your agent is that great, why don't you just trade it yourself? Why do you want to share it with people?

Alex: That's a great question. So first of all, we never say that we will hand you alpha. We think that if I can guarantee you alpha, that's an oxymoron. It just means that I know the lottery number and Bonnie, I'm going to give you the number. It doesn't make any sense.

So kind of want to reiterate — we think agents are here to genuinely help trade better. Just because more information overlay getting you to the habits of a pro trader. For example, from pre-trade, during trade, and after trade of managing positions, managing risk, and really attending to the market in a more emotionless manner to follow your risk profile. We think that's the ideal of what agents can help you with. It gets rid of a lot of the grunt work and it gets you more personalized. And it should not be advertised or it should not be guaranteed: here's the alpha, put your money in.

九、如何评估 Agent 的好坏？

Bonnie: I've been talking to some of the builders that are building AI agents and a lot of them are financial related. How do you know your agent is better than theirs?

Alex: These days it really depends on which level you're building at. So when we say your agent is better, there must be certain evaluation metrics that we compare with.

  • Common ones are for example financial Q&A.
  • Another common set is instruction following — just because after you build financial agents for a while, you figure out that it's not really throwing information at it and just making it figure out a thesis. It's really about executing something that is semi-deterministic.

In finance, when you do valuation, you need to do DCFs, you need to do comps, you need to do quantitative stuff — and it's all pretty much governed by code. It's not really letting the agents run wild and putting numbers with hallucination.

So we benchmark how well the agent follows instructions. We benchmark whether it can place the numbers diligently such that tasks or information does not get leaked out. We do not evaluate whether a certain idea or thesis correlates with P&L — because this is totally stochastic. A great idea reasoning by an agent still could lose you a lot of money. A super stupid idea can do the vice versa.

So never eval on the meta processes or results. Eval on the semi-deterministic processes that bring you closer to trading, becoming a better trader.

十、Varsity Trader 画像与完整用户旅程

Bonnie: Let's say you're not building True North and you want to use an AI agent for trading. What would you be looking at?

Alex: Me as a varsity trader — I trade three to four times a week. I do not have all the time in the world to look at the market. I have a bunch of ideas or I heard from somewhere, I just don't have time to build a model to go about tracking the data.

So my agent — what it should do for me — is that: ingest my ideas, go to work, formulate the trade for me and monitor on my behalf. When the time hits execute, enter for me, monitor this continuously, when it hits my take-profit or stop-loss, exit on my behalf.

So it's an automation process for me, but instead of me clicking to the order flow, it's me expressing the intent at a higher level for more sophisticated trade compositions that could happen. That's the journey that we are looking at right now.

Bonnie: For somebody that hasn't used your product, walk through the steps and what they're going to see.

Alex: We have a very specific target audience we call varsity traders. These traders — they're not the pros that have six screens, 40 tabs open. They're not the very normie people that don't know, for example, what a trading view chart looks like. They like trading. Their problem is that they don't know what good looks like.

So good trading constitutes of certain habits in three stages of user journey:

  • Pre-trade: scanning markets, 50,000 tradables — what are the gems that you need to find?
  • During trade: a certain asset — how do I overlay confluences to make the call, long or short or DCA?
  • After trade: you enter a position, continuously monitoring it — when to trim, when to TP, when to SL.

So that's the full journey that you're going to get on True North once you log in.

And do note that after you place in a trade or your idea, in your agent, runs in the cloud. So then I close my laptop, I go touch my grass, I have it on my TG, I have it on my WeChat, my LINE — that's where I go to for my instant messaging. So that experience in itself kind of closed loops the entire cycle of investment. And that's our user journey.

十一、5-10 年后，所有人都用 Agent 交易吗？

Bonnie: Do you think in 5 to 10 years — okay, 5 years — people are just going to be using AI agents to trade? Everybody — even grandma, grandpas — are they all going to be doing that?

Alex: I think there are two types of users that will exist.

For one, a lot of our current users are actually the ones that really enjoy trading as a hobby. It's a dopamine thing. I tend to joke that casinos have existed for more than centuries. People do like to put their judgment to really bet on things, to put money where their mouth is. So that need will not go away. What is different is that AI is helping you turbocharge it in a sense — things you didn't know about before, things you need to spend a lot of time finding, now it's readily available. So this co-pilot like trading experience I think it will persist for quite a while.

There's another set that we just talked about — the autonomous trading side. I do firmly believe that in 6 to 12 months people will be expressing their idea to their agent. It may exist on any major AI app that you see these days, and it will tap into an infrastructure that helps you dissect the trade, track it, place it on-chain, and go about putting your capital to work. And that's what we're kind of building. We firmly believe this is going to happen pretty soon.

十二、与大机构 AI 的竞争：选对层级

Bonnie: I talked to John from Coinbase Institution and he was talking about: like, big institutions, AI will be better than your AI. So don't compete.

Alex: I think if I understand correctly, the context is that if you're competing at the general harness level — meaning you're trying to beat Anthropic at certain benchmarks in finance — it's going to be a losing battle. I completely agree with that.

I think the future distribution for a lot of consumer AI will happen at the Muses of the world, the dots of the world, the Grok bots of the world. Leading labs are already competing on this front.

From my understanding, every vertical AI to certain extent should be building at the doors — to become the necessary infrastructure, plug-in, connection, whatever you call it — to facilitate the process of the underlying either experience or capability. In our realm, it's about trading securely and safely to composite whatever you want to be achieving for your personal finance goals. But never on a front where it's general intelligence evolving as such an exponential curve. It's a losing battle on that front.

十三、人类的 Alpha：AI 做不到的事

Bonnie: When you trade, there has to be a human element, your judgment that makes you a good trader. What are some qualities that AI agents still cannot do?

Alex: I think AI agents are very good at branching off of a thesis or a hypothesis that you have, but it never replicates your initial hypothesis or judgment of how a trade would take place.

I like to tell this story. I used to do professional investment at Temasek, and there was a very senior management there. He told me a story of his past experiences of beginning as a consultant. He actually learned about the energy bills in Texas. Nobody's really interested in that. It's very boring stuff.

But I mean, to this date, you actually find that that energy bill is going to impact significantly on the power grid capacity and the supply demand buildout of data centers. So there is a certain bet there to long or short certain suppliers.

Now do mind that this trade made him tens of millions of dollars in one or two months — and the thesis could not have came from AI just telling it to figure something out and make me tens of millions of dollars. The initial starting point of the entire search space need to be specific to a point where AI comes back with theses, building ideas that help you elaborate.

So that's where I still believe humans have a lot of alpha in where they're thinking and placing their bets. AI is there to help them out in this process.

Bonnie: So information that AI doesn't have?

Alex: It's information that AI can find. Its thesis is that it cannot pinpoint in a search space that is so big to begin with. You kind of need to help it narrow down.

十四、超级智能、"鸡与人"的类比与AI末日论

Bonnie: Have you seen The Diary of a CEO and they're talking about how AI is going to kill us all? And there was this so-called AI godfather says: if you want to imagine a being smarter than us, just think of yourself as a chicken.

Alex: Yeah.

Bonnie: So AI will be the human in this world. If that is the case — I don't know if you agree with that — but if that is the case, then supposedly chickens are not supposed to have information that humans don't have.

Alex: I think public information these days — it's already super abundant compared to like 5 years ago. Just because agent implies search and infrastructure has been built out extensively over the past years. And you can argue that agents already have the data corpuses of humans of the past centuries of information.

To an extent, I think the agents that you see these days — or the AI that you see these days — have certain intelligence capabilities that are reminiscent of human developed intelligence over history for the past centuries. So I tend to think about it as a very smart person that knows everything from history. So it can make good inferences of patterns in the past. It's a pattern recognition machine to an extent that is referencing off of past memories that is being trained of and real world events that are evolving.

So still trying to find patterns. But I think in the course of human history, we kind of see that there are patterns that come back and forth. There are cycles that come back and forth. But there's always inflections that are happening outside of technology evolution. I think AI is one of them. I do believe we're in an inflection of that capability.

So maybe I will someday become a chicken, but I hope that before I become chicken nugget, I do know that there is a much more superior intelligence where I can get the information from.

Bonnie: So you do believe that might happen?

Alex: I do believe that maybe with the next generation of AI models — that's not just purely inferencing off of past history — there may be a capability where it would drive the inflection itself. And when that happens, then that scenario may be more legit.

十五、超智能峰会、监管与国家博弈

Bonnie: Now since we're talking about this, did you follow the super-intelligence meeting at the White House with Trump?

Alex: I think people kind of reference the idea of regulating nuclear weapons. If this is something that has such a significant impact on national security or even the livelihood of humans — but we kind of all knew how nuclear regulations panned out when interests are not aligned in a consortium. I think there are always bad actors that will do things for their own benefits.

So I'm not saying that this is not a good cause. I do think that everything developing with certain guardrails or regulations will actually benefit in the long run. It cannot grow like super super wild.

Because let me give you one example. When AI advances at a speed that is so fast, you kind of see it eat into every industry out there. Like 24 months ago, you start seeing Anthropic eating into legal, now finance, now every professional services. It's kind of like the productivity — if you place it from number one to number 10, it can already do everything.

So, if you look at it from an antitrust perspective — wow, that's a huge conglomerate that's forming out there. There's so much pricing power. Like 50% of what you do every day is consumed by it. It's pretty dangerous if it's not regulated in certain ways.

So in that regard I do feel that whatever super-intelligence meeting consortium that is happening — it's a global awareness thing that people need to keep in mind.

Bonnie: Global awareness, but other countries won't follow.

Alex: I guess the ideal of having the betterment of the humanhood has always been a mutual interest. Whether other countries will follow, we cannot guarantee. But it doesn't mean that we shouldn't be voicing the concerns and the consequences if this thing is not regulated — especially when we see there are certain signs that it could get out of control. That's how I feel.

十六、AI 与黑客攻击、链上资产的两难

Bonnie: Do you think recent hacks — there are so many hacks happening — you think it has something to do with AI?

Alex: To be super honest, I do think that AI — if it can crack a lot of the mathematics problems that you see these days — it definitely has a lot of capabilities to probe into holes in cyber security that people did not find decades ago.

There's no direct correlation that we can draw saying that oh, because of certain models, so there are more hacks. But I would say that the malicious actors behind it now have a better arsenal to do bad.

Bonnie: I want to tie it back — because you say every asset will be on-chain, which I believe as well. But this is code, and since AI is going to improve these hacker skills unfortunately, how do you feel safe having your whole network on-chain versus — okay, if I have a real estate here, at least I know hackers won't take them away.

Alex: That's a good question. But then again, a lot of physical assets like your real estate may be tokenized in the future. So your shares of ownership may not be like paper. It may be something that is existent on-chain or custody or put into custody in other entities that can provide you trust — or even you put in as collateral to do something else financially.

What I do think is very very important is that: when everything starts to go on-chain, physical, non-physical — AI helps the malicious actors but AI also helps the ones that are guarding this thing as well. So when you're building out the guardrails, there's also better capabilities to plug in the holes to get rid of the leaks. And I think this has always been a battle between the two parties. So we will co-evolve together.

Start with things that can limit blast radius — that's why we talked about the agent wallets, giving it certain permissions and start slowly. Your assets will not be 100% delegated to AI, but I do think a decent 5 to 10% maybe per year starting from now will be a good trajectory to build the trust and the comfort that you need to delegate in agents.

Otherwise, if you basically all-in all the eggs in one certain basket and it just so happens that the guardrails were not built timely enough — then it's a very bad investment decision in terms of risk control.

十七、信任如何建立？从 FDIC 到 Agent 的类比

Bonnie: What do I have to know for me to put all my net worth to, let's say, True North, and be like, "manage this for me"?

Alex: Realistically trust building is a process. We ourselves do our best to guarantee that we will not leak any of your stuff. We put your stuff in enclaves and TEEs, so it's executing very securely. We give you the white box of things in transparent processes of your signage of your approvals — starting with you as the human still in the loop to do a lot of the kind of okay. I think that's a very important point to start with before we move to a point where autopilot is just kind of on the run.

Now, if you put that analogy into: why are you okay putting with your money in banks? It's because in the US you have FDIC. It insures you for 250k — there's certain insurance there. And you trust it because it's an entity that is managed or governed by the government. So I think these are the things that humans believe in.

Now I do think that agents will probably believe in something differently. For example, they will audit certain security measures that we are providing. There may be certain standards that will emerge in the next 6 to 12 months that say — hey, in terms of these metrics you kind of need to hit like SOC Type 2, something like that. I'm making it up, but obviously there will be certain things that give you a check mark and users are looking for these kind of proxies, because they don't understand what this certain metric in encryption in whatever means. They just need to understand that there is a trustworthy party, there is trustworthy metrics that they can easily sign off to. And I think that will be put in place when this entire thing starts to take off.

Bonnie: Or maybe that thing has to be in place for that to take off.

Alex: Yeah. Chicken-egg problem.

Bonnie: Well, are you seeing people building this?

Alex: I think a part of this is built by us as operators of this. But I think for it to achieve a scale where people are comfortable to deploy capital, even move fiat, right over, or let agents tap into wherever their piggy bank is right now — it needs to be a co-built effort with regulated entities, with operational entities that provide the services. It's a co-effort.

十八、Alex 的个人仓位与业绩

Bonnie: Do you have a portion of your capital following your True North suggestion?

Alex: As a founder, I have to trust my product in order for others to trust it. So I myself put more than 80% of whatever capital that I have on this platform to test it out diligently to verify its capabilities. And of course within this process I discover myself as a user, so to enhance the performance. Yeah, that's what I do.

Bonnie: 8% you said?

Alex: 80%.

Bonnie: 80%.

Alex: 80%.

Bonnie: Oh, I thought you said 8%.

Alex: No, 80%. Stables, denominated trades can go into RWAs, can go into crypto, can go into whatever.

So if I was, you know, trading on, for example, Charles Schwab in the past, or Robinhood — we tend to think about them as like the past generation of the brokers. And these days when you have self-custodial assets in cold wallets and hot wallets, I can place it on any liquidity venue that I would like — with that running my own strategies, or using a venue that can genuinely help me trade better — is what I truly believe in. So putting my money where my mouth is.

Bonnie: Okay. How long has it been? How is your performance? I know everybody has different strategies but I want to know yours.

Alex: For me it has started the moment that I decided to do the company.

Bonnie: Which is when?

Alex: Which is January of 2025.

Bonnie: Okay. It's been a while.

Alex: It's been a while. I wouldn't say I'm a very aggressive trader. I'm a firm believer of, for example, NVIDIA — we talked about it. It's a DCA for me.

But the problem that I'm using my platform for is that during certain events of FUD, or in certain events of people being more bullish on the AI thesis, I can very well get the feedback of what the agent sees as where the consensus is shifting. And that shaped a lot of my decisions into long-term investments or confidences to hold or trim positions.

Bonnie: For example, what would the agent tell you?

Alex: I think in 2025, when I started to do this, AI was on a trajectory run where I think fundamentally the models were improving at a super exponential speed. I felt it myself because I was building. But then the general public had a strong consensus that — oh, actually this thing may work — and the implied supply chain just kind of benefited from this thesis.

Everyone was betting in, but how can I know this early on? It could happen on socials — social sentiment is picking up. It can happen on certain flows that we're monitoring on-chain — whales are placing bets or monetary flows are going here and there. I think these kind of clues give me a lot of confluence in how I should believe about my trade.

I would say how much NVIDIA has appreciated over the past 12 months is roughly how I performed. Because there are certain positions that I also hold that are net kind of negative compared to the gains I'm getting from.

Bonnie: Then the next question is: how much has NVIDIA appreciated?

Alex: I think it has done very well — 50 to 100% at least.

Bonnie: Oh, that's amazing.

十九、财务自由、创业初心与责任

Bonnie: Have you heard of the FIRE movement? The FIRE movement looks for the number to stop working. So you reach a net worth and then you stop working completely. Apparently it's very popular among young people. What does financial freedom mean for you?

Alex: That's a very good question. I never tend to think about this, to I'm just being very honest.

I did True North because I felt it's something I genuinely like doing — even if I weren't starting a company. I was in AI chips in the past, basically my whole life, B2B, did two companies.

So financial freedom to me is just whatever I can do moving forward attending to my interest. I think that's financial freedom to me. It's not a certain number. I would not underpin like 10 mil, 20 mil USD with like a 5% whatever rate on top of inflation. I'm just saying that I can comfortably do what I love to do. That for me is financial freedom.

Bonnie: What you're doing is pretty expensive — starting businesses.

Alex: Yeah. It is pretty expensive. But I think we're building for something bigger. To drive that vision to help everyone trade better using our product. I think that's the ideal. So despite it being expensive, we got to do it.

Bonnie: What wakes you up every day?

Alex: I think what wakes me up every day these days is customers not being able to fully use our product to its potential. And that has a lot of implications in making the product better in every aspect of UI/UX, in the agent performance, and even in the vision that we have of autonomous trading securely.

So all of these — I think when we started AI startups, it's racing with time. Everyone is racing with time. So the urgency that I have waking up every day is that I don't have enough time to build the things in time for my users to really enjoy the experience.

Bonnie: Do you feel a sense of responsibility that you want your users to make money?

Alex: I don't have a sense of responsibility for our users to make money. I have a lot of responsibility and sense for users to trust this process and for us not to make them lose their assets in a malicious way. So it's more about giving them the trust and securing whatever they have running on us, but not guaranteeing that it's going to be, you know, green candles.

Bonnie: Of course you cannot guarantee that. But I mean, if you're building something, it is your baby and you want this thing to benefit more people — meaning in your case, make people money.

Alex: I would phrase it as: I would genuinely love people to trade better. And trade better means a lot of things, because people look for very different things.

There are people that can accept 100% drawdowns at 10x, 20x — that's a type of people. There's a type of people that can accept 10 to 15% of gains but with zero drawdown. So very different cohorts. I can't guarantee anything for them.

But when I say genuinely trade better, it's what? It's to find better opportunities for the people that like to punt the 100x to the moon. It's providing better guardrails in execution of following their endeavors for the people that want to pursue a very steady pace very diligently and not lose the capital.

So that's my definition of helping users trade better. Whether they can follow through this, whether they can stick to this experience — a part is my responsibility to make it good, but it's also a part of them to believe in the process of using agents using AI to assist them.

二十、交易日记：面对亏损的"外包"机制

Bonnie: Can I share my trade with this AI agent and ask this agent to tell me where I do wrong?

Alex: Yes. That's actually a killer use case that a lot of our users love right now in trading. They call it trading journal. It's actually a very important process of professional trading, because humans tend to not like to face their losses — it's just human nature. But it's these losses — if you can emotionlessly summarize and get back to the user — that's what helps them trade better.

So within what we're building these days, let's say Bonnie, you connect your wallet, we kind of know what positions you had, held for how long, which ones are winners, which ones are losers. So our agent would tell you: okay, so you've been trading this way too much. And if you're doing it again, it would actually say — "hey, you know, it's quite angry — don't don't do this. You're going to lose. Think about it." Or if you're compounding on certain habits or skills, keep on building it better.

There needs to be a reference or a memory of you as a trader persona. We call these trader metadata. This trader metadata compounds with your usage on platform. So agents know more about you. You know more about you. So you trade better.

Bonnie: If in the future agents are trading against me, then they have all the information.

Alex: These days you're already trading with — I tend to call institutions — agents that I tend to call institutions. Retail is always in this battle. There's always another side, or you're always in a game. You're trading with someone else. So you're evolving your skills, other people are evolving their skills. That's why we tend to say help you trade better in the sense that you're compounding your skills faster than your counterparty. So that the entire game kind of evolves holistically. It's just inevitable.

二十一、上手指南与时间表

Bonnie: If people want to try out — let's say my neighbor wants to try out today — what do they need to do?

Alex: They need to have some stables in a wallet. And you just need to log on to our platform. Select the venue that you like — the most popular ones are already available. So select it, connect it, start trading.

Bonnie: Hyperliquid, I saw that.

Alex: We connected Hyperliquid. We connected to Aave Perp. We just did Lighter, and there's a whole lot that we will be expanding to centralized and decentralized venues.

Bonnie: Centralized as well?

Alex: Yes. And centralized is even more straightforward because it's just your whatever OAuth authorization that you'll be doing like on Gmail. So very simple to connect — same set of APIs. We never can transfer your funds out. It's only delegating the trade authorizations to these agents so that you as a human in the loop approve it. And very soon the agents can take your delegation, execute and part safely on your behalf.

Bonnie: Okay. Very soon meaning how soon?

Alex: Product-wise 3 months.

Bonnie: Oh.

Alex: Yeah, 3 months. And I think vision-wise — we talked about all the regulatory, all the guardrails — I think it will start to take shape like 6 months from now. So my personal hypothesis is that 6 to 12 months from now, people will be very comfortable to put at least 5% of their total AUM for agents to trade autonomously. That's sort of my thesis.

Bonnie: I haven't tried but I would love to try that.

Alex: Oh, okay. Yeah, please do. Happy to spot you.

Bonnie: Thank you so much.

Alex: Thanks, Bonnie.
