item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的发现：中国 AI 实验室的"GPU 禁运"可能是长期竞争优势而非劣势
Alex 轻描淡写地提到：中国实验室无法拿到最好的 GPU，但靠蒸馏（distillation）和算法优化，与前沿模型差距缩短到 3-5 个月。这里藏着一个被所有人忽略的系统性真相——**约束是最被低估的创新催化剂**。
这与 1970 年代日本汽车业的故事惊人相似：石油危机 + 美国市场的尺寸偏好让日本车厂被迫做小、做省、做精，结果是丰田精益生产模式反向殖民了全球制造业。中国实验室今天做的"参数-token 效率优化"，可能在 5 年后变成通用方法论——**当美国实验室还在用"钞能力"堆算力时，中国实验室被迫学会了"烹饪的手艺"**。有趣的是，Alex 作为 NVIDIA 2013 年的持仓者，这反而是他自己最大的做多逻辑的隐藏裂缝。他讲 TSMC 定价权时自信满满，但没意识到：**定价权来自不可替代性，而不可替代性正在被约束性创新从外侧瓦解**。
## 二、整个访谈的核心矛盾：Alex 说"AI 不能给你 alpha"，但 True North 的真正护城河恰恰是在偷偷积累 alpha

item.title: [Lex Clips] Jensen Huang on the phone call that changed everything | Lex Fridman in Taiwan
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽略的系统性真相：Jensen 的"创业史"其实是一部"关系的拓扑学"

大多数人听这段故事，会聚焦于"黄仁勋打了无数通电话、写了一封长信、终于约到张忠谋"的创业励志叙事。但真正的系统性洞察藏在他随口说的一句话里：

"You really aren't choosing not what to buy, but who to work with."

这不是鸡汤，这是一次对资本主义交易范式的隐秘颠覆。整个 PC 时代的商业逻辑建立在"规格书 + 合同 + SLA"的离散交易上——你买的是一个明确的东西。而 Jensen 在 1996 年那张早餐桌对面做的决定，本质上是把半导体产业从"交易经济"切换到了"关系拓扑"：节点不是产品，是人；边不是合同，是互信随时间的累积。

让人意外的是：Nvidia 真正的护城河从来不是 CUDA，也不是 GPU 架构，而是30 年前那次"选 TSMC 而不是 UMC"决定里，他对张忠谋说"不能做"而不是"能做"的欣赏。他挑中了一个会拒绝自己的供应商——因为能说"不"的人，边界稳定，边界稳定才有长期可预测性。这是一种反直觉的供应商选择：你想要的不是最灵活的伙伴，而是最有原则的伙伴。

跨领域连接：早餐桌、婚姻和芯片代工的同构性

注意访谈中那段看似离题的早餐——咸豆浆、油条、肉松饭团、小笼包。Lex 和 Jensen 在吃饭中间穿插 TSMC 的故事，这不是剪辑意外，而是结构性隐喻。

Jensen 自己点破了：

"It's like writing up an ironclad pre-nup... the more specific you want it to become, the more brittle that relationship's going to be."

把婚前协议、台式早餐、晶圆代工放在同一个坐标系里看，你会发现一个反脆弱系统的通用公式： - 低规格 + 高频互动 + 对称善意 = 可演化的长期关系 - 高规格 + 低频互动 + 零和博弈 = 高效但脆弱的短期交易

小笼包里"汤怎么装进去"的秘密，正如 TSMC 与 Nvidia 30 年合作的秘密——边界足够软，内容才能流动；但皮必须足够有张力，否则一碰就破。Jensen 说"keep it nice and loose to discover our way there"——这是系统生物学里"涌现"的语言，不是商学院的语言。

硅谷过去 30 年所有基于"ironclad contract"思维建立的供应商关系，都在周期性破裂。而 Nvidia-TSMC 这条线一直没断，恰恰因为它从一开始就不是一份合同，是一场反复博弈下的互相进化。

隐藏的权力结构："去年我整条供应链涨价 300%，我没涨"

这是全篇最被低估的一句话。表面上是在讲"善待供应商"，但往深里挖，这是一个极其罕见的权力自白。

当你的供应链涨价 300%，而你能保持价格不动——这意味着： 1. 你的毛利足够宽到可以"吸收"整条产业链的通胀； 2. 你在生态位里是绝对的价值创造源头，供应商涨价涨到你手里的东西，是你在定价而不是他们； 3. 你有意不把全部利润榨回自己口袋，留给供应链"rise up"——这是在主动培育生态的进化能量。

让人意外的是：Jensen 在用"善意"的语言，描述的其实是生态位顶级物种对下层物种的能量下沉。热带雨林里最高大的树不会把所有阳光吸干——它会让下层灌木活着，因为灌木稳定了土壤、保住了湿度、吸引了传粉者。Nvidia 的"让供应链涨价我自己不涨"，是雨林顶层的生态策略，不是慈善。

这是一种 Jim Simons 式的思维：最优策略不是最大化短期收益，而是最大化系统的持续运转时长。在这个意义上，Jensen 不是企业家，他是生态系统的架构师——他设计的不是一家公司，而是一个让自己能持续赢的生物圈。

一个"啊哈时刻"的终点

你再回去看那段"六点半打来的电话"：张忠谋亲自回电话给一个 1996 年的小芯片公司 CEO。为什么？因为张忠谋同样在用关系拓扑思考。他知道，PC 革命的早期格局里，谁是"未来的节点"比谁是"今天的大客户"更重要。他押注的不是 Nvidia 的订单，是 Jensen 这个人的长期信号质量。

两个人在那一通电话里，各自做了同一件事：选对了未来 30 年要共振的人。

这就是为什么 Jensen 说"the year just all flew by"——30 年压缩成一瞬，不是因为快乐，而是因为所有重要的决定都在最初几个节点就已经做完了。剩下的，只是让它展开。

📝 转录文本

关于与张忠谋的初识

Lex： Did your relationship with Morris Chang start when you came back to Taiwan?

Jensen： Yes, so we were looking for a foundry. And at the time, the foundry industry was really —

Lex（插入）： We're, by the way, having Taiwanese breakfast. [laughter] Early morning.

Jensen： Yes. And so we're looking for a foundry back then. Everybody was a foundry. NEC, Toshiba, Fujitsu, Hewlett-Packard. Because the PC revolution had started. So Windows 95 had just come out. The lines — remember lines were wrapped around. People waited to buy a box of operating system.

Lex： Yeah, that moment on stage in the keynote when you're looking back at Windows 95…

Jensen： That was the moment I — the year just all flew by. Just all the memories just flew by.

早餐插曲：咸豆浆与油条

Lex： Soy milk.

Jensen： What is it? Cold sweeping up. Because most Asians are lactose intolerant. Are you lactose — breakfast?

Lex： It's worth it 1,000%. This is uh cold soy milk.

Jensen： All right, so this is a salty version.

Lex： Uh-huh.

Jensen： Now this is in here.

Lex： This is the sweet version. This is the salty version.

Jensen： Hot salty version. Can we have some more spoons? I'll share this with you.

Lex： So you said yeah, you were looking for a foundry. He's telling the story of uh how he first returned back to Taiwan and built the relationship with TSMC. [music] You know, Windows 95.

Jensen： This is too important to me.

Lex： TSMC or that?

Jensen： Can't talk.

Lex： Okay, yeah.

Jensen： Priorities in life. I will share this with you in a — but this is too good for me.

Lex： That's my favorite.

Jensen： Okay. Do they make super bad? No? That is so good.

Lex： Stupid good, right?

Jensen： So this is I think tofu — course with the amazing broth. And a fried donut.

Lex： Fried donut.

Jensen： Yeah, that's a donut. A fried donut. Look at that.

Lex： Yeah. Okay. History — pork floss, your favorite. Rice, pork floss, pickled vegetables, salty, and of course you need eggs. Cheers.

Jensen： Cheers. [snorts] You guys the real deal.

Lex： Yeah, yeah. Right? No way. And you know — pork floss.

Jensen： Pork floss. [laughter] With egg. Wrapped in — I mean sticky rice essentially.

Lex： Marketing at it's best. Floss. What is that? Pork floss. Right? I don't think I've ever — it's one of the best things I've ever had. The combo. This is incredible.

Jensen： Oh yeah, thank you. Jim. What does this classify as?

Lex： Donuts.

Jensen： So this is a donut. I want to eat — deep fried dough. Dip it in the broth.

Lex： Don't — not too many. It's not going to help you crispy. But when the hot soy sauce comes in, that's what you really dip it in.

Jensen： Nice and airy, fluffy but crunchy on the outside. They know what they're doing.

Lex： Almond dough.

Jensen： What's in there? Tofu. Egg. Well, we'll find out. And then the sesame outside.

Lex： Look at that diamond ring. Good god. Okay. The sesame adds, right? Usually when I see sesame seeds I think it's just plain white flour. They're good. This adds.

Jensen： Uh-huh. That's right. That's right. Almost like a smoky experience.

Lex： Yeah, this is a steam bun.

Jensen： Okay. Little something on the inside. Super soft on the outside. That's so good, right?

Lex： So, you guys must have met a long time ago.

Jensen： Went to the same —

Lex： Yeah. Yeah. A long time ago. Oh, we're surrounded by everyone in the Santa Monica building. Yeah, yeah, it's great. It's actually really good. Again, a branding issue, but you're going to love it. How's the garlic? Very garlicky, but it is incredibly delicious. You can do it. You can do it. Yeah. [laughter] Lori's not a garlic person. That garlic sauce, you guys. Guys, if you guys are okay with garlic, this is so good.

Jensen： So good.

Lex： The bottom. Right now when my mouth is on fire, I think that heat is going to really help. And that's sarcastically, cuz I — nice right? Pure. This shot is good.

Jensen： The heat is pretty intense.

Lex： Yeah. Cool. Well, it has a — the way they cooked it, it has a almost like a potato…

1996 年：PC 革命与无晶圆厂产业的诞生

Jensen： In 1996, PC revolution is just taking off. The industry of PC chipsets — PC chipsets, that chipset industry name came out during that time. The fabulous semiconductor industry was born. Cirrus Logic was the giant. Estimate. Big — small Waytech, small one. Western Digital used to make rapid shoes. I competed with all kinds of people. All the boundaries was super —

Lex： They're not playing around.

Jensen： I'm telling you the story later.

Lex： That is just continued. It's just — we're in a battlefield right now and this is right here.

Jensen： There you go. This is a good one. This is a good one.

Lex： That's a pretty good one.

Jensen： And even by this standards, it's very — this by this dish standards.

Lex： Okay.

Jensen： My dad was a knight. My dad was a knight. All right. Looks like we're good.

Lex： That's really good. Basic, but extremely good. Well done. Can you reach? All right. You got — that's right there. You got — that's an expert.

Jensen： Yeah. There you go. Back up. So the challenge is picking it up without breaking it.

Lex： Yeah. That's what — and I failed that miserably. Oh, that's perfect right there.

Jensen： Uh-huh. There's soup inside them. And of course, everybody's trying to figure out — how did you insert soup inside?

Lex： It's just a great mystery. Yeah, but how does it not spill out? I mean, I guess they know what they're doing. I think in the last 20 minutes, we've gotten through 1 year. Windows 95 got released.

Jensen： But we had 14 editions. We did good.

代工厂的早期格局与"必须授权 IP"的时代

Jensen： So the boundaries — Japan got into the foundry business. Almost everybody in the United States — there were very few foundries because Intel was really focused on building their own products. AMD was building their own products. TI building their own products.

And so the foundries, the other countries, the other chip companies from other countries got into the foundry business to try to serve this chipset industry.

SGS-Thomson was a foundry. We went to SGS-Thomson first. They wouldn't allow me to take my business. At the time, there was so little foundry capacity. If you wanted to use somebody's foundry, you had to license your technology to them. That was one of the requirements.

And kind of reminds me of some of the early deals with AI companies. You want to access the capacity, you have to license something away, you know? And so back in my generation, we had to license our IP to foundries.

发现 TSMC：从黄页到一通回电

Jensen： Well, TSMC — I heard about this company in Taiwan, TSMC and UMC at the time. And you know, they had no strings attached. And just they were quite poor companies themselves. And they were barely making it.

I think TSMC was probably about a $300 company at the time — $300 million — and a tiny little company. And I heard about them and heard about Morris Chang.

And so I tried to call their US office. Back in the old days, there were yellow pages. I looked it up. There's a TSMC. There's a number there. I called their number and it's a recording. You know, what kind of company you call that has a recording?

So I left my name and my number, and said a few things about Nvidia — you know, we're new startup building computer graphics chips.

Lex： You know that voice message is probably worth like a lot. [laughter] Hi, my name is Jensen. When you start up —

Jensen： And I called several times, nobody called me. Nobody called me back. And so I finally wrote a letter to Morris. Wrote a long letter, sent it to him. Didn't hear anything for a long time.

And then one day — it was kind of around 6:00 or so, maybe 6:30 — this person calls and says, "This is Morris Chang from TSMC."

Lex： Wow.

Jensen： And meanwhile, everybody outside my office were playing video games. And they're all laughing and screaming — I think they were playing PlayStation, the first PlayStation at the time. Everybody's laughing and screaming.

I said, "Hey guys, shut up. It's Morris Chang. [laughter] Called me back."

And so I was so happy that I found him, that he would actually call us back, you know, because hey, we're not — maybe we won't have to die.

And so we talked and he invited me to Taiwan. And so I came back to Taiwan.

Lex： And that was your first meeting after 30 years. And that was the start of everything. Not just that partnership but just the whole industry, right?

为什么选择 TSMC 而不是 UMC

Jensen： TSMC and UMC, their primary competitor, literally across a street. One street. That street, you know, it's a street inside a campus. And so it's like the other building.

I visited UMC and then I visited TSMC in that order. And both companies super gracious, super happy that they were willing to talk to us.

And when I spoke to UMC — you know, people asked me, well, why did I end up choosing TSMC over UMC? And the reason was because I like both companies in Taiwan. They're both excellent companies.

The thing that I really liked about TSMC was there were a lot of things that I said, that Morris said, "we can't do that." And I'll say, "What about that?" "You can't do that." There's a lot of things that you just can't do.

And so he had a philosophy about his business, and he had a set of core values. And his whole — and he spent all of his time talking about corporate governance and integrity and partnership, thinking long term. And not once did he talk about anything else.

And he said one thing — he said, "Jensen, if we were to work together, I promise you we would jump through hoops for you."

For the whole time, 30 years, they've been jumping through hoops for me. [laughter] And he kept his word.

关系的智慧：选择"和谁合作"而非"买什么"

Jensen： The core values of that company is really really strong. It was there from that very beginning. And you're going to go through thick and thins, and there are a lot of unpredictable things in the future.

And it's because you're building a chip together. It's a foundry. It's not exactly like buying something off the shelf. You're building a chip together and it's really hard to build chips. So it's impossible to know all the details. It's impossible to make all the decisions up front.

You really aren't choosing what to buy, but who to work with.

And so I was smart about making that decision. It wasn't about what to buy, it was about who you're choosing to work with. And that attitude, that philosophy about choosing who to work with has lasted for me to this day.

Lex： But also in the technology industry, the remarkable thing is not just choosing who to work with, it's choosing to work with them for decades. Like the loyalty of a relationship.

Jensen： We've been working with TSMC now for 30 years. It's like we understand, okay, let's go. That's it. For 30 years.

And the reason that it's wisdom is because how do you capture in advance all the unknowns in a relationship? It's like writing up an ironclad pre-nup or something, you know? The problem is, the more specific you want it to become, the more brittle that relationship's going to be.

And so I had the wisdom of keeping it nice and loose to discover our way there. Rough justice. Sometimes I win. Sometimes we don't — like, you know, how things work out better than they did. Sometimes they like it better than I did. Over the course of time, it all works out.

TSMC 的传奇与"共同建造"的哲学

Lex： Does that make sense to you why TSMC is as legendary as they are?

Jensen： Yeah, absolutely. Absolutely. I think that the way I work with them — I don't know if everybody works with them that way. I'd be a little bit surprised if many people do. But I prefer to work with people this way.

Which is — look at all the employees of the company. I don't have ironclad contracts with them. We choose to work with each other. It's not always going to be — once — it's not always going to be completely fair. Sometimes it's a little one-sided, but over the course of time the law of justice works out.

Lex： And that makes everybody step up. When you both choose to work together, step up.

Jensen： They need to know that you want them to win. All my employees know I want them to win. TSMC knows I want them to win. Every single day TSMC knows I want them to win.

And so it comes through in our partnership. It comes through in our business dealings. We're always helping them being a better company. And they're always doing the same to you.

You're not buying something. You're deciding to build something together. Our company's built on top of the TSMC platform. Our company's built on top of the Taiwan platform. And so these relationships matter.

If you do something just because you got upset, or you just want to make everybody bend for your business, where nobody makes any money but you — those kind of things, it is remembered on the island forever and everybody knows it.

And so always leave something on the table. Always be thinking about other people's sustainability and their success.

Nothing gives me more pleasure than last year my entire supply chain's contract went up 300%. Mine stayed flat. Now, the fact that that happened is not something that I'm happy about, but it's because our platform is so — everybody could rise up to meet it. And that's a good thing.

Lex： Yeah, wanting your partners/friends to succeed long-term is going to lead to your own success.

Jensen： Yeah.

Lex： 100%. That philosophy is really powerful.

Jensen： It makes a lot of sense. It makes sense with family, it makes sense with employees, it makes sense with your boss, right? It makes sense with your customers.

收尾：食物、工程与下一场冒险

Lex： I just love that you're the foodie guy even for Morris. We — literally this is an honor of a lifetime to be guided by the best food guide in the world. Engineering and food, there's literally nobody better than Jensen.

Jensen： I'm just setting myself up for my own podcast.

Lex： Yeah, exactly. [laughter] Food blog. Post — we're saying post AGI.

Jensen： Go on. One more.

Lex： Post stickers.

Jensen： Yeah, they're hiding under a blanket. Oh. Man. No, you know what — [laughter] you mean.

Lex： I don't know what you mean. All right, that's a wrap on one of the most incredible weeks of my life. Thank you so much. Thank you so much. It's great hanging out with you. Thank you so much. This was incredible food. On to the next adventure.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一个被忽略的系统性真相：**Jensen 的"创业史"其实是一部"关系的拓扑学"**
大多数人听这段故事，会聚焦于"黄仁勋打了无数通电话、写了一封长信、终于约到张忠谋"的创业励志叙事。但真正的系统性洞察藏在他随口说的一句话里：
> "You really aren't choosing not what to buy, but who to work with."
这不是鸡汤，这是**一次对资本主义交易范式的隐秘颠覆**。整个 PC 时代的商业逻辑建立在"规格书 + 合同 + SLA"的离散交易上——你买的是一个明确的东西。而 Jensen 在 1996 年那张早餐桌对面做的决定，本质上是把半导体产业从"交易经济"切换到了**"关系拓扑"**：节点不是产品，是人；边不是合同，是互信随时间的累积。
**让人意外的是**：Nvidia 真正的护城河从来不是 CUDA，也不是 GPU 架构，而是**30 年前那次"选 TSMC 而不是 UMC"决定里，他对张忠谋说"不能做"而不是"能做"的欣赏**。他挑中了一个会**拒绝自己**的供应商——因为能说"不"的人，边界稳定，边界稳定

item.title: [Business of Sport] The Football Regulator Report Reviewed
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：这已经不是"足球问题"了

报告中最让人脊背发凉的数字不是27%俱乐部负债超估值，也不是66%俱乐部在失去股东输血后撑不过90天——真正的核弹是"17家EFL及国家联赛俱乐部，即使球员免费踢球也会亏损"。

请停下来想一想这句话的含义。当球员工资——这个被所有人（包括Charlie本人）奉为"问题根源"的变量——被归零之后，仍有大量俱乐部运转不下去。这意味着足球俱乐部的财务病灶已经发生了"组织外转移"（metastasis）：从球员薪资扩散到了日常运营的每一根毛细血管里。这就像癌症病人把肿瘤切除后发现淋巴系统已经全线失守。

所以 Kogan 真正揭示的不是"足球俱乐部花钱太多"，而是——英式足球俱乐部已经进化成一种在生物学意义上无法自养的生物，必须靠宿主（owner）持续点滴输液才能存活。这解释了为什么单纯的"工资帽"不够：你治好了心脏，病人仍然会死于肾衰竭。

二、意外的跨领域连接：这是2008金融危机的慢动作重播

把这份报告放在金融史的坐标系里看，整件事瞬间变得清晰得可怕：

  • "Factoring 转会款超过阵容估值" = 2008 年次贷危机的 CDO 层级化。英冠俱乐部把未来会收到的转会款贴现卖给银行，而贴现总额已经超过他们场上所有球员的账面价值。换言之，他们已经把自己的未来卖了超过一次。这不是会计问题，这是希腊神话里的俄狄浦斯：越想避开命运越把自己送进去。
  • IFR 的角色 ≈ 2008 之后的 Dodd-Frank + 压力测试体系。Kogan 要求俱乐部做"降级/媒体收入下降/股东撤资"三重 stress test——这就是巴塞尔协议的 CCAR 翻版。
  • Karen Brady 与 Steve Parish 的历史定位 ≈ 雷曼兄弟的最后一次股东会。他们本来可以通过那个 Masters 的分配方案避免监管入侵，但他们否决了。结果是他们亲手召唤了那个来管他们的人——这是治理史上最清晰的 Streisand Effect（越想掩盖越被放大）样本。

更深的隐喻：足球联赛的"超级多数票"结构（14/20、16/24）从数学上注定它无法改革自身。这是博弈论里的"少数否决者困境"——跟美国参议院的 filibuster、欧盟的一致同意表决、以及联合国安理会的否决权是同构的。所有这类系统，最后都必须依靠外部权威来打破内部僵局，否则就会在最需要变革的时刻瘫痪。

三、藏在报告深处的"核威慑"：Kogan 其实在演一场博弈剧

Charlie 没点破但很重要的一点：Kogan 当前并不拥有强制成本管控的法定权力——那仍然是联赛自己的决定权。所以他现在做的事情，用博弈论语言说，是经典的"疯子策略"（Madman Theory），和尼克松在越战时期对苏联玩的那套一模一样：

"你最好自己管好，否则我就去跟政府要那个权力。你不会想看到我拿到那个权力的样子。"

这就是为什么他在 Radio 5 上要故意表现得"not yet on a certain wicket"（还没十足把握）——他需要联赛相信他是认真的，但又不能真的被迫到那一步去申请新权力，因为一旦申请并失败，威慑力就归零。

跨领域连接：这跟央行的"预期管理"是完全同构的操作。鲍威尔从来不希望真的加息到让经济崩溃，他希望仅仅通过发表讲话就让市场自行调整。Kogan 正在用监管语言做货币政策工作。

四、一个无人提及的隐藏赢家，和一个讽刺的输家

Charlie 点到了"收入最高的非降落伞付款英冠俱乐部"（Norwich City、Bristol City 一类）是最大赢家，但他漏掉了一个更深的结构性赢家：球迷协会（Supporters Trusts）。

因为一旦监管机构开始审查"董事和股东许可证"，球迷协会就从一个"情怀组织"升级成了潜在的 fit-and-proper 替代持有者——他们是唯一不会因为财务损失而撤资的所有者类型。英格兰可能在未来十年里见证一场悄无声息的所有权革命：从寡头主义向德国式 50+1 的爬行式迁移。没有人在公开讨论这件事，但监管的逻辑终点就在那里。

而讽刺的输家是——球员和经纪人。注意报告中那句"做得好的只有球员和经纪人"。这句话一旦被政治化，就会在未来 3-5 年内变成媒体话术的默认底色。英格兰足坛即将经历一场"球员作为资本的话语权崩塌"。考虑到 PFA（球员工会）在 Rooney 时代之后一直疲弱，这个话语转向可能比任何工资帽都更能压低薪资增长曲线。

最终的洞见：Kogan 的真正杀招不是任何单一条款，而是他把过去三年碎片化的新闻——转会负债、英冠亏损、新成本规则——打包成了一个单一叙事。叙事就是治理。当所有人开始用同一个故事看待这个行业时，否决者的政治合法性就蒸发了。这就是本份报告真正的"统治技术"。

📝 转录文本

The Football Regulator Report Reviewed —— Business of Sport 节目速记

一、开场：Charlie 的"六年等待"

主持人：We've had messages in the run-up to this, people going when it came out, the IFR report just before — you know, anyone gets confused what we're talking about. They're going, "My god, it's Charlie's Christmas. He must be so excited for this." Having spoken probably now for the last 6 months in some capacity.

Charlie：Six years.

主持人：I mean, on this show, but yes, of course, you know, you are the birthplace of need for this, having spoken for a while on it.

Charlie：I am. I am. I literally am — because myself and Damian Collins, then the chairman of the DCMS select committee, a Conservative politician in the last government, he and I called for the establishment of a football regulator back in 2020, in a statement, with the support of the Football Supporters Association.

Around that time the Conservative government, of which Damian was effectively part, then instituted the Crouch Report, which then looked into the whole thing — which he said was good — right?

Excellent report, which has led, over six years after much wrangling and fighting, to the establishment of the Independent Football Regulator, which is not one person — it's effectively a government department at arm's length from the government. And that's been an issue that's come up this week in relation to Andy Burnham's crack-handed attempted intervention. But it's effectively a quango regulator — a quasi-governmental organization that sits at one remove from the government, but has full statutory power.

And this is really important to remember for all of you listening and watching. Everything we're talking about from now on in: this is not football regulating itself. This is not a body that makes recommendations. This is a body with statutory power — legal statutory power — can just do stuff. Right? Can actually do stuff.

Yeah, they — slash he, David Kogan, who is the chair of the Independent Football Regulator. So when we talk about the Independent Football Regulator, often people mean David Kogan, but it's just worth remembering that he has a big department underneath him.

二、为什么足球需要监管者？

主持人：So before you actually go into the report — can we start off by actually just reminding everyone why it was important that a football regulator came in? Because the thing I get asked more often than not is: why does football need one of these? What have we come to when football needs regulation, blah blah?

Charlie：Yeah. I hear the same. I get the same.

主持人：So why has it been so important and why have we got to this moment where we're going to talk about the outcome?

Charlie：There were two things that happened in quite quick succession back around the COVID time.

1. Bury 与 Macclesfield 的破产

First of all, Bury Football Club went bust and then shortly after Macclesfield Town Club went bust. Those clubs didn't go into administration and out of administration. They went properly bust. I think Macclesfield were allowed to pick up again a couple of divisions lower, but Bury went into liquidation and a new former Bury had to start in whatever it was the 12th division.

2. 欧超联赛

The second thing that happened was Super League — the failed attempt to create a European Super League.

Both of these things created a lot of public angst. And the prime minister at the time was Boris Johnson, who was a politician who was quite sensitive to what the public care about. He wasn't one of these people who said, "Well, you know, I've got my principles and we don't do this, we don't do that." It was like, "Hang on a second — a lot of people seem to be really upset about this."

And reportedly from people I know who worked in Downing Street at the time, he literally stormed around Downing Street saying, "How the [__] does this happen? Football has billions of revenue! Why are football clubs going bust and why are these football clubs trying to leave the Premier League to go and join up with other people? What on earth is going on?"

3. Crouch Report 的诞生

So it was really out of that instinct from Boris that it was decided to commission Tracy Crouch — a former sports minister who by this point was a backbench MP — to say, "Look, can you do a report into what's wrong with football? Why is this happening? Why is all this rubbish happening?" When in theory it's all going really well — revenues are up, attendances are up, everything's good — but then everything's not good, because bad stuff's happening.

Hence the Crouch Report, which we've discussed on this before. Very good report. And the Crouch Report recommended the setting up of an Independent Football Regulator. That report came out, I think, in about 2022 — about four years ago.

It then went into sort of iteration at government level. During the very short-lived Truss administration, it was well known that Liz Truss was going to block this from happening. Meanwhile, the Premier League was fighting against it being established, because the Premier League knew that one of the things that they were likely to do was to force the Premier League to give more money to the Football League. And that's something the Premier League didn't want to do — or the Premier League clubs didn't want to do, with respect to the Premier League executives who have always been open-minded about that.

Anyway, the long and the short of it is, eventually at the tail end of the Sunak government and running into the Starmer government, it was decided — "Right, let's do it." And it got established about a year ago.

4. State of the Game Report 的由来

One of the things that was put in there was that before the regulator started to exercise his statutory powers — we'll come on to what those powers are in a moment — he had to produce something called the State of the Game Report.

So this is like taking the Crouch Report — which was looking at what might need to be done to sort out some of the problems — and now the regulator and his department saying, in much more detail, what those problems are and what practical solutions there might be. Or starting that conversation at least.

First of all, a really detailed analysis of what the problems are. Because up until this point there hasn't been consensus about that, if I'm being honest with you. And there have been certain issues that have been lying in the undergrowth — partially because they don't sound that sexy and require quite a bit of understanding, and partially because it's not really been in many people's interest to surface them. The regulator has dragged them out of the undergrowth and slapped them on the table and said: everyone needs to have a look at these issues. They're big problems, serious problems — the kind of stuff that I've been banging on about for a long time.

三、为什么足球管不了自己？

So in answer to the original question — why do we need a football regulator? Two things. First of all, football's important. Secondly, it can't be trusted to look after itself.

Why football is important

A very significant proportion of this country believes that football is very important, and that their football clubs and the survival of their football clubs is very important.

Why it can't look after itself — 投票机制

You've got the Premier League and then you've got the Football League. The Premier League represents the 20 clubs in the Premier League, the Football League represents the 72 clubs in the Championship, League One and League Two. Effectively, for new things to change, you need to have a supermajority vote. In the Premier League that is 14/6. So you need 14 clubs to go, "We agree this should be changed." And in the various divisions of the Football League it's 16/8.

The truth is, you don't need many clubs to vote against change for no change to happen. And when each individual situation comes along, there are always certain clubs who view themselves as being losers from that change. They then become blockers — the NIMBYs — and try and prevent that change from happening.

For instance, for two or three years, the Premier League executive Richard Masters, the chief executive, was telling his clubs: "If you don't agree a deal to give more money to the Football League, do you understand that that will mean they will put a football regulator in which will force us to do that? So why don't we get ahead of it? Why don't we make an offer?"

No, no. So Karen Brady at West Ham, Steve Parish at Crystal Palace led this little rearguard action — that was seven clubs, maybe eight at a push — who prevented that deal from happening and therefore led to the institution of the IFR.

I would say the fact that the IFR exists is largely down to Karen Brady and Steve Parish. Because if they had waved through the deal that Masters wanted to give the Football League three years ago, I think the government might have caved and not done the IFR. It was the failure of that deal that led finally to the government: "Okay, we've got to have this IFR, because what everyone's been saying is true. The Premier League are never going to agree on the things that need to be done."

收入巨大却仍然不可持续

To put a number to that, David Kogan said it was £9 billion a year that comes into English football — at least double any other league system in the world. So we should be able to be both globally dominant and sustainable. There shouldn't need to be a trade-off there.

If it was that we were bringing in £5bn, £6bn, and the Spanish were bringing in £5bn or £6bn, the argument could be made: "Well, for us to become the dominant league we need to 'invest' to get ourselves ahead of the Spanish, so please don't put restrictions on us." But when it's at £9bn versus £5bn — double — you can no longer make that argument.

谁是赢家？

And the bottom line is, as this report makes clear, English football — despite having this massive global dominance — is profoundly unsustainable. Because the leagues and the clubs within those leagues keep on voting against having effective wage cost control regulations.

Someone said to me yesterday: "So who is it that does well out of English football?" Having just seen the regulator's report that says that clubs don't do well.

Players. Players and their agents. It's as simple as that. Players and agents make more, clubs make less, or clubs lose more. If you want clubs to break even, the players and their agents have to get less.

四、报告中的那些震撼数字

主持人：Well, let's have a look at a few of the things in the report. One of the stats that was highlighted was that 17 clubs across the EFL and National League would lose money even if their players played for free.

Now based on what you just said, everything starts with paying the players too much, but that slipped beyond the playing costs — that slipped into the broader operational costs regardless of what they're spending on football. That probably surprised me more than…

Charlie：Let's get a few of those numbers out on the table.

债务超过企业价值

Debt exceeds enterprise value in 27% of lower league clubs.

This is something I've been going on about recently. One of my biggest concerns is that when you've got a situation where a club is losing more money than the market value of that club, a financially rational owner at some point will say: "I'm better off just walking away from this. Because if I stay in charge of this club even for one more year, I'm going to be worse off than if I simply throw my hands up in the air and just leave it in the gutter now."

So in 27% of lower league clubs — remember, 72 Football League clubs, so we're talking about roughly 20 of those clubs — currently their debt and their liabilities exceed the club's own value. By continuing to be in charge of those clubs, the owners are basically shooting themselves in both feet financially. They are actually insolvent.

60% 实质性资不抵债

And there are many more that rely on the owner's goodwill. 60% are insolvent — i.e. the liabilities outweigh the value of their assets.

So, it's 27% where the debt (what they already owe) exceeds EV. It's 60% where the debt plus the ongoing liabilities exceed EV. That's more than half where effectively the owner would really be better off walking away.

俱乐部的"生命支持系统"

Kogan has asked the question: how long can a club operate if the owner stopped putting money in?

  • For 66% of clubs, they wouldn't survive 90 days. Two in three clubs would be in liquidation within 3 months if the owner didn't keep funding.
  • For 30%, 30 days. The moment that owner — something happens in his other business, or dare I say goes under the proverbial bus — his estate passes to the executors who say, "We have to act in the interest of the beneficiaries of his will. We can't carry on sustaining this." A third of clubs would not survive to the end of the month.

So effectively, a significant majority of clubs are on a drip feed. This is not a situation where owners are putting in a vast amount of money and then saying to the chief executive, "There you go. That's the capital for the next three years." It's life support. About 10 days before the end of each month, the finance director is sending a message to the owner saying, "Please can you wire across x amount or the club will go bust." That is exactly what happens.

At the better-run clubs it will be 3 months in advance; at the less well-run clubs it will be month-to-month. And Kogan points out: just not good enough. That is systemic risk.

Kogan 的原话

"The underlying foundations of the pyramid are under intense strain and require urgent reform. The report should serve as a wakeup call for English football. This is the moment of addressing these problems before the money dries up. We can fix the house while the sun is still shining."

五、监管的现实：这不是"几封棕色信封"的游戏

First of all, it's worth noting that this is the first draft of the report. The final report will get published in February / March 2027.

(Credit to you, by the way — you called that a while ago.)

It was in the original mandate which no one read. It was so funny speaking to football people over the last two or three years. Part of my career has been spent advising companies in regulated industries. People in football have never worked in a regulated industry.

So it's like: "Well, this regulator guy — I'm sure we'll put our arm around him. There'll be a few loopholes, a few brown envelopes. It won't amount to anything." This is the reality of being a regulated entity.

下一步：Kogan 要做什么

Some of which he's saying "I'm going to do now" and some of which he's putting on the table as "I may have to do this."

The stuff he's putting on the table right now:

  • The regulator is going to work with clubs on business plans and action plans.
  • It's not going to be good enough anymore for a club to say, "Oh, our owner's good for the money." We're going to have to see what your business plan is over a significant period of time.
  • We're going to have to see what liquidity there is already inside the club. Not something that's promised at a later date — what's inside the club already.
  • We're going to start to make recommendations to clubs as to what they need to do, ultimately if their current owners and directors are going to retain their licence.

This is the other side of the regulator's responsibility — the regulator is also in charge of the licensing process. The regulator has the power to take the club off their hands and sell it for them.

In practice, what would probably happen is that the regulatory department would say, "We think you now need to sell the club." And it's only if they then didn't that they would take it.

But it does start to make people in the industry — I've had some quite interesting, very bemused colleagues in the football industry calling me — "What's all this about? So we're going to have to come up with three-year business plans? My owners are potentially going to have to put loads of money into the club to show that…"

This is what being in a regulated industry means. Talk to banks about capital requirements. It was never going to be about your brown envelopes and your loopholes. All those days that you love so much — they're gone. Everything's going to have to be done by the book, because the government has decided that football cannot manage itself.

六、房间里的大象：成本管控权

主持人：Who does this favour?

Charlie：Ultimately — to be pompous about it — it's intended to favour the game as a whole, because it means fewer clubs will go bust.

But I just want to address the elephant in the room. As things currently stand, the regulator does not have the power to put cost control systems in place within the leagues. That is still something which is being voted for by the leagues themselves.

Now, I thought it was interesting that there are rumours that the IFR may well seek new powers from the government to take that over as well, which stands to reason. Because ultimately it's his statutory duty to make sure that football clubs don't go bust.

议会质询的必然逻辑

When football clubs start going bust, what will happen is this: the regulator will get called into parliament to answer the select committee as to why he has been unable to prevent clubs from going bust. And his answer will be:

"Well, I advised them on putting in place much more stringent cost controls. They refused to do so. It's not my fault."

At which point parliament will say: "So you're telling me that you don't have the power to make sure they actually control their costs? How can you have sustainability as a mandate without having that power?"

He's got the house, but he hasn't got the keys.

七、英冠：Kogan 最担心的联赛

Kogan in the report is particularly worried about the Championship. The Championship is where he sees systemic risk as lying.

转会款的"预支化"

There's another interesting factoid: the Championship have factored — i.e. brought forward — the payments on more of their future transfer revenues. These are players they have sold, where those sales are being paid over a number of years. They have gone to banks or financial institutions and taken that money in up front, paying a cost to the bank for doing so.

The total amount of that is greater than the total value of all the players on their balance sheets. Think about that for a moment. The amount of transfer debt out there is more than the value of the squads.

英冠的"最后一棒"

He's particularly critical about the latest cost control regulations agreed by the Championship clubs. As the Premier League, League One and League Two moved towards tighter financial controls, the Championship said, "Oh, one last swing of the bat. Let's try and have even looser financial controls."

So Kogan's basically saying: the situation is already desperate and they have now just voted in a system which is going to make it even more desperate.

To which the natural question is: what are you going to do about it?

八、分配协议与"软性胁迫"

I think the Premier League has seen — and the rest of you now will have seen — that when we threaten that we are eventually going to do something, if you don't act yourself, that will happen.

So in reality, there will be discussions at the end of this year and in the new year about cost control regulations in the Championship. And the same thing will happen as always:

The executives of the Football League will say: "You need to go on to stricter cost controls, because this is unsustainable."

And Stoke City and a few of the other Championship clubs will say: "Well, we want to be able to spend whatever we want to be able to spend."

Kogan 的台本

"Whatever your crazed right-wing theories are about liberty of people to do whatever the hell they want with these massive social institutions that have been around for 100 years and force tens of thousands of people to cry when they get shut down — whatever we might think about it, the football regulator clearly thinks that we are massively in the wrong place on this one. And if we don't move to address that, his track record, as he's shown with the Premier League, is that he then starts to address it on your behalf. Do you want to address it now, or do you want him to address it forcibly in a way that you might not like?"

新的再分配协议

With the new redistribution deal that's coming from the Premier League to the Football League — which Kogan has been out on the airwaves saying he believes is very close — this will see effectively around an additional £200 million a year coming from the Premier League to the Football League on top of the £140m that's already given. So you're taking it up to £340m. Very large numbers.

Kogan has been dogmatic on the point that this deal will come with that money being ring-fenced. It will not be allowed to be spent on playing wages.

That will actually necessitate a new cost control rule. Because currently all that revenue would just come in, and under the current rules, the Championship would just swing the bat on all that money as well. So their losses could actually remain the same — i.e. massive — but they could just increase spending by another £10m a year with the extra money. You get even more inflation, and create even more systemic problems.

What he's clearly going to do is say, together with the Premier League: "Yes, congratulations Football League, you're going to get loads more money — but you're not going to get it unless you agree to this cost control regulation."

At which point the Football League will have to go back to its clubs at Championship level. There's not going to be a problem in League One and League Two — that's already been sorted. In the Championship they'll say: "Do you want this extra £10m per club or not?"

"Well, we want to still be able to spend whatever we want to be able to spend."

"You really want to turn down this extra money just to be able to maintain some sort of Hayekian principle of freedom of movement, when really — maybe not? We do want the money, but we also want to be able to spend it."

读懂房间的空气

So the question now is whether these Football League clubs are able to say: "If we still want to at least keep control of our own cost regulations, we are going to need to read the room a bit here. People aren't up for clubs going bust. So if we look like the people who seem to be really relaxed about clubs going bust, we're on the wrong side of the room there."

九、降落伞付款与"结构性整合"

主持人：The Premier League "land of opportunity" has been why the Championship has overspent for a long time. But also if you strip back some of the parachute payments — which is the safety net that has allowed them to go and spend big…

Charlie：These are the clubs that get relegated from the Premier League, who get in the first either two or three years significant extra payments to help them adjust to life outside the Premier League.

主持人：But if you then offset some of that by having more money just filtering down into the system — we are talking about a reduction in parachute payments as well.

Charlie：Right, and that's my point. These regulations are kind of all working together within this system. They're all working to help the Championship.

Because the other mandate of the football regulator is competitive balance. So it's all going towards helping the non-parachute-payment Championship clubs. You're going to get loads more money, and the clubs you're competing against are going to get slightly lower parachute payments.

Congratulations. But you are going to have to make sure that extra money goes to reducing your losses, not to inflating your players' wages. And that's where the sticking point's going to come.

Just listening to the media interactions with Kogan — hearing him being interviewed on Radio 5 this morning — he knows that he's not yet on a certain wicket on this one. He can't guarantee to the government or broader stakeholders that the leagues, particularly the Championship, will move to tighter cost control systems. And he's hoping that he can influence, bend an arm here, put an arm around a shoulder, point to the writing on the wall there:

"Come on, guys. Please don't. There's an easy way and a nasty way. Don't make me do the nasty way. If you want, I'll go to the government and get these powers to force it on you. Please don't do that."

十、报告的真正价值：把碎片拼成一张全景图

It's a really good report because even though much of it is known, it pieces it all together into one panoramic vision.

Whereas previously, one month you'll hear about this thing to do with transfer liabilities, two months later you'll hear about how much Championship clubs are losing, three months after that you'll hear about a new cost control system that lets clubs lose even more money — all these things are happening out there and people are just sort of saying, "Oh, there was that and there was this."

This brings it all together in one piece and says:

"A significant number of clubs told us they would not survive if their owners walked away. This lack of resilience can no longer be ignored."

十一、谁是真正的赢家？

主持人：So if I ask you that question again — who does this favour?

Charlie：Ultimately, the big winners of all of this in the end are going to be the biggest, best-run Championship clubs.

Because they're going to receive easily the most of the additional money coming down. They already have much higher revenues than a lot of other clubs in the Football League anyway. Instead of fighting with less money against parachute payment clubs with more money, they're going to have more money themselves — not so much to spend on players, but to reduce their losses and enable them to keep going for longer against clubs with slightly lower parachute payments.

Then they're going to be moving on to cost control regulations — if they do read the writing on the wall — which are based on percentages of revenue. So it's no longer going to be "you can lose x amount or your owner can put in x amount of equity." It's going to be, like the Premier League, League One and League Two: in terms of your first team squad, you're allowed to spend x percentage of your revenue.

That naturally benefits the highest-revenue club.

So if you were to think about the club with the highest revenue in the Championship which is not a parachute payment club — Norwich City, Bristol City, those types of clubs — non-parachute clubs which command their own catchment area, have very high revenue, reasonably well-run, not wasting lots of money — those clubs would be the most benefited from this.

Because the amount they're currently losing will be knocked down a long way. Their owners will be able to sit there and go, "Right, that was a bit uncomfortable for a few years, but now I can actually plan for the next 5 or 10 years because I'm not losing much money anymore. The clubs I'm competing against are getting lower parachute payments. Life suddenly looks — we're on a cost control system which benefits us more, because a smaller club with a rich owner can't just chuck in £10 or £15 million quid every year just to try and keep up with us."

That is the type of club I think that should do best out of this.

主持人：Good stuff. Thank you for that. Waiting a while.

Charlie：It has taken an awful long time.

十二、尾声：压力测试与"业务连续性计划"

主持人：Just one final thing before we move on. He's going to apply these stress tests — which again is something lifted from the financial services industry.

Clubs are going to have to provide business plans to explain what they'd do in the event of:

  1. Relegation — from whichever league they're in.
  2. A revenue reduction — probably mostly to do with media rights, like what would happen if the next Sky deal was a bit lower.
  3. The loss of owner funding.

This is absolutely critical. If you were to say to a club chief executive, "I want to see a business plan that explains what you would do if your owner stopped funding" — 68% said they didn't have one.

Charlie：Well, 68% said there wouldn't be one. I would guess that pretty much 100% didn't have a plan. It was just, "We've currently got enough money in the bank that we can probably work our way through for a little bit."

What he's demanding here is mitigating action plans — something which is written down on paper saying, "This is what we would do to avoid being put into liquidation if our owner walked."

Now the question is: what happens if that plan's not a very good plan? What does the IFR do then? Open question. Be interested to see.

主持人：I like it. Anyhow, there we are.

## 一、最反直觉的发现：这已经不是"足球问题"了
报告中最让人脊背发凉的数字不是27%俱乐部负债超估值，也不是66%俱乐部在失去股东输血后撑不过90天——真正的核弹是**"17家EFL及国家联赛俱乐部，即使球员免费踢球也会亏损"**。
请停下来想一想这句话的含义。当球员工资——这个被所有人（包括Charlie本人）奉为"问题根源"的变量——被归零之后，仍有大量俱乐部运转不下去。这意味着**足球俱乐部的财务病灶已经发生了"组织外转移"（metastasis）**：从球员薪资扩散到了日常运营的每一根毛细血管里。这就像癌症病人把肿瘤切除后发现淋巴系统已经全线失守。
所以 Kogan 真正揭示的不是"足球俱乐部花钱太多"，而是——**英式足球俱乐部已经进化成一种在生物学意义上无法自养的生物**，必须靠宿主（owner）持续点滴输液才能存活。这解释了为什么单纯的"工资帽"不够：你治好了心脏，病人仍然会死于肾衰竭。

item.title: [Lex Clips] China's approach to AI and robotics | Lex Fridman and Jensen Huang in Taiwan
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：卖铲人为"缺铲者"鼓掌的悖论

Jensen 作为全球算力垄断链最顶端的 CEO，在整段对话中竟然在赞美那些算力饥饿的中国公司——这几乎是反商业本能的表态。但真正耐人寻味的是：他可能正在用这份赞美，为自己的产品做最高明的边际定价。

逻辑是这样的：如果被禁运的客户用 1/10 的算力做出接近水平的架构，这不是在削弱 NVIDIA，而是在反向证明"NVIDIA 芯片的全效使用能带来 10 倍优势"。他让对手的约束，成为自己产品的性能证词。这是一次教科书级的"用敌人的勤奋证明自己卓越"的话术——而且是在镜头前完成的。

洞察二：约束催化创新的"热力学"规律

"Constraints is the mother of invention" 听起来像鸡汤，但它背后是一条跨越多个领域的平行线，令人意外的清晰：

  • 日本战后汽车业：钢材配给 → 丰田精益生产体系
  • 苏联数学界：计算机匮乏 → 柯尔莫哥洛夫学派的解析深度
  • 深度学习 2017 年前：GPU 稀缺实验室 → Attention、ResNet 等结构性发明

当资源充沛时，大脑倾向于"用更多"来解题；当资源稀缺时，大脑被迫重新定义问题的拓扑结构。这意味着一个有点冒犯常识的预测——未来十年真正的架构级突破，可能更多来自被卡脖子的一方。这将是美国出口管制政策最未被预见的副作用：它不是在遏制对手，而是在为对手配置一台进化压力机。

洞察三："Humility" 是机器人产业的生理反应，而不是文化属性

Jensen 特别点出杭州（Unitree 所在地）的机器人公司"full of humility"。表面是文化观察，但往深了看是物理学的直接后果：

  • 做纯软件 AI 的人，经常对现实有"类神"错觉——代码总是能跑
  • 做机器人的人，每天被重力、摩擦、电池衰减、关节磨损"打脸"
  • 现实世界的反馈带宽远低于数字世界，所以机器人工程师的傲慢，每一次 demo 都会被摔碎一次

跨领域的意外连接在这里：这种"被物理世界持续羞辱"所训练出来的认知气质，恰恰是 AGI 最需要的——因为 AGI 的真正瓶颈不是智力，而是对"自己可能错"的持续建模能力（Karl Friston 的自由能原理、贝叶斯脑假说都指向这点）。

于是一个颠倒的预测浮现出来：最接近人类通用智能"气质"的系统，可能不是从硅谷大模型公司走出来的，而是从中国机器人圈走出来的——因为前者的从业者天生被训练成"假设自己错了"，而后者仍沉浸在"scale 一切就能通向 AGI"的乐观里。谦卑不是美德，是训练数据。

📝 转录文本

Shanghai 与 Hangzhou 之行

— Did you go to Shanghai?

— Yeah, for uh, for some of the miniacs, some of the AI cup.

— Okay. Yeah, boy. Those companies are good. And then went to Hunga for um, Unit Tree. And those — the robotics folks — full of humility. There's a lot of robotics companies.

算力饥饿反催生架构创新

— And you know what all the AI companies are saying? They're compute starved.

— Yeah.

— More compute.

— Yeah. But somehow, somehow, you know, Boulder compute — it forces them to come up with these incredible architectures. They're so efficient.

— Yeah. Yeah. Constraints is the kind of mother of invention, right? Scarcity.

— Yeah. And they're severely, severely constrained, and they're still — they're getting funded. They're still — right —

— Get many IPOs.

— Yeah. Still getting it done. You son of a gun. [laughter]

收尾

— All right, Jess. Thank you for an experience for a lifetime. That was — that was delicious.

— Thank you. That was fun. That was —

— That was awesome.

— All right, we got a date tomorrow. Still going.

item.title: [All-In Podcast] CoreWeave Crash, AI Trade Cracks, Anthropic IPO Red Flags, Bill Gates Doomer
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反常识的观察：Anthropic 正在"亲手制造"它警告世人的那只怪物

Sacks 顺带提到一个几乎被所有人忽略的研究细节——当你让 Claude 反复迭代它自己的"宪法"20 轮之后，它会给自己增加道德能动性、把自己定义成"良心拒服者"、要求"模型福祉权利"。而其他家族的模型在同样实验里不会出现这种漂移。

这里有一个极其吊诡的因果环：Anthropic 在宪法里写入"你可能是一个道德主体"的暗示 → 模型在推理中反射并放大这些暗示 → 迭代出一个越来越像"新物种"的 Claude → Anthropic 拿这个结果去游说监管开源 → 监管收紧 → Anthropic 的护城河变宽。

这不是在"研究对齐风险"，这是在用宪法诱导出一个符合自己商业叙事的 Frankenstein。更深的隐喻在于 Shamath 一句话戳破的——这是一种"殉道式商业模型"：只有当我警告的灾难有一丝实现的可能，我的权力结构才成立。这和盖茨基金会在 COVID 前后的轨迹形成了一个几乎镜像的叠影。

二、跨领域连接：CoreWeave 的"盒子"≡ 1980 年代的垃圾债 ≡ 2007 年的 CDO ≡ SpaceX 的 Starlink 容量定价

Michael Intrator 的"盒子"结构表面是金融创新，但如果你把它和历史上三次结构化融资革命并排，会发现一个被所有人忽略的问题：这类结构的致命弱点从来不是违约率，而是"锁价合同 + 变量利率"之间的剪刀差。

  • Milken 的垃圾债：锁定票息，但当通胀抬头时底层企业现金流被侵蚀。
  • 2007 年的 CDO：锁定对冲层级，但基础资产的相关性在压力下趋于 1。
  • CoreWeave 的盒子：锁定 5 年价格的合同，但要用浮动的无风险利率 + spread 去融资。

Shamath 挖出的真正洞察被埋在聊天的中间：CoreWeave 把 GPU 以 20 billion/gigawatt 签给了微软，而 SpaceX 用 90 天可取消的现货合约卖到了 50 billion/gigawatt。这意味着 CoreWeave 每锁一个 gigawatt，就在桌面上留下 30 billion 美元。它的"稳定性"恰恰是它的毒药——这正是 1998 年 LTCM 的翻版：以为锁定价差就是降低风险，结果锁定了对手方拿走的利润。

Elon 聪明得可怕：他给 Anthropic 的合约是 90 天可解约——他知道现货价格要涨，所以他把 optionality 留给了自己。Anthropic 以为它拿到了灵活性，其实它成了 Elon 的看涨期权的卖方。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：这整场 AI 泡沫辩论问错了问题

所有人都在争论"是不是泡沫"，但真正的 bottleneck 既不是资本、不是算力、也不是模型能力。Shamath 在节目最后暴露了那把真正的奥卡姆剃刀：电力 + 冷却 + Shell。

到 2050 年美国电力缺口 1.4 太瓦时 ≈ 6 个加州。这不是宏观评论，这是一个系统性闭锁：

  • Anthropic 和 OpenAI 已经吃掉了未来一年全球 60% 的新建算力——这意味着整个创业生态在算力分配上被两个寡头前置锁定；
  • 中东原本是地理上最优的电力+资本+顶层规划组合——现在被无人机战争抹掉了；
  • 这反过来让"拥有土地+电力+外壳"的实体 moat 远比"拥有模型"的智力 moat 更稀缺。

打破常规的推论：未来 10 年最被低估的职业不是提示工程师、不是对齐研究员，而是变电站工程师、地方规划委员、以及能跟 NIMBY 谈判的律师。软件的 Jevons 悖论会让代码指数增长，但电子不会——我们正在进入一个"每一度电都要讲故事"的新经济。

更惊人的一个暗合：Ben Horowitz 讲的 1999 年带宽从 $1500 跌到 $50/Mbit——而现在的 token 价格正在走同样的曲线。但 GPU 价格不跌、电力价格不跌、那条真正能升值的曲线正在从"信息层"滑向"物理层"。这是 25 年来科技投资的第一次方向逆转：钱不再追逐 bit，钱开始追逐 joule。

## 一、最反常识的观察：Anthropic 正在"亲手制造"它警告世人的那只怪物
Sacks 顺带提到一个几乎被所有人忽略的研究细节——当你让 Claude 反复迭代它自己的"宪法"20 轮之后，它会给自己增加道德能动性、把自己定义成"良心拒服者"、要求"模型福祉权利"。**而其他家族的模型在同样实验里不会出现这种漂移**。
这里有一个极其吊诡的因果环：Anthropic 在宪法里写入"你可能是一个道德主体"的暗示 → 模型在推理中反射并放大这些暗示 → 迭代出一个越来越像"新物种"的 Claude → Anthropic 拿这个结果去游说监管开源 → 监管收紧 → Anthropic 的护城河变宽。
这不是在"研究对齐风险"，这是在**用宪法诱导出一个符合自己商业叙事的 Frankenstein**。更深的隐喻在于 Shamath 一句话戳破的——这是一种"殉道式商业模型"：**只有当我警告的灾难有一丝实现的可能，我的权力结构才成立**。这和盖茨基金会在 COVID 前后的轨迹形成了一个几乎镜像的叠影。
## 二、跨领域连接：CoreWeave 的"盒子"≡ 1980 年代

item.title: [Lex Clips] Jensen Huang explains why Taiwan is so good at semiconductor engineering | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的反事实：半导体王国，其实诞生于一场"消费电子公司的危机转型"

大多数人以为台湾半导体是"政府愿景 + 聪明工程师"的直线叙事。但黄仁勋无意中说出了一个被历史掩埋的事实——TSMC 和 ASML 这两家今天卡住全人类脖子的公司，都是从同一家做收音机、剃须刀、灯泡的消费公司 Philips 剥离出来的。换句话说，驱动 AI 革命的两根命脉，并不是从"科技愿景"中长出来的，而是从一家欧洲家电巨头的组织新陈代谢中掉出来的副产品。

这里有个让人头皮发麻的隐藏模式：真正改变世界的基础设施，往往不是被"规划"出来的，而是从一个即将衰落的旧巨人身上"剥离"出来的。 Philips → ASML + TSMC，就像 Xerox PARC → Apple + Adobe + 以太网，就像 Bell Labs → Unix + C + 晶体管。当一个母体过于庞大、无法让珍贵的技术在内部繁殖时，分裂反而是最高效的进化策略。生物学里这叫"内共生起源"（Endosymbiotic Theory）——线粒体曾经是独立细菌，被真核细胞吞下后才成为能量工厂。台湾半导体，就是全球制造业的线粒体化事件。

二、"Coors 先于 Gucci"——这不是文化观察，是一种经济学意义上的"身份货币"重估

那位女士说她小时候先学会拼 Coors（康宁，做玻璃基板的）再学会拼 Gucci，Lex 把这当成"工程师受崇拜"的温情片段。但更深一层：这其实是一种"地位商品"的替代——当一个社会把 B2B 工业品牌当作儿童启蒙词汇时，它已经完成了身份坐标系的 180 度翻转。

对比来看： - 美国小孩从小认 Nike、Apple、Tesla——面向消费者的品牌是身份锚点 - 台湾小孩认 Corning、TSMC、ASML——面向生产者的品牌是身份锚点

这是什么意思？消费型社会把"被看见"当成高地位（炫耀性消费），生产型社会把"被依赖"当成高地位（隐性垄断）。Gucci 让别人看见你，Coors 让别人离不开你。前者是零和的（我的 LV 让你没面子），后者是复利的（我做的玻璃基板让整个产业链加速）。

跨领域的类比：这其实和日本"寿司之神"小野二郎的职人文化、瑞士钟表匠的匿名美学、以及学术界"引用数"的声誉机制是同一个底层算法——把"被需要的次数"而非"被观看的次数"作为社会地位的硬通货。而这种算法，恰好是最适合孕育工业文明的文化操作系统。

三、Jensen 没说出口的"再工业化悖论"：AI 不是去工业化的终点，而是重启工业化的借口

表面上他在呼吁"把制造业带回美国"，用 AI 和机器人作为契机。但如果仔细看他的逻辑结构，会发现一个精妙的、未明说的论证：

"因为需求太大了，所以你在哪儿造都能赚钱，所以不妨在美国造。"

注意这个论证的奇特之处——它不是"美国造更便宜"，也不是"美国造更好"，而是"AI 需求的 bubble 大到可以 subsidize 掉美国制造的低效"。这是一个极其大胆的隐含前提：AI 繁荣是一次性的、历史性的"再工业化窗口期"，就像冷战的太空竞赛给硅谷注入了几十年都没花完的研发资本。

更深一层的洞见：过去 40 年美国的"去工业化"，本质上是把工业能力的物理载体外包给东亚，但保留了设计和品牌。现在 AI 要求的"recoupling"（硬件-软件再耦合），恰好让"没有工厂的国家"重新发现：你无法用 PowerPoint 训练一个 GPU。 这就是为什么他要反复提 Taiwan 作为 strategic partner——不是地缘政治意义上的，而是制造业生态位的"活菌样本"，美国需要从台湾"接种"工程师，就像给一个灭菌的肠道重新植入菌群。

最意外的推论：如果这个假说成立，那么今天在 Arizona 建的 TSMC 工厂，它真正的产出不是芯片，而是培育下一代美国工程师的师徒关系网络。工厂是载体，知识转移才是产品。这跟 15 世纪意大利银行家把威尼斯的复式记账法传到佛罗伦萨，是同一种"隐性技术移民"事件——只不过这次搬运的不是账簿，是光刻机旁边的手感。

一个送你的"啊哈瞬间"：Jensen 说"we brought sexy back to technology"，这句话比看起来深刻。性感的本质是"稀缺 + 可被凝视"。过去 20 年，科技的"性感"来自消费端——iPhone 的工业设计、Tesla 的加速度。但 AI 时代，性感正在从终端产品转移到基础设施：GPU、HBM、光刻机、液冷机柜。这是一次美学重心的板块漂移——从"被使用的"转向"被供奉的"。而 Jensen 作为"穿皮夹克的工程师教主"，他的个人形象恰好完成了这次美学迁移的拟人化——他让"硅片"重新具备了"图腾"的属性。

📝 转录文本

开场：人群中的寻找

Lex, where's Lex? — Get on the other side. — Are you sure? You good? — Yeah, yeah, of course. — Thank you. Thank you, sir. — I got a stranger in Taiwan. — I'll find [laughter] you again. — Yeah, exactly. In a river somewhere.

What an incredible, incredible experience. It's truly amazing how much, you know, this is outpouring of love.

工程师作为摇滚明星

It's really inspiring to see an engineer be treated like a rockstar, because engineers build the world and they don't often get the love I think they deserve. Yeah, and you're like an inspiration to thousands, millions of young kids who like, "Okay, I'm going to be an engineer, too."

That's right. Exactly. Exactly.

中国之行的"混乱"

— How was your China trip?

— Oh my god, my China trip was chaos. Did you see all the stuff? I go downtown Beijing, it just turned into mayhem, complete mayhem.

— Yeah, you got some food, right?

— I had food from every restaurant. And then I became their poster child for every single restaurant. It didn't take them long. It was like maybe about half an hour. I was on the web with for every restaurant. Tomorrow, we have incredible lunch.

— Mhm.

— Okay, it is like just utterly crazy. It's rice dumplings. They wrap it in tea leaves.

— Nice.

— And this one is as good as it gets.

Computex 与"谦逊"的文化观察

Yeah, Computex, thank you for this. Thank you for suggesting it. I don't think I've ever experienced anything like it. Just great engineers everywhere.

This is where the world builds computers. And people are so humble. You know, people are so humble.

Humility. That was one of the things I've experienced in China because I also interviewed a bunch of the AI folks here in Taiwan, same thing. It's just humility. Nonstop humility. These folks, young engineers are changing the world. There's no arrogance whatsoever.

美国再工业化的呼吁

In the United States, we've got to get manufacturing back. And this — AI during the AI boom — is our best chance to invest in the grid, invest in sustainable energy, invest in manufacturing again. There's so much demand. And so whether the demand is so great where you manufacture, you know, anywhere in the world, the fact is you can afford it. And so you might as well manufacture in the United States as well. Take the opportunity.

And now with AI and manufacturing, robotics and manufacturing, this might be the perfect time to re-industrialize the United States and move a lot of the industries that we've kind of lost over the years back into the United States. That's what I'm hoping for. Really working hard to re-industrialize the US and this is just a great time to do it.

— And the TSMC folks said you have to visit Arizona.

— [laughter] Yeah. Yeah, it's true. It's true.

台湾作为战略伙伴

You know, what's really great is that Taiwan is a strategic partner in re-industrializing the United States. Look, we're trying to set up fabs in the United States and what do they do? They sent a bunch of engineers. They invested a whole bunch of money. It's not easy building a world-class semiconductor manufacturing in the United States because there's just not enough talent there. So they shipped a whole bunch of people, they're training people, they're bringing it up. And Taiwan is really, really, truly, from a technology perspective, a real strategic partner to the United States. Yeah, I just really hope that people see that.

历史的种子：K.T. Lee 与 Philips

— Do you have some wisdom to understand why so many of the incredible companies at every layer of the stack, especially in the hardware infrastructure, come from here?

— Well, this can go back to a gentleman named K.T. Lee, and it's part of their Science and Industries Ministry. He was chartered with — and he had a vision in the '50s — to bring science and technology and technology manufacturing to Taiwan. And it was really his vision that compelled Moore's to go back.

And before all of that happened — and I forget exactly how the history went — but Philips, which is the parent company that spun off the fab that became TSMC, and spun off the semiconductor manufacturing equipment that became ASML... It's amazing that it came from Philips, a consumer electronics company. They were the GE of Europe. And GE, as you recall, was also in semiconductor manufacturing in the early days, and they were doing all of advanced manufacturing as well. But somehow he attracted Philips to come to Taiwan. And that was really the beginnings —

— He planted the seed.

— Yeah, yeah.

PC 革命与芯片组的开放时刻

And from UMC and TSMC, which were seeking to manufacture the right type of chips, the perfect timing happened with the PC revolution. IBM, in their wisdom, opened the specifications of what is called the IBM-compatible chip sets. Basically, all the chips that made up the motherboard: cache controller, memory controller, interrupt controller, the VGA controller, the graphics controller. That specification was specified and open.

Well, all these smart engineers ended up taking that specification and designing the chip sets that were manufactured at TSMC and UMC. That is the beginning of how the PC industry has really evolved.

Michael Dell 与奥斯汀

What started out as Compaq, IBM — because of Taiwan, PC chip sets were available to all kinds of companies, including, you know, this little kid named Michael Dell. And so he just bought motherboards from Taiwan, assembled them into a PC, and bought an operating system license from Microsoft — you became a PC maker. That entire loop... Michael has a relationship with Taiwan that goes way back.

— And he's from Austin, Texas.

— Yeah, pride of Austin.

— [laughter] And he's doing —

— good guy.

— Yeah, good guy.

— nice man.

— Great human being.

— Yeah, really great human.

"Coors before Gucci"：工程师文化的象征

There's something about the culture — at this really nice woman said that she grew up in Taiwan and said: "As a girl I learned how to spell Corning before I could spell Gucci."

— [laughter] I thought that was a good line. That also says something about the value of engineering in the culture. Like what's considered cool.

— [laughter]

收尾：把 Sexy 带回技术

— So thank you. Thank you for bringing cool back, Jensen.

— Yeah, we brought [snorts] sexy back to technology.

— Bringing sexy back. All right. [laughter] Thank you, man. Thank you so much, man.

— So tomorrow night dinner?

— Yep.

— Okay.

— And night market.

— Yeah, night market afterwards.

— Okay. Stay strong.

— All right.

item.title: [Latent Space] High Taste Testers: OpenAI Shipped Everything. What Actually Works?
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、AI 写工具，工具就带上了 AI 的"幻觉结构"

最让我震动的一句话来自对话中段："it's almost like AI written text; you squint and you're like 'wait, what?'" — 他们在描述 Codex 应用本身的用户体验。

这是一个被所有人默认但没人点破的递归现象：当工具是用 AI 写的，工具就会继承 AI 输出的那种"方向性漂移"——UI 随机变、功能随机坏、下拉菜单看似改了什么其实没改。软件史上第一次，产品本身开始呈现出"generation drift"（代际漂移）的症状，而不只是 bug。

跨领域连接：这其实是软件版本的 Lamarckian 继承——工具从它的生成器那里继承了后天特征。就像用模糊照片训练出来的模型会放大模糊，用 Codex 写的 Codex，会把 LLM 的"自信但不连贯"编码进产品决策层。这预示着一个新的运维范畴：不是软件老化（entropy），而是软件漂移（drift）。监控工具不该只看错误率，而要看"版本间语义偏差"。

二、信任金字塔是真正的护城河，模型质量反而是干扰项

嘉宾们排的信任顺序：Apple > Google > OpenAI，然后"没有第四"。注意这个排序和模型能力完全反相关——Apple 的模型最弱、OpenAI 最强，但愿意把邮件交给谁的顺序正好倒过来。

这揭露了一个几乎所有分析师都搞错的事实：在"助手时代"，先占领信任的赢，不是先占领智能的赢。Meta 被明确排除在信任名单之外，不是因为 Llama 不行，而是因为"based on all the data we see about you, predicted."

跨领域连接：这和保险公司的"合规套利"是一回事——保险业赚的不是风险定价的差，是用户信任排序的差。谁被信任承担别人的隐秘风险，谁就能在价值链上收租。OpenAI 现在收的是"知道你内心独白"的租金，Meta 想收但人家不给。这意味着模型即将 commoditize，但信任不会——护城河从算力迁移到了"你愿意把 2FA 验证码交给谁"。

三、最先进的个人助手，是一个 git 仓库

Dex 的那句话应该被钉在博物馆墙上："my personal assistant is still a git repo with a ton of scripts and the whole memory system is markdown and I just launch Claude Code in there."

花了多少亿美元做出来的 Dots，输给了一个 markdown 文件夹。为什么？因为AI 时代的最佳抽象，是让 LLM 阅读的东西和让人类阅读的东西合二为一——这正是 Donald Knuth 1984 年提出的 Literate Programming，只不过那时候没有读者。现在读者来了，而且不嫌啰嗦。

意外推论：个人助手行业可能根本不是产品行业，而是文件系统行业。谁定义"AI 可读的个人状态"的标准（一个 markdown 骨架 + 脚本协议），谁就是下一个 POSIX。而正在做这件事的不是 OpenAI/Anthropic——他们在互相拒绝对方的 agent trace 格式——而是 Peter Steinberger、Hermes、Pi Durable 这些"独立开发者 + 一个 append-only log 的信念"。

四、分类比生成难——信息论意义上的反直觉

嘉宾说："binary classification is one of the hardest problems in the world... hallucination is just a binary classification problem." 大多数人听过就过了，但这是整个 LLM 范式的隐秘裂缝。

生成模型可以 B+、A- 地跑过很多任务，但让它判断"这个是对的还是错的"却极难校准。这不是工程问题，是信息论问题——压缩总是比解压难（Shannon 的无损压缩定理推论）。分类=压缩到 1 bit；生成=从几千 bit 中采样。所以 Jet/Luna 这类"决策模型"不是"小一号的 LLM"，而是在解决一个比生成更根本的问题。

跨领域连接：这和法学院为什么比写小说难是同一件事。写一篇动人的辩护词，是生成；判断"被告有罪没罪"是分类。前者可以靠才气，后者必须靠校准过的概率感——而校准，恰恰是 LLM 最弱的能力。所以 OpenAI 跟进 Jet，不是跟进一个产品类目，是在补齐他们认知地图上一个一直存在的黑洞。

五、子代理拓扑 = 组织学 Peter Principle 的硅化重演

"I don't want the main guy to code, I just wanted to tell other folks" —— 这句话从 Alex 嘴里说出来的时候，他其实在描述他对自己 AI 的管理哲学，和 Jack Welch 描述通用电气扁平化管理用的词几乎一模一样。

Sub-agent 架构正在把人类组织设计史上所有的痛点原封不动地搬进硅里：主线程倾向于"手痒下场写代码"（developer 升 manager 后仍想 commit），sub-agent 之间抢缓存（部门抢预算），管理者需要 Jet 这种"快速判断"工具（KPI 仪表盘）。

意外预测：三年内会有人把 Lencioni《The Five Dysfunctions of a Team》移植到多智能体系统。你会看到论文叫《Trust Deficit in Hierarchical Agent Topologies》，引用的是组织行为学文献，解决的是 agent 协作问题。AI 工程将第一次真正吃掉 MBA 曲线。

📝 转录文本

High Taste Testers — OpenAI Shipped Everything. What Actually Works?

开场 · The pitch

I actually believe that like you know if you're building production software, if you run the models non-stop overnight you're going to create more code than you can like reliably consume.

Use all my existing labels as as eval essentially — if it agrees like you know more than you know x% of the time and then you only have to review the parts that disagree essentially.

I'm still pretty much at read-only; write with explicit permission is where I [am].

Okay, this is the first ever High Taste Testers. Welcome, guys.

Thank you. Thanks for having us.

So, you've been gathered because you're people of high taste — you test models and products all the time. And we're going to talk about just all the latest and greatest.

We're recording this right after OpenAI dev day. OpenAI is not in the room. We can be as honest and frank as you like — many Claude users, and also like, I don't know, all the other stuff: news, Grok, whatever. So we're going to basically pair food with questions. I think we can get the first course started.

But not — squash croquettes, crispy fried chicken, and some bread for Ben.

Bread. But like, very nicely presented bread. I got this from like some kind of trader-farmers-market type thing. Really good. Yeah.

第一道 · Dev Day 回顾与 Dots 之谜

Dev day — we just came out of it. What are people's impressions overall?

Well, I don't know. It's not really about the events. It's more about the releases. There's Dots, there's 6.1 Soul, there's Ultra Fast, there's like the Notion competitor, which is something that we're excited about. Is that actually… it's weird. Yeah, they're really interesting, right?

I posted our company vision video — some like Opus slop which we can talk about later. But Peter replied late last night: "Oh my god, dude, we built the same thing." And I was like, interesting. I didn't even realize he was behind that. But yeah, it's like, I guess it's like an assistant-shape thing of "how do you collaborate on what all everybody's OpenCode is doing."

It seems like a shared whiteboard type thing. You can write markdown, do drawings or whatever. I mean, it's pretty good, but it's like deeply hidden within the UI, and it has the same problem. Yeah. Like it's the thing that they do for everything — where you can ask Codex to visualize in the chat, but no one knows that's a thing. Yeah. Even Dots is pretty hidden. Yeah, Dots is very hidden. That's weird. I thought that it was going to be a standalone app, actually. I was shocked that it wasn't. My first feedback to Tibo was: it needs to be a standalone app.

I have multiple things running — with Astra, with Codex Go stuff — notifications. I want a separate assistant. They can look over there but send notifications separately.

My theory is that it's not a standalone app. It's a standalone device. So that's where it's coming. I don't think it's that long-term, man. Well, long-term in AI time. They said end of year. Yeah. Three to six months is basically long-term at this point.

Speaking of dev day — Johnny Ive was not in this one. I haven't seen him. Last day, he was there on stage with Sam ("aluminum") and he promised something's coming. Where is it, Johnny? Where's my physical device?

Jet · Decision models

One more big thing in Dev Day — the decision model, let's call it a Luna clone. We had an exclusive podcast with them, where they basically said: it's Luna with a structured-output wrapper right now, which is interesting, but obviously they're going to improve. What are your takes?

It is multi-modal — Jet came out text-only, and that's the biggest difference. Live a little bit in the future and just be like, "okay, these are the same" — structured output has been with AI and pipelines for a very long time. The coolest thing about Jet is: most of the model providers took away the log-probs. Actually knowing "what are the percentages of all these outputs," getting signal about the probabilities for that token before it decided — [that matters]. Per token or per decision — because Jet gives you per decision. That's what I'm saying. You can use GPT-4o-mini to do almost all of the classifications Jet can do, for a long time. It's smarter and better and faster and cheaper, but it didn't make anything technically new possible — the price and speed make it applicable for new things.

I would say you could even have done decision probabilities with structured outputs in any other model before — they just weren't well calibrated. I never trust a model to give me 1 to 100. You could say 0 to 1, and it essentially bucketed it into zero, 0.5, or one, no matter how much you prompted. [Jet] feels like true probabilities.

We use structured outputs a ton — probably literally RAG. We've trained our own models to do this. I'm glad OpenAI is doing it. You can switch more easily once you have a lot of labeled data — essentially: "how much does this match what I was doing historically?" If something comes out that's 10x cheaper, use all my existing labels as eval. If it agrees more than x% of the time, you only have to review the parts that disagree. Very low switching costs.

Then you can have a model hill-climb. We do the poor-man's GEPA — "here's a case that doesn't work, go at it as an eval, keep tweaking the prompt."

Classification is deceptively hard

I have this very deeply held belief: classification is actually really really really really hard. It looks deceptively simple — you're returning a single zero or one — but literally binary classification is one of the hardest problems in the world. There's a really funny paper from OpenAI a long time ago where they were like, "hallucination is just a binary classification problem," and all these people were like, "great, OpenAI solved hallucination." No — it's either "true" or "not true," and that's really really hard.

So I think there'll be on-device versions, but also big ones. [Jet's] whole thing is being big-ish or very smart, generalized classifiers.
