If you're trying to do a super heavy long-running loop, that is definitely the best way to do it. The only way I got Astra to burn down some insane problems — none of the models could do it — was Ultra, give it tons of sub-agents, tell the main thread "your only job is to send off sub-agents, put a timer on them, if they stop or get lazy, keep pushing. It is the pushing machine."

It's like the pattern in bigger companies — developers rise to the level of their incompetence as a manager. Companies want the developers to keep developing while managing other people. For me, I don't want the main guy to code or run tools — I just want it to tell other folks in the best way possible, then review and bring it back.

That is Dots, right? That is the idea of Dots. You can slash-command that. I don't think that's all Dots is. I think it's my personal assistant.

How I use it — it does shell stuff out, it can fire off Codex threads.

It's very non-deterministic how it does that — more aggressively than I would like. I don't trust it. There's something really broken with the whole model of "where is execution happening." It's so confusing — Codex and Dots and… it's really confusing.

其他模型 · Haiku, Terra, Muse Spark, Grok

Keeping on the model discussion — we talked about the two big ones. Other models you've been trying?

Where's Haiku? The one-year anniversary is coming up next week. Haiku 4.5 is almost one year old. It's in [its] birthday. Luna is not having the small-fast kind of [slot] now. Luna is great for speed, for small stuff. Terra — where's Terra? What happened? I love that they had the lineup "Terra, Luna, Terra Soul" — this beautiful thing, like OpenAI pixels — and then "6 Astra. Wait, 6.1 Soul, and you're looking for Luna." Like, what happened to Terra? "That's out now." One week after 6 — one week later. I thought OpenAI finally got their [stuff] together with the naming — saw Terra and Luna, beautiful and easy to understand — screwed it up. No one used Terra. I think they did 6 Soul because the brand was good. That's all it was. [6.1] should be Soul; Soul should be Terra; and Luna should stay the same. They should have the model with Terra — No, OpenAI needed a Fable-class model. They needed something better than normal. They couldn't call it Soul.

Sam refers to the next models as whatever next-hugest celestial body there is.

Nova. Supernova. Got to be Galactis. Nebula.

I may be the only person I know that uses Muse Spark.

I use Spark. I love Muse Spark. Oh my god, you're such a Muse show.

First of all, it's 1 million context, multi-modal. Other models don't give me that.

What do you use it for? Speed. And where — coding or newsletters? No, definitely not coding.

The cheapest — until Jet came out and started to rethink a lot of stuff — I would just chuck huge chunks of text [at it], especially the contributor room. But multi-modal as well — you can send it videos: "hey, when did Ben say this thing?" Not transcription-wise — it can hear. The claps, for example.

Gemini also does that. They've done that. Gemini is kind of behind on that. Wait — you think Muse Spark is better than anything Gemini has? Muse Spark is more useful and significantly cheaper. Muse Spark is cheaper than Gemini. Including the "train on me daddy" mode — the contributor mode? Yes. Oh, that is so cheap. "Cheating on me daddy." And they will. Don't worry. Muse Spark is what's running Muse as well. It's good enough for most assistant tasks.

Grok?

Grok 4.7 was a disappointment. Oh my god. I was like, "all right, the Cursor folks will give Elon the data he needs to train the models — finally." Walk me through — someone releases, you download, what do you try? What's your bench?

Two sides. One: pricing. They were hyped to say it's a better model but the same price — that's just flat-out not true. If you go over 200k context, you double in price. Turn on fast mode, you double. Both at the same time, nearly triple. Ends up being a very expensive model. Two: token efficiency is awful. It will do so many steps, so much reasoning.

It doesn't — I don't know what purpose it serves. It's not the fast model (that's Muse), not the cheap model (Muse or Luna), and not the capable model (that's Opus). You're paying Opus prices on Grok. The only thing that feels good is Grokbot — they RL'd the model on Grokbot. That's what I feel happened: they sacrificed it to Grokbot.

Grokbot — and the Grok tool itself. Grok is not only the model; Grok is also the product (grok.com) and inside X, which has access to real-time data from Twitter that no other model has — gives it superpowers in research. Has anyone used Grok in X.com?

Yes, all day. Every day. It's the best research model. Why? I try using it all the time, and it always says it doesn't know my username. They fixed it. There was a bug for a month and a half. I hated this. So ridiculous. I would be like, "pull up the tweet where I said this." "Hi, I don't know who you are." You know what's funny — a month. The built-in integration within X didn't know who you are. Grok.com knew who you are because you're logged into that person. It was literally a bug.

The Grok Build CLI is actually a great CLI, but the most useful thing is you can have other agents call it as a sub-agent — because it has native X API capability, unlimited, for free. Instead of an MCP to Twitter, just say "if you need Twitter stuff, go." Have it call that to get posts or whatever.

I don't know if it's unlimited. Because they released this — the OAuth connector to X — Pi and Hermes and everyone can use the same thing without even their tool. Just add it and OAuth, and it works. Is the tool exposed when you do that? I don't think it adds the MCP to Pi or whatever. You can search Twitter without paying for XAI / X API tokens. In Build CLI you can, but I don't know if that tool just magically gets exposed when you sign in with [OAuth]. The search-Twitter tool? Yes. Let's check this after.

I know my Hermes agent used to do the Bird CLI that Peter Steinberger released with OpenCode, and then — because it was frowned upon to use, they were starting to ban folks that used the cookie-via-browser thing — I switched to that via OAuth, and it works.

Oh, I could totally see the OAuth working. I just don't know [about] the tool — you would have to give it the tool somehow.

开源 · The chasm

DeepS — I don't know if people are deep into that. Basically, open models vs closed — how are you feeling about the general landscape?

So I have four DGX Sparks. When GLM 5.3 Flash came out — as soon as I saw the size of the model, I was like, oh okay, these are going to spike in value. So I instantly texted my dad and had him go to Micro Center back in Ohio and get the Sparks for me before they went up in price. I actually got a pretty good deal on them. I've made money off of compute — which is stupid. It should not be appreciating in value.

I've been using V4.1 Flash on the Sparks — it's really cool. It can get stuff done. Fun and kind of useful for any hill-climbing problem where you can grind it down with verification. It is not useful for true day-to-day work. There is such a chasm between the frontier from OpenAI and literally everything else, that I don't think it's all that viable at the moment.

There was a moment where open-source models were six months behind — then Opus came out, 5.5, and 6.1 — the frontier shot straight up again, and open source is not there. Maybe a year.

Opus felt super sold out. I run this benchmark called SlopCodeBench, out of a lab in University of Wisconsin. I haven't looked at the new data, but for the 10 problems we did: Opus 5.5 wrote three times as much code as Sonnet 5 at the time, as Opus 4.8. Both had about 10,000 lines. This thing wrote 30,000 lines, and literally half of it was tests — more than 51% of the code was tests, whereas the other models wrote 10 or 15% as tests. Really excited to publish the Opus 5.5 stuff. Yeah — Claude just flattened out. Fable was interesting, but none of their daily-use models were. Suddenly it's like, "okay, the new conversation is—" The new is the new hot.

Capability generations

Model capability — the "generations," quote unquote — there are these lines of capability that everything almost approaches, and then doesn't quite cross. Right up next to it, can't get past, until you break through that ceiling, and then you get to the next plateau.

End of summer, before Astra, 5.1 Fable, everyone was getting up towards that ceiling of the last generation of sub-agent orchestration, long-running tasks, capable of solving a lot of problems — but didn't quite have the power and discernment that are in the new models.

There's a certain something that's a step function above. Now, 6.1 Soul, Astra, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 — to me those are the only ones in this new category.

Can you name the category? The big ones in this new generation: really good swarming behaviors. The ability — it's hard to put a strict word on it. Anything other than trust. There's a certain level of trust that these new models have. Also — there's always some meme thing that has to go viral when the new generation comes in. The blender slop, or the video. That's just marketing, right?

I agree. If you think about it, people are connecting their email to models now — giving the ability, especially, to send email. You could have done that a year ago.

No. Or two. You could have added a tool that would take in text and send an email, but no one in their right mind would have done that on their actual email. Now you would. And not — 'cause all the emails would — I said no one in their right mind. I was very specific. How else would you get a helpful personal assistant if it doesn't know you? No, I'm saying a year ago.

I got so many emails. In fact, we had our Azure rep — our company Azure rep — we got OAuth messages from their OpenCode on our dedicated support chat. We're getting these from people I knew personally.

Prompt-injection progress

When I saw — on the record — that Pliny the Liberator cannot liberate Matthew Berman's OpenCode, and then I saw a bunch of benchmarks they're doing about prompt injection specifically — in the latest models, Astra, I think it started with Astra and Opus 5.5 — they have benchmark jailbreak prompts and prompt-injection benchmarks. These models do not trust anything that comes outside of the system prompt. You cannot inject into that level. They have a very high hierarchy — their constitution (which is post-trained), then the system prompt (which the creator/developer gives), then the content. They always wrap this: "this is from here to here, this is an email, this is whatever." Really hard to jailbreak with a prompt injection.

I'm not — prompt injection is definitely not the only thing I'm worried about. There are a lot of other ways to cause your life a lot of harm that is not other people trying to do it. The models actually trying to be helpful is much more dangerous.

I guarantee there are ways of doing — I don't even know if prompt injection is the right word — but as soon as you have your model responding to emails and you want it to give information some of the time, it is going to misclassify what it should or should not share. I believe that to be true.

I'll ask for evidence — have you seen this on [X]? You follow a lot of people, they try a bunch of stuff. Instinct has a very — someone asked their friend's Instinct for the Netflix 2FA code from their email. It just gave it. Instinct, I think, uses open-source models — don't quote me — but I don't think they can scale right now. Maybe later, but in the beginning they were different. I have mine set up such that it will give me a permission prompt before — Grokbot — I use Grokbot for all this. With your emails connected? They are connected, and I do use them there, but it is not allowed to send anything until I can see the actual draft and hit send myself.

In this little expander thing that you have to scroll to the right to see — the worst UI ever for reviewing what it's about to send.

No — the one in Grokbot's great. It just shows as a message. It's great. But what I've noticed: it's rare, but I'd say one in five times, there is details and things in there that I do not want to have. It's a support email and it'll be like "hi, I'm this person's Grok" — let it fire-and-forget.

Let's draw a line here. Ben was talking about a year ago, people would not connect their emails. There is a line between read and —

Oh — I don't send willy-nilly. I review what it sends. I was talking about sending. Reading is a different thing.

I mean, especially a year ago, people were a lot more closed-off. Now people are just connecting everything — to work stuff, personal stuff, you can post on Twitter, has your email.

Memory diaspora

Here's a problem I'm noticing after using a lot of these tools: I wonder if people will just choose one and stick with it, because there is an attention-span cost at switching between those tools. I'm now at a point where I don't remember which conversation I had with which assistant.

I agree.

Importing their memories one to another — that's not good enough, because their memories move in different ways. If you think about them as clones, the clones start living different lives at some point. This one knows about this thing, this one did this thing — "is it use-case-based? Do I go to Grok only for work stuff, use [X] for personal management?" How do you deal with that?

I don't have a good solution. I have a solution — it's not good. I've been trying to rip things out, the idea of an MCP gateway. One of my friends is building a company around this — it's called Executor. It's a big MCP gateway that has all my connections: Gmail, Google Drive, Notion, etc. That lives on one of my Linux boxes at home, and I have a Cloudflare DNS proxy so I can get to it on any device. Now whenever I set up a personal assistant, I do one MCP connection, I log in — and that now has all of my tools, including skills to use them, prompts, config for each. My core connections layer, which is the obnoxious part to set up, is centralized. All my devices share it. Change something there, it's changed everywhere. The actual interface for working ends up being pretty lightweight.

Integrate with Grokbot — you said Grokbot shows you what it's about to send over email. Will that generalize? Instead of their Gmail connector, it will go to your connector and still show you the preview? It works pretty well. There are a couple of things I need to work out. Some connectors per thing I do still use natively — like the finance connector. I really like the finance connector in Grokbot. Useful. I'm not going to do that over a direct MCP.

Just to note — he said a year ago people will not connect their emails. Now you're talking about taking your bank data.

Well — read-only vs. write. Read-only is the line. I'm still pretty much at read-only; write with explicit permission is where I am. The only one I want write for: I want to be able to create — I have people who are very sophisticated about every single vendor getting a different virtual credit card. I'm way too lazy. If I could tell my agent, "hey, go make a virtual card on Mercury." That's link.com — that's their wallet. Exactly what it does. You give your agent that skill. It generates a virtual card for every purchase your assistant does, and then you approve it. Through Marketing? No, Link from site. I need [to look into it]. They're all still charging my one card, so I can't set individual limits or expirations. No idea what [link] does. I still haven't figured out. I don't want to give my agent a card thing. I just want a different card for AWS vs. G Suite vs. etc.

第三道 · 收尾 · 现在你在用什么？

Dessert — lemon-blueberry cake and dark chocolate crémeux mousse.

I use Instinct for things that don't need my data — just communicating with businesses and helping book events. My personal assistant is still a git repo with a ton of scripts; the memory system is markdown. I launch Claude Code / Codex in there when I want to do stuff.

Mine is pretty much Grokbot for work-administrative stuff, but I still do a lot of the management through Codex itself. I'm using Poke, Lindy, and Instinct at the same time — and it's hell. All dry message. I like the bridge into Slack. I'm realizing how silly this sounds as I say it. Dots, very recently. Devin, I've seen that a bunch — as an assistant, not an agent. Can you show us both? Codex. My own thing that I built that has access to my own little Google Drive setup — essentially stacked. There's zero trust on anything. Email — I'm very like — you get 2FA codes in some cases to your email. Even for read, I'm scared of it. There's a long tail of other assistants — Orchid, Instinct, etc. — Orchid, or I was Orchid. 2 million views on Twitter, right? This was the one where the guy was planning an anniversary date. Actually good. And Muse too, for marketplace, shopping — surprisingly good browser use. Muse is surprisingly decent.

For me — I use Codex, and I don't really do anything else, really. I just connect to Codex, have all my tools, and alternative harnesses that we're building. I have a Hermes agent that I keep up to date because there's a lot of stuff there I built. Then Grokbot — around 30 of them doing different things. I like the pattern of cloning one bot to do a specific thing, and they talk. Recently Muse and Dots — probably Muse the most. And Instinct, yes.

Wait, so how do you section them?

That's a problem I want to bring to the table. Grok is mostly for work stuff, personal company management. I have a chief of staff over there, a PM. I have a Linear connector between all of them — they all talk through Linear to ticket, so they can tag each other. That pattern is working. Muse — for one-off; seems best when I talk to it to do something, like record the voice message: "hey, how far is my hotel from this place, or when do I need to leave?" That's immediate.

And I send all three of them stuff that doesn't have dependency, or doesn't know how to pronounce the word. If there's a task all three can do without causing harm, I send to all three — just copy-paste — to see who's better, who's faster.

For Grokbot users: do you ever have it dispatch to Devin or Codex or anything like that? Grokbots have Cursor integration, and it's amazing. Grokbot can work as a chief of staff for you, and kick off a Cursor cloud agent. With any — well, now they're not getting Astra; they're only getting the Soul models — but it can kick off Opus 5.5. You can tell it, "hey, don't do this yourself on your computer. Kick off a Cursor cloud agent with Opus 5.5." Significantly better than Grok 4.7 that's on the line. That's the pattern to get it to do actual stuff. Even writing — you can ask Grokbot to always write via Claude in Cursor. I feel like I have enough code. Between Codex and Devin, I'm kind of good right now. Cursor is good, but to get anything good out of it, it's so much work. Set up cloud environments for every project, get the environment variables, make sure scripts are good. It's easy for the agent — it's so much work. It also loves developing. If you ask it to write something, it will send a PR. I don't need a — I just need an answer, write this in. But it has a pull — it loves a good pull request.

One thing I love about Devin — maybe Cursor has fixed this — I saw almost every company fall in the same trap. Devin by default is just a computer — an agent on a computer. You can create a repo, find an existing repo, work across repos — just a computer. Super flexible. So every wild idea I have, that's where I go. Whereas Codex — I think it'll die as soon as I close my laptop — and other things, "which repository do you want to work in?"

Figure it out. You have the GitHub connector, right? Sometimes you don't even want to be in a repository. You just have an idea. If it's trying to work within a repository, it's like, "oh well, I'll add it to this page" — I just want to see this, try out this new model, try out Jet, try out whatever. So nice to just have a sandbox.

This is the difference between assistants and coding agents built for coding — they're trained to do the diff work, write a markdown file, connect, compare, shove it in a doc. That doesn't execute, write tests, whatever. Just tell me — "write the thing and give it back." They're all that. The whole system prompt's like: "well, I can't do that. What do you want to code today?" I don't want to code. I just want you to be — unh — my model for me. Thank you.

隐藏推荐 · Under the radar

Any things, other than these common names, that you think deserve more recognition?

This isn't on personal assistants, but it is very relevant. 6.1 Soul is much, much better than I think most people think it is, because of just weird branding stuff that's happened — 6 Soul happening last week and 6.1 Soul happening this week. It's weird. I agree. It's an incredibly good model for an incredibly good price. Worth looking at and driving. It's basically to compete with Opus 5.5. It is literally just kneecapping [Opus].

Between the lines — don't want to name sources — it wasn't named to be Soul, and last-minute marketing decided we need to make up on whatever happened.

The headline was that they had an extra and he pulled it.

For me — it will be personal assistants, if you don't mind. I think it's an incredible unlock for regular people. We're developers, all of us; we do stuff with these models all the time; high-taste testers test between the models. The normal person does not care. What personal assistants give to normal people is just time-unlocking — doing stuff that otherwise would take time. The labs now understand this — this is why they're all pivoting towards the simpler use case.

They also get the benefit of tokens per user. Most people still use ChatGPT or Google — type in a query, get a response. Most people don't run agents 24/7. Now, with a personal assistant, suddenly they're hooked on that sweet, sweet streaming of tokens that the labs enjoy. And they get productivity and time back.

So it's cool to talk about use-cases, not just products — because in the limit most of them do the same things. Most can do booking, reply to emails, scan them. Interesting to talk about what people can do.

Weekend-plans bot

I'll give you one. An assistant can do a better job than a coding agent before. I woke up one weekend with my kids early to take them to a karate class — that was closed. I arrived there and it was closed. I got so pissed that now, in the 2026 proactive-assistants era, there's nothing that alerted me — "hey, you're going to a class that's closed" — that doesn't know my schedule.

So I built a weekend-plans bot for kids and for my wife as well. Every weekend, as it comes up, it goes and searches all the local places — all the places I would never go to — websites like "cheap-and-fast" or "good-and-expensive" — plans and says, "hey, if you want, here's a bunch of things. Oh, and by the way, the stuff you're meant to do is closed within as well." Now I know that corner is covered.

Google AI overview

I think Google AI Search Overview — super underrated. Really? So underrated. Every question I want a fast answer to, I Google it. Really fast. 300 milliseconds — by the time the page loads, the answer is there. In ChatGPT, I'm always in the max-reasoning setting. Change it, and then make a new chat and it's on that stupid setting. It's 10–30 seconds for an answer. You can keyboard-shortcut to Instant — it's still there. I should look that up. Actually, the way I do it is Recast. Command-Enter, type your thing, Enter. Done. Is it good? What does it use? Whatever you — whatever you want. I set it to whatever.

It's interesting you said this about Muse — "where's my hotel?" I've started using Instinct instead of Google. I was traveling, got off a train at midnight in Amsterdam — "where's the nearest train station?" "Can I pay with a tap?" "Yep, you can tap your card, make two rides out of the door." Not probably as fast as Google, but much less overwhelming if I just want a yes/no or a short answer. I'm not going to open the ChatGPT app for all the reasons just said.

No — actually everything you guys are doing is suboptimal for your best experience. Which is: one thing should have all your searches ever. Exactly. You shouldn't route. Routing is bad. But you can't be a high-taste tester without testing. You have to test around to know the differences.

Hardware integrations

The thing I'm super excited about is hardware integrations. Grokbot now exists in a Tesla — once they release it a little bit, the Ultra tier now sits Grokbot in your car.

Amazing. I have a Tesla. Really? Not Grok — Grokbot specifically. You just do voice-to-text with Grok, "hey, go tell this bot to do this thing," and it's sending it to the bot. Then it will tell you, "oh, the bot responded with whatever." Car drives itself.

Car drives itself and does stuff for you. What a beautiful future we're living in. Integration into hardware is something that excites me. Muse — own glasses, use devices like the charm thing.

Small prediction. The charm thing that Zuck showed — the little Tamagotchi Muse lives in — is going to get sold out immediately. I think I have plans in my agents to buy like six of them — every agent is going to buy one. If you think about people new to ChatGPT, new to assistants, and they get onboard on Muse — that's a perfect Christmas gift. A perfect "hey, here's the thing — Charm — a Tamagotchi."

Why has this not happened yet? Why is it not on the [Apple]? You want to get into why Apple is not in the race? Not — I know why Apple is not. Your phone — and everything else won't be your phone either.

My feeling: the number of things to charge is saturated. Some people are responsible enough to handle a watch, but it's actually a pretty small number. The reason I don't have an Apple Watch is I would always forget to charge it.

This is a solved problem. Just bring those little battery chargers. No — then I have to remember. The solution to another thing to charge is to get another thing to charge the thing. Does not work. $15. Buy four of them. Put it everywhere. It doesn't work for me. It doesn't work for you.

片尾 · Plugs

We're almost at a wrap. Thank you guys so much. What's one thing people can do for you? How do they find you, give you money, whatever?

The one thing people can do for me — or to me? Is — I would always appreciate a massage. A random on the street approaches me, starts a massage — it's going to be fine.

I want people to unlock their imagination about what's possible with AI systems. We're moving into a new era where a lot of people will get a lot of benefit from AI finally. Important to counter doomerism — there's one thing to see "oh, it's coming for us" on the news, and another to see "oh, it actually booked me a hairstone and saved me five minutes." Once people feel that tactile "helps me, saves me time," they will move towards "oh, AI is helpful." Very important all the companies move there. The one thing they can do for me: unlock the imagination, try AI assistants. If they want to know which ones — we talk about this on my podcast, called Thursday AI, every Thursday.

Okay — I'm at RC. We're doing a lot of models that are going to be pretty good and open-source, coming out soon. Also building harnesses. Check me out on Twitter — @Allisonology — would be good. So in addition to being a shitposter on Twitter, I also run a very serious AI company that makes agents more reliable. We work with Fortune 100 healthcare, a bunch of Fortune 500 companies, and some of the fastest-growing AI new startups. Give it a try — it's free for most people, if you're under a thousand runs a day. What's it called? Raindrop. Sorry — detail. Yes. CTO.

I have a YouTube channel and a podcast — look me up on YouTube as Ben Davis, or Nerd Snipe — you'll find me there.

I work at a company called — I'm founder of a company called Human Layer. We're building the software forge. We're saying software forge instead of software factory now. The forge of the future. Because factories fail. Not all of them. Factory reference. No comments. Your AI talk went super viral. It was misinterpreted. Everyone saw it and said, "oh, you're the 'don't like software factories' guy." No, no, no — there are things you could do that would cause them to fail, and I'm going to tell you what those things are, so you can not do them.

Anyways — I'm Dexory on Twitter. Check out Human Layer. Welcome to the future, I guess.

Well, until the new future comes in three months.

Personal reference for Dex — I met Pacock, one of your guests, who said there are a few folks whose skills he trusts, and Dex was one.

Talking about markdown skills — I'm not skilled in real life. I'm talking about markdown skills. I think if I give you an [intro], you can — I submitted Maya for consideration next time.

This has been a great first episode. Thank you guys for being part of it. This has been High Taste Testers. The thing you can do for me is like and subscribe. There we go.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、AI 写工具，工具就带上了 AI 的"幻觉结构"
最让我震动的一句话来自对话中段："it's almost like AI written text; you squint and you're like 'wait, what?'" — 他们在描述 Codex 应用本身的用户体验。
这是一个被所有人默认但没人点破的递归现象：**当工具是用 AI 写的，工具就会继承 AI 输出的那种"方向性漂移"**——UI 随机变、功能随机坏、下拉菜单看似改了什么其实没改。软件史上第一次，产品本身开始呈现出"generation drift"（代际漂移）的症状，而不只是 bug。
跨领域连接：这其实是**软件版本的 Lamarckian 继承**——工具从它的生成器那里继承了后天特征。就像用模糊照片训练出来的模型会放大模糊，用 Codex 写的 Codex，会把 LLM 的"自信但不连贯"编码进产品决策层。这预示着一个新的运维范畴：**不是软件老化（entropy），而是软件漂移（drift）**。监控工具不该只看错误率，而要看"版本间语义偏差"。
## 二、信任金字塔是真正的护城

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让人意外的观察：紧张感是他的护城河

黄仁勋说"每次公开演讲都紧张"——注意他的解释：因为所有东西都在最后一刻聚合，根本没时间排练，没有提词器，连自己要说什么词都不完全知道。

大多数人会把这当作劣势来掩饰。但请换个角度看：NVIDIA 的护城河机制和这个演讲状态是同构的。GPU 架构、CUDA 生态、Blackwell 的推出——每一代都在"最后一刻聚合"，因为前沿本身就是不可预先排练的。一个能在聚光灯下不用提词器的 CEO，和一个能在技术拐点处不用路线图的公司，是同一种"实时编译"的能力。他不是"克服了紧张"，他是把紧张作为专注力的燃料——这是一种罕见的反脆弱型表演。

跨领域连接："几万亿美金的算力" × 台湾庙宇的香火经济

他讲到要在台湾卖出几万亿美金的计算，需要整座岛的生态都"想要、理解、被激励、感觉自己是其中一员"——这不是采购语言，这是宗教语言。

有意思的是，这和台湾庙宇体系维系香火的方式惊人地相似：不是靠一次性的大额捐献，而是让每一个信众都觉得自己是"宇宙秩序的参与者"。TSMC、ASE、Foxconn 这些厂商要掏出数千亿美金 CapEx，光靠合同锁不住他们——他们需要叙事信仰。黄仁勋的 keynote 实质上是在做一场香火仪式：让整个供应链相信他们不是在"接单"，而是在"共建一个新物种的身体"。

这揭示了一个被忽视的系统真相：在超高 CapEx 的产业里，CEO 的真实职能不是销售，而是神话工程师。

隐藏的系统性模式："游戏玩家"是他的锚定仪式

他反复强调"不要忘记根"——"don't let your feet leave the ground"。但为什么是游戏玩家，而不是别的？

深层机制在这里：游戏玩家是 NVIDIA 唯一一个"不买账"的客户群。超算中心会因为合同买账，数据中心会因为路线图买账，车厂会因为战略买账——只有游戏玩家会因为帧数掉了 5 fps 骂你三天。他们是最严苛的实时反馈回路。

当一家公司市值冲到 4 万亿美金的量级，最大的死亡风险不是技术失误，而是反馈信号衰减——周围所有人都开始说你想听的话。黄仁勋把"gamers"保留为仪式性锚点，本质上是在人为维持一条不会撒谎的信号通道。那个 First Robotics 签名、那个把球递给小孩子的动作，是同一种机制——让自己持续暴露在"没人给你面子"的受众面前。

这和达利欧的"radical transparency"、贝索斯的"Day 1 letter"是同一个物种：所有超大规模组织的掌舵人，都在设计某种私人的反神化装置。 黄仁勋选的是游戏玩家。这个选择比它看起来重要得多。

📝 转录文本

开场：掌声与问候

[cheering]

People are nice. There's so much nice, so much kindness. Yeah.

关于 Keynote 前的紧张

Were you nervous before the keynote? The whole world was watching.

Jensen： Nervous. I was super nervous. But I'm always nervous. You know, every public—every public speaking, doesn't matter what it is.

Take it sharp.

Yeah, well, I don't take it for granted. And you know, I want to do a good job. And it's because everything comes together at such a last moment. It's hard to practice at all—and we don't. And so, you know, so I don't know exactly all the words that I'm going to say, and there's no teleprompter.

几万亿美金的算力蓝图

If we're going to go build and sell a few trillion dollars of computing over the next several years, this entire island has to be part of it. This entire ecosystem have to be part of it.

Every single one of these companies are going to have to invest hundreds of billions of dollars over the next several years. And so they've got to—they've got to want, understand it, be inspired by it, want to be part of it, and understand how they can benefit from it.

And so, you know, in the keynote I tried to distill that down to as few words as possible.

对游戏玩家的爱

By the way, Jensen shows—I mean, obviously shows—he might give some amount of love to me that I don't deserve, but he shows love to everybody, everybody. And he gives some love to the gamers too.

Jensen： Yes, I love the gamers. That's where we all began. You know, don't forget your roots. You know, no matter how high you are, don't let your feet leave the ground.

Some of the most passionate humans on earth are gamers. And some of the happiest moments in my whole life is playing video games on Nvidia hardware.

Look at that. Look at that. Look at all these people. It's unbelievable, man.

现场互动与告别

It's an honor of a lifetime. Thank you. Wow. Well, I really love hanging out with you. Okay, are we going to go get it done? Let's get it done. Let's go get it done. Can you sign this for me?

First Robotics Challenge.

Oh, wow. Love this. Look at that, 2026.

Young engineers building robots. Most of them probably running on an Nvidia brain.

Love that. Now, you got a son, too. I'll hold that for you. Thank you, sir. Keep going. There you go. So good. So good. Good job.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] When Should an Army Stop Attacking? - Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

1. 两种失败的几何学：战略本质上是一个"最优停止问题"

克劳塞维茨真正偷偷告诉你的不是"打仗要狠"，而是——攻击本质上是一个"过早停下"和"过度延伸"都会致命的停止问题。策略的几何形状不是一条上升曲线，而是带有隐藏拐点的凸曲线：越过那个点，边际收益不是递减，而是反号。

这个结构其实并不属于军事学。它和下列问题是同一个数学对象： - 投资中的凯利公式——下注过小吃亏，下注过大归零； - 概率论的"秘书问题"——过早定下人选和拖到最后都是输； - 扑克里的 "fade"——该离桌时继续加注，赢的那一手会亏掉之前所有筹码。

真正令人意外的是：Paine 把"第三方介入"作为识别顶点被越过的唯一外部信号。这暗示战略家无法从内部判断自己是否过线——系统必须依靠外部反馈才能知道自己已经崩了。这是一种军事版的"反脆弱"：世界会用俄国的介入告诉拿破仑他已经输了，但在那之前，他感觉自己正越打越好。

2. 俄国人没看见的护城河，和你公司"被低估的资产"

整段演讲最反直觉的一句是——俄军其实还有 3000 匹可食用的马。他们没有缺粮，缺的是对自己价值的认知。

Paine 把 "fleet in being"（存在舰队）扩写成 "fortress in being"（存在要塞）——这个一闪而过的概念，其实揭示了一个跨领域的秘密：最有价值的资产常常不是通过"做"产生价值，而是通过"存在"占用对手资源。

一个旅顺要塞牵制了乃木整整一个军（45,000 条命，占日本总兵力 1/4）。可俄军从没把"我被围住"这件事当作筹码来运作。

这就是企业战略里永远被看漏的那一类护城河： - 一个难缠的客户让竞争对手不敢进场——你却把它当成"客户集中度风险"； - 一个慢但稳定的老产品线占住了心智——你却嫌它拖累增长； - 一个"落后"的技术栈让新对手进来必须重写一切——你却天天想迁移它。

防御者最常犯的错误，不是守不住，而是不知道自己正在守什么。

3. 词汇即战略：Paine 在偷偷教你把"模糊"从思维里拔掉——而日本自己栽在这一点上

Paine 花时间批判一个词——"decisive"（决定性的）——这件事本身，才是整段演讲真正的"元课"。

她建立的三分法并不是修辞游戏： - lopsided（一边倒）——伤亡悬殊，战术层； - pivotal（枢纽性）——改变未来可能性集合，作战层； - decisive（决定性）——结束整场战争，战略层。

三个词刚好对应战争的三个尺度。换言之，词汇的分辨率就是思维的分辨率。你没有这三个词，就只能用"重要"描述一切——然后你就同时处理不好战术、作战和战略。

这个洞见跨领域地锋利： - 编程里 "naming is design"——变量命名的精度决定抽象的精度； - 心理治疗中的 "affect labeling"——给情绪一个精确名字，杏仁核活跃度就会下降； - 维特根斯坦："我语言的界限，就是我世界的界限。"

真正让人起鸡皮疙瘩的"啊哈时刻"：旅顺口不是决定性的，而是枢纽性的。可日本赢了这场战役之后，被自己的胜利路径依赖困死——他们学到的教训是"再难的要塞也要正面硬攻"，这段肌肉记忆一直延续到 1941 年珍珠港和瓜达尔卡纳尔。他们混淆了 pivotal 和 decisive，于是用赢一场战役的方法去打一场战争，然后输了四十年。

俄国人没弄懂自己的要塞是什么，日本人没弄懂自己的胜利是什么。两方都死于同一种语言贫困。

📝 转录文本

从克劳塞维茨的两个"顶点"说起

According to Clausewitz, most attacks only lead up to the point where their remaining strength is just enough to maintain the defense and wait for peace. So he's talking about the culminating point of attack in terms of a battle or a succession of battles, which is called a campaign.

He says beyond that point, if you go too far, the scale turns and the reaction follows with a force that is usually much stronger than that of the original attack. That's what we mean by the culminating point of attack. Go too far, you ruin yourself.

攻击顶点 vs 胜利顶点

So culminating point of attack — operational term — applies to a battle or succession of battles. Culminating point of victory pertains to the entire war.

In a battle it may be: "I'm going to reduce the fleet in Port Arthur, get rid of it." That might be my battle objective. That's not my war objective. My war objective is Russia [out of] Manchuria, or something.

In either case, if you don't go far enough — you don't reach your culminating point of attack or victory — it means you could have achieved more at acceptable cost, and you failed to. If you exceed the culminating point, you've either assumed risks and costs that exceed any benefits of whatever it is you do, and you're probably weaker as a result.

One of the key indicators that you've gone beyond the culminating point of victory is a third-party intervention that may change the nature of the war, if the third party is a big one.

选择旅顺口作为案例

So that's the term. And then I'm going to apply the terms, and I'm going to start with culminating point of attack and pick a particular battle. Here's some choices for culminating points.

I'm going to choose Port Arthur — looking at when is the culminating point of attack for the Battle of Port Arthur. Why? Well, that's the battle that starts the war, goes on for nearly a year, and as a result of winning it, Japan destroys Russia's fleet in theater. So it's a significant one.

乃木的四万五千人

So if you look back at these frontal assaults that General Nogi is sending one after another, because he's desperate to reduce this fortress — and you're going, well, when's the culminating point?

One of the takeaways here is: Nogi loses about 45,000 men by the time he's done with these frontal attacks. That's the size of a Japanese army. Japan's only got four armies. That's a lot of people to lose.

203 高地：一周架炮，三日沉舰

And here's why he really wants this 203-Meter Hill. It's just — I think it's interesting to look at it. So this is from below, but if you're up there and you have a spotter, you can adjust the line of fire about what thing is getting sunk there and what isn't.

Once they take 203-Meter Hill, it takes another week to get the guns in, and then — if you look — it's like three days they sink everything in harbor, and then the Russians scratch their heads for about a month, and then they decide to capitulate.

俄军的盲点：被忽视的"要塞牵制"

However, if you look at all the food they had there — the Russians could have gone on for at least another month and probably longer, because I look up there and they've got 3,000 highly edible horses if they really want to stick around, right?

And what the Russian war plans had never considered is the use of Port Arthur as a fortress-in-being: that it tied up tons of Japanese. You're pinning a lot of Japanese assets. And if the Russians had been a little more clever, they would have thought of how to use that to their advantage. But they didn't.

回到问题：什么是攻击顶点？

So back to the question: what's the culminating point of attack? If someone asks you this analytical question, you can pick various points.

And I'm going to choose 203-Meter Hill and say: once Japan's taken that, that is the culminating point of attack. But I'm also going to show you an alternate way to answer the question — it's about how you use evidence and come to your own conclusions.

论点与反论点：两种解法

So if you want to say 203-Meter Hill is the culminating point of attack, the sort of argument that you might make is that the fleet-in-being there is key, and without the hill, Russia no longer has sanctuary for that fleet — so it's going to lose it. It's just a matter of time.

But you could have a perfectly good counter-argument. Someone who has a completely different thesis says: "No, no, no — it's really the destruction of the fleet. Until you've done that, you haven't reached your culminating point." And why? Because the fleet pins so much of the Japanese army and navy, and the destruction of the fleet is the operational goal. So if you haven't achieved it, you just aren't there yet.

And then you'll notice that the rebuttals, depending upon which way you go, are different. You don't want to, in the rebuttal, repeat your main argument. But I think it's really useful thinking in terms of arguments and counter-arguments about which way you actually think you would argue. Maybe you come up with a different thing that I haven't even got up there. But that's one way of looking at it.

"决定性战役"概念的厘清

Anyway, a related concept that might help you with culminating points of attack and culminating points of victory is decisive battle. And I'm going to use the term the way Mao and Clausewitz mostly used it.

And here's Clausewitz. He said: "Campaigns whose outcome have been determined by a single battle have become fairly common only in recent times." So that's a campaign — it's not a war. "And those cases in which they've settled an entire war are very rare."

So I'm going to use "decisive" meaning war-winning battle, because if you use it to mean "important," you're actually not conveying anything. Important in what way?

精确用词：lopsided / pivotal / decisive

For instance, I would use different words for a battle where the casualty rates are really skewed. I would use the word lopsided. And if I use the word lopsided, you immediately get it: one side lost a lot more people than the other.

Another alternative would be pivotal battle. Port Arthur is not a decisive battle — other battles follow — but it is pivotal. Once that happens, certain things are foreclosed for Russia and certain things are opened up for Japan, and they're terribly important.

结语

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] Why Taiwan dominates the semiconductor industry | Lex Fridman and Jensen Huang
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、山地的"反直觉红利"：地理劣势如何锻造出芯片密度

一个很少被提及的悖论——台湾 2/3 是山地，这意味着全岛人口被压缩进狭长的西部走廊。表面看是劣势，但这种被迫的空间压缩，本质上是在宏观地理层面上预演了芯片本身的逻辑：把尽可能多的功能、尽可能多的供应链节点、尽可能多的工程师，塞进尽可能小的物理半径里。从新竹到台南的高铁通勤圈，几乎等于全球最先进半导体生态系统的直径。你无法在德州沙漠里复刻这种"密度"——不是因为缺钱、缺人，而是因为那里的物理空间太宽敞，供应链不会被迫咬合得这么紧。TSMC 的 3nm 工艺之所以难以搬迁，不是光刻机的问题，而是一个"地理尺度上就是一块晶圆"的岛的问题。

二、金字塔比喻的真正含义：静态遗迹 vs. 活着的工艺

Lex 把台湾比作哥贝克力石阵、金字塔，看似浪漫，但这个类比里藏着一个被他自己也没完全说破的洞见——金字塔之谜是"过去完成式"：我们不知道它怎么建的，但它已经建好了，静静地站着。而台积电是"现在进行式"：每一代节点的 know-how 必须被每天重新执行，一旦工艺停转三个月，隐性知识就开始衰变。这意味着台湾半导体的"不可复制性"远比金字塔更脆弱、也更强大——它不是一座建筑，而是一场永远不能停的仪式。这反过来解释了一个跨领域的现象：为什么顶级芭蕾舞团、米其林三星后厨、SEAL Team Six，都会在"连续运作"这件事上近乎偏执——所有依赖隐性知识的系统，都靠"不停转"来对抗熵。TSMC 和巴黎歌剧院芭蕾舞团，是同一类生物。

三、"Foodie"不是闲笔：夜市文化与良率文化是同构的

Lex 结尾那句"黄仁勋是个 foodie，没有比他更好的台菜同伴"听起来是人情味的调剂，但如果你把它和前文的"工程文化"并置，会出现一个让人意外的结构同构——台湾夜市的运作逻辑和晶圆厂的良率优化逻辑，几乎是一回事：极小批量、极快迭代、师徒制隐性传承、对"一碗牛肉面今天比昨天好一点点"的病态执着。胡椒饼摊和 EUV 工艺的共同底层算法，是"微小改进的复利"——这是一种文化操作系统，不是一种产业政策。

这里引出一个跨领域连接：荷兰之于金融（17 世纪）、新加坡之于转口贸易、以色列之于国防科技、台湾之于半导体——所有"小岛/小国 + 极端专精"的组合，背后都是同一个生存方程式：资源贫瘠 × 外部威胁 × 教育崇拜 = 被迫在某一维度上做到世界第一，否则死。台湾不是"选择"了半导体，是地缘政治和地理条件把它推到了一条非走不可的路上。这也解释了为什么美国造一座 Fab 容易，造一个"必须靠半导体活下去的集体心智"几乎不可能——富裕的大陆国家没有那种生死压强。

四、一个藏在"humility"里的技术预言

Lex 两次强调黄仁勋的"humility"（谦卑、会倾听）。这看似人物素描，但放在半导体语境里有技术含义：3nm 以下的工艺，物理极限开始压过人的意志——电子会隧穿，原子会抖动，再聪明的 CEO 也不能"命令"一个硅晶格就范。一个长期沉浸在"必须对物理谦卑"的工程文化里的 CEO，天然会把这种姿态带到人际关系里。所以黄仁勋的谦卑不是人格修养的偶然，而是一种被工艺训练出来的职业习惯——这也是为什么硅谷里真正强势的 AI CEO 大多反而不像华尔街的 CEO 那样张扬：你无法对一个 EUV 光源发脾气，这种克制会反向塑造一个人。

📝 转录文本

初访台湾

Visiting Taiwan, first time for me. Uh, I'm part to hang out with Jensen Huang, the CEO and founder of Nvidia, which is the world's most valuable company and also one of the most consequential companies in the history of human civilization. And I'm also here to attend Computex, which is this gigantic conference, just to see engineers—uh, at the heart of the land of engineers—in Taipei.

一座岛，撑起全球最先进的芯片

Now, Taiwan is this island that's 2/3 mountains. And this one island is responsible for more than 90% of the uh most advanced semiconductors in the world. Basically, every computer, every smartphone, every GPU, every AI data center would not exist without this one place. Virtually impossible to replicate anywhere in the world.

像古代奇迹一样令人费解

You know, I often think about ancient uh history, human civilization, and uh places like Göbekli Tepe or the Egyptian pyramids. And there's a lot of mystery about how was it built? And it's humbling to know that there's places on Earth—like those ancient constructions—that we still don't quite understand how it's built.

How is it that Taiwan comes to dominate so much of the uh semiconductor industry? And of course, there are answers. Some of it is culture. Some of it is uh the education system and how much uh engineering is prized within the education system. And of course, all of that has huge implications—technological and geopolitical—for the coming years, decades, centuries.

竞争，但保持朋友关系

I, of course, want us to compete but remain friends. And I think a big part of that is uh understanding each other, understanding each other's culture, each history, and respecting it, but also working together. And the interlinked uh economies, technologies, supply chains—but also humans talking to each other, marrying each other, drinking beer together, eating together—all of that.

And that's what I'm trying to do, and that's what I'm trying to do here, and it's a huge honor to be able to do that amongst so many incredible engineers that come from all across the world.

关于 Jensen

And to also be able to do that with the one and only Jensen—a great human being that, after all of these years, is able to maintain uh humility, and to truly be able to listen, to recognize everybody around him as a human being, including me. It's a huge honor.

Plus, the guy's a foodie. There's no better person to be eating some uh great Taiwanese food than with Jensen.

All right, let's go.

观看原视频 →
